speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour. subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO WORKERS DISPLACED BY AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on Friday last I had a meeting with representatives of the automobile manufacturers as the first stage in developing appropriate programs. Further discussions will be held by the officials of the Department of Labour and the Department of Industry with the automobile manufacturers. subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO WORKERS DISPLACED BY AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
May I ask a
supplementary question of the Minister of Labour. subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO WORKERS DISPLACED BY AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
The discussions with the automobile manufacturers on Friday last confirmed the statement already made that there will be a substantial increase in total employment and total jobs available in the industry as a result of this agreement. There will be dislocations, and the purpose of our discussion is to mitigate or minimize these dislocations where practicable and possible; that is the point of the exercise. However, it should be borne in mind that these adjustments will
April 12, 1965

take place within the context of expanding employment within this particular industry.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO WORKERS DISPLACED BY AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT
speechtext: A further supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In view of the widespread uncertainty as to the precise plans of the government in the area of dislocation, can the Minister tell the House when he will be in a position to make a firm statement of Government policy in this regard?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO WORKERS DISPLACED BY AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT
speechtext: The purpose of the discussion, Mr. Speaker, is to isolate and pinpoint as accurately as possible the sources of dislocation. Until that is accomplished more accurately it would be impossible to develop plans such as my hon. friend suggests. This is one of the purposes of the further consultations. I think it is fair to say that it would be wrong to create apprehensions and fears at this stage about potential displacement.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF EARNED REMISSION WITH RESPECT TO PAROLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Justice could I pose a question to his Parliamentary Secretary and in this way give notice of the question, because it may require reference to some files and documents. I base my question on a letter which I have just received, and it is necessary to quote two brief sentences from it in order to make my question intelligible. The letter relates to a former inmate of the British Columbia penitentiary, one Raymond Johnson, and according to the letter:
In Johnson's case he was sentenced to ten years in 1957, was paroled in July, 1962, found that because of the new Penitentiary Act 468 days that he had earned under the old Act was added to his parole period, thus in effect he was having to serve this time over again. He claimed in the writ-
That is a writ of habeas corpus.
-that earned remission under the old Act could not be considered statutory remission under the new Act. Johnson appeared before Mr. Justice Ruttan and was ordered released.
I am wondering, Mr. Speaker, what the Government or the Department is doing in respect to all other inmates who find themselves in a similar position, or all other exinmates who have been released on parole since that time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I should like to congratulate the mover (Mr. Cashin) and the seconder (Mr. Chretien) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They have performed their tasks singularly well; they praised the speech to high heaven. Both their speeches were magnificent examples of a torrent of words devoid of any ideas.
The speech from the throne we heard last Monday was merely the icing covering the budget cake to be served to us in a few days. What will the budget speech contain, we do not know as yet, but it will reflect the future policy of the country's financiers put forward by their go-between, I mean this government.
This speech is particularly noteworthy not for the solutions it brings but for the acknowledgements it contains.
Upon careful reading of this speech, I mean the speech from the throne, one wonders whether the Liberal party awakening from a bad dream is not telling us this bad dream is about the results of its policies which have lacked administrative foresight during the 33 years it has been in office in the last 45 years of the country's administration.
We have at least learned one thing from this speech from the throne: Poverty does exist in Canada. For the past 25 years the Credi-tistes have repeatedly pointed out that poverty existed in Canada and have succeeded at least in opening the eyes of the Liberals who finally have admitted and acknowledged that poverty does exist. After having been in office for 33 years out of the last 45 years of the country's administration, the Liberals have finally admitted that poverty does exist in Canada and that the Creditistes were right in speaking about poverty.
The worst off in all that are the poor themselves who had to live for those 33 years under a Liberal administration and who had to live and suffer from Liberal policies.
I should like to quote here a few lines from the speech from the throne in order to show how ridiculous it is:
Our country is achieving a high rate of economic growth. Trade is expanding. With growing industrialization. Canadians are enjoying rapidly increasing employment opportunities; incomes and living standards are rising; the number of people

out of work has been reduced to lower levels than for many years.
And immediately after this, we find that:
All the great potentialities of our economy are not, however, being realized. The talents of some of our people are wasted because of poverty, illness, inadequate education and training, inequality. in opportunities for work.
The measures to correct that misery, as set forth in the speech from the throne, are yet unknown. But the adoption of "O Canada" as the national anthem is mentioned in order to enable all Canadians to sing officially their national anthem, including those who are in misery and poverty because of Liberal policies especially, and also of Conservative policies for that matter; indeed, at the rate debts, taxes and poverty are increasing at present it will soon be more accurate to sing: "O Canada, our home and taxing land".
In 1963, at the time of the last federal election, everyone remembers the dirty publicity campaign launched by the Liberal party against the Social Credit to the tune of at least $5,000 a day, in the newspaper La Presse. Those full page ads were headed:
Social Credit means poverty.
But it is not the Social Crediters who have been in office in Ottawa since 1963 and yet one can read in the Liberal government's speech from the throne that there is poverty and want in Canada.
The poverty which is mentioned in the speech from the throne did not spring up overnight among the people. It results from the administration of the two old-line parties which have succeeded one another in office since confederation. Poverty is the offspring of past governments which, through their systems, sowed and today are reaping poverty and want. They have never had any policies to prevent hardship and poverty. On the contrary, they have always allowed hardship and poverty to grow worse from day to day.
What with taxes and debts, the two old-line parties do their utmost to drive people to poverty and keep them there. Every day and in every way, we are told that our country is tremendously rich in all sorts of things. That is true. So much so that we hardly know the real value of our natural and other resources. And yet, this same country, in spite of all its wealth, is forcing its own people to live in insecurity, sickness, poverty, unemployment, to such an extent that they need unemployment assistance, public welfare and charitable institutions. The people know what bankruptcy and poverty are.
April 12. 1965

We have a rich, an affluent country, due to our national resources and the labour of our people, but we have poor and indigent people because of the political and economic system of the old-line parties.
While Ottawa was considering waging war on poverty, the provincial budget made public last week in Quebec brought us a shower of new taxes, an increase in taxes which will increase the number of poor and poverty in the province of Quebec. Poverty in Ottawa and taxes in Quebec. Liberal in Ottawa, Liberal in Quebec. Grits in Ottawa, Grits in Quebec.
I would like to quote an article by Leslie Roberts published in the Montreal Star, Saturday, April 10, 1965, page 5:
[DOT]	(11:40 a.m.)

Between Ourselves Dirty Word "Thrift"
What makes me dubious is the fact that as a people we have totally abandoned all notions of respectable frugality, all ideas of pay as you go, nowhere more than at the highest levels of government.
When Mr. Gordon, the Minister of Finance, tabled his estimates for the Federal Government's new fiscal year which began on April 1, his proposed spending figures for the period which will end on March 31, 1966, topped $8,000,000,000, with more to come later in what are called "supple-mentaries."
Assuming a population of 20,000,000 Canadians, what this means is that the federal authority alone plans to spend $400 for every man, woman and new-born babe in the country.
If you proceed from this point to regard five people as comprising the average Canadian family, you arrive at a figure of $2,000, representing what Mr. Gordon proposes to spend per household this year-and in most households I would guess the bite is carved out of one income.
This is just the federal tab. After that the province and your municipality still have to collect their share.
As Quebec has just budgeted for expenditures of approximately $2,000,000,000 and we are 5,000,000 Quebeckers that's another $400 per household of five.
Another fascinating item here is that of Mr. Gordon's eight billions, at least $1 in every eight he raises (whether in taxes or new borrowings) will go into what is politely called "servicing the national debt."
[DOT]	(11:50 a.m.)
What this means, in the kind of language laymen use to communicate with each other, is that $1 in every eight Mr. Gordon acquires by taxes or new loans will be expended solely to pay interest on money we already owe. This is $1 billion for which the Canadian people will not get a damned thing in return-a steadily rising total which you may as well jot down on your reminder pad as the high cost of deficit financing.

This article criticizes the financial system which we have unceasingly denounced for
The Address-Mr. Rondeau more than 20 years. We are now subject to an inflationary system and it is because we have known this inflationary system that we of the Ralliement Creditiste move today an amendment in order to balance one aspect of our national economy, family allowances.
The Family Allowances Act was passed on August 15, 1944, more than 20 years ago, and the first benefits were paid under this act on July 1, 1945. This was an act for which the Government of the day had reason to be proud. It was the same party as the one which is in office now, the Liberal party. We are wondering if the present Government does not regret the enactment of that piece of legislation since it has let the purchasing power of family allowances fall to nothing or practically nothing. In fact, the cost of living has tripled since 1945. Everything has gone up and increased threefold and often more, such as the indemnities of members of parliament and of members of most provincial legislatures. Only family allowances have remained at the same level as in 1945, which means that they are only worth one third of their original value.
Whereas they permitted the purchase of a quart of milk for children, in 1945, they now permit the purchase of only one third of a quart. It is the same thing all along the line. Milk which sold for 10 cents a quart in 1945 now costs 25 cents.
In 1945 a 24-ounce loaf of bread sold for 10 cents while it now sells for 25 cents in 1965. Compare the cost of living in any area and you will realize that what cost 100 per cent in 1945 has gone up 300 per cent today.
In 1945 an hon. member's indemnity was $4,000 while it is now $12,000 in 1965. Hon. members' expense allowances were $2,000 in 1945, while they have gone up to $6,000 in 1965.
Family allowances have remained at the same level since 1945. When an employer cuts his employee's salary by half it is because he is not satisfied with his services and he would have no regret if he were to quit his job. Should we conclude the same thing in the case of family allowances whose value is reduced to one third of their initial value? And to think that the Liberals would prefer that such a legislation had never been passed.
I see government members vehemently denying those charges. Why, then, do they leave family allowances at the same level as in 1945? Why did they reject every year motions to raise family allowances in order to give them back their initial value? Every
April 12. 1965

The Address-Mr. Rondeau session we of the Ralliement Creditiste made new attempts to have family allowances raised to put them in line with the cost of living index.
There is no electoral approach in this plea. We are only concerned with the welfare of families raising children. The party in office does not care for the welfare of families between general elections, but waits for the eve of new elections to give a thought to family allowances. Why wait until the next election to think about children and families? Thereby, the Liberal party proves once more that its hunger for power is stronger than its concern for the well-being of this country.
The government knows where to find young people when it launches a military crusade, but it cares a lot less about the families where are born and will grow those who will be 20 a few years from now.
The amount paid as family allowances should be tripled to meet family needs and to counterbalance cost of living increases since 1945. By so doing, families could buy three times more products than they can now afford. Stores have a surplus of products, industry is always ready to produce more, farmers find it difficult to sell their products. They are all waiting for orders from the families who need this production.
If the government has compromised itself with financiers who control it, if it cannot make capital serve production by taking money from the Bank of Canada in order to satisfy production and if, out of respect for financiers who had it elected, the government has to resort to taxation, well, it should dip into the national defence budget, into the armaments budget, in order to increase family allowances.
Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac (Mr. Latu-lippe):
That the following words be added to the address:
We respectfully regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to propose legislation to adjust the family allowances according to the rise of the cost of living index since 1945, and no longer enjoy the confidence of the house and the Canadian people.

speechtext:
It
is indeed an honour for me to take part in this debate. I too would like to join with my colleagues in all parts of this House in congratulating the Mover and the Seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. I am more than proud to belong to a group in this House which includes such energetic and aggressive members.
I do not intend to spend very much time on the contents of the Speech from the Throne. At the outset, however, I wish to put on record some comments which appeared in an editorial published on April 6 in the Toronto Star, since these comments express my own views.
The Speech from the Throne which opened the new session at Ottawa yesterday may fairly be called an historic document. It outlined what is probably the largest, boldest and most sweeping program ever submitted to a Canadian Parliament.
Then it goes on:
This Speech from the Throne remains a tremendous challenge to Canada. It is nothing less than a call to bring the economic and social forces which dominate, and sometimes wreck, the lives of Canadians under public control.
I compliment the Government on the contents of this Speech from the Throne which is so challenging, so ambitious and so visionary, if I may use that word. However, I feel there has not for many years been a debate in this house on a most important topic. I refer, of course, to the subject of the St. Lawrence waterway upon which a debate took place in 1951.
That debate was probably one of the most important which has ever taken place in this House. I certainly wish to make some comments on the present Seaway because of the contribution it has made to the economic life of this country, to job opportunities and to the industrial development of Canada.
The St. Lawrence Seaway has been described as the world's greatest engineering project. Its most remarkable feature is the Welland ship canal, a navigational facility unequalled anywhere in the world. It was designed, constructed and paid for solely by the Canadian people at a time when Canada had yet to achieve the proud place it occupies in the world today.
The first Welland ship canal was constructed in 1829 in the face of incredible difficulties, physical, financial and political. It was 22620-151
The Address-Mr. Macaluso the opening of the present canal which did so much to ensure the progress and prosperity which Canadians have since enjoyed. We should never forget, however, that the first canal was opened only after a long and bitter struggle, and that all subsequent improvements were brought about by courageous and determined men who fought deeply entrenched opposing interests.
In 1932, the Welland ship canal was deepened to 25 feet, giving impetus to the growth of industrial development throughout a large area. As a result of this demonstration of what a canal 25 feet deep could do, it was further deepened to 27 feet. This work was completed in 1959.
The canal is the most crucial part of the St. Lawrence Seaway. In 1964 the cargo throughput was 51.4 million net tons. This was nearly double the tonnage handled in
1958	before the Seaway was completed. Despite the fact that the Seaway operates only eight months of the year the project has encountered opposition from those who have always feared and resented its existence. In
1959	the Seaway from Montreal to Lake Ontario handled 20.4 million net tons of cargo, and in 1964 this figure rose to 39.3 million net tons, an increase of more than 92 per cent. I submit this explains the vociferous opposition which the Seaway has engendered since its inception.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
A great part of this cargo tonnage is being attracted away from the United States Atlantic coast ports. Last year it is interesting to note that the United States North Atlantic Ports Association, which represents 13 port districts, told a United States Senate subcommittee:
The greatest share of traffic that today moves via the Seaway once moved via the ports along the seaboard. Without doubt those who have suffered the greatest loss as a result of the Seaway have been the North Atlantic ports.
In January, 1965 the Association of American Railroads issued a statement which, in part, had this to say:
Prudent judgment would indicate that there is no alternative except to raise Seaway tolls to a more realistic level. Our interest in this subject is stimulated by the Seaway competition with railroads.
Also in May of 1964, Mr. Speaker, the National Association for a Non-Subsidized Seaway, with headquarters in Baltimore, Maryland, and which represents United States Atlantic, Gulf and west coast ports, issued a statement before the same Senate sub-
April 12, 1965

The Address^Mr. Macaluso committee; and its chairman, a Democratic Congressman from Maryland, characterized the Seaway at that time as, and I quote, "a monstrosity". He said:
We hope this Senate subcommittee will recognize that the good of the Seaway, the good of the nation, and indeed of expanding world trade will best be served by raising tolls on the Seaway.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this is an absurd statement and in the interests of the continued good relations between Canada and the United States I will not comment further on this very extraordinary statement.
Canadian railway and truck operators have benefited from the heavy flow of traffic along the St. Lawrence Seaway, and it is important to bear in mind that every pound of the 39.3 million net tons of cargo which transited the Seaway from Montreal to Lake Ontario in 1964 was transported at one step or another by rail or truck in Canada. So much so, Mr. Speaker, that in 1964 Mr. N. R. Crump, the chairman and chief executive officer of Canadian Pacific Railway, said that the movement of bulk cargoes in export have been a factor in the favourable showing made by railroads in 1964. There is a reflection of that movement found in the fact that in 1964 tonnage of Canadian steel consumed by Canadian builders of railway cars and locomotives increased by 135 per cent over 1963.
One of the principal reasons for the construction of the Seaway, which was put forward back in 1951, was to facilitate the movement of Canadian forest products, iron ore and coal from the lower St. Lawrence and Nova Scotia to ports on the Great Lakes, and of Canadian wheat to overseas ports. The St. Lawrence River ports in 1964 handled for export 270 million bushels of Canadian grain. It is obvious that without the St. Lawrence Seaway it would have been quite impossible to commit ourselves to supply such enormous tonnages of wheat to Russia and to other iron curtain countries. Iron ore from the lower St. Lawrence destined for United States Great Lakes ports furnished the greatest tonnage of any commodity transiting the Seaway.
Therefore in my view, and in the view of many others, the Seaway has provided an increase in traffic for Canadian ports, for Canadian railroads and Canadian road haulers; and has also performed a most notable economic, political and social service to the whole of Canada by making it possible to create a whole new civilization in the lower St. Lawrence valley. This in turn involved millions of dollars of Canadian investment, created new and substantial markets,

continuing and growing markets, for Canadian products and manufactured foodstuffs.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, more important than this today, about 85 per cent of the bulk cargo transiting the Seaway and the Welland ship canal is carried in Canadian vessels. This is most interesting, because one of the most important reasons put forward in 1951 for the imposition of tolls on the St. Lawrence Seaway was that United States vessels would provide the bulk of the revenue. But this is not the case. The movement of Canadian raw materials through the St. Lawrence has stimulated Canadian shipbuilding industries in Ontario, Quebec and New Brunswick, and this has been a direct result of the construction of the Seaway.
I should like to refer to the book "The St. Lawrence Seaway" written by Hon. Lionel Chevrier, the present Canadian High Commissioner to Great Britain, which was published in 1959. In discussing the matter of tolls Mr. Chevrier had this to say, as recorded at page 114 of his book:
The question of tolls was often used as a political and economic argument to make the Seaway impossible. The powerful interests in the U.S., when they could no longer stop the construction of the Seaway, tried to get the tolls pinned at hopelessly high rates, high enough to scare all shipping away from the Seaway.
At that time Senator Wiley was piloting the bill through the U.S. Senate, and Mr. Chevrier says:
Wiley emphasized that the U.S. must have a voice in setting tolls. She must be able to watch for the possibility of reducing tolls when possible. ..
The U.S. could not permit Canada to dominate the Seaway. For the same reason she was loath to see Canada planning duplicate facilities during construction of the joint venture.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, the revenue from tolls is not coming from United States vessels but from Canadian vessels. Canada reluctantly accepted, under duress, the principle of trying to make the Seaway self-liquidating through tolls within 50 years, a hitherto unheard of provision in the history of North American navigation, both coastal and inland. When the Government announced last year the twinning of the remaining locks in the Welland ship canal at a cost in excess of $180 million, it also announced its continued adherence to the unique and highly discriminatory principle of trying to recover capital costs of this public work through tolls.
Presently, Mr. Speaker, tolls on the Welland ship canal are suspended, if I may quote the Minister, "for the time being". The tolls on the St. Lawrence Seaway from Montreal to Lake Ontario are frozen at their 1959 level
April 12, 1965	COMMONS
until July 1, 1966. Therefore I bring this matter to the attention of the house at the earliest opportunity.
We might ask ourselves, what is the burden of tolls? The largest type of Canadian bulk carrier, fully loaded with Canadian iron ore or Canadian coal upbound from the lower St. Lawrence, or loaded with Canadian grain downbound from the Lakehead, pays $12,400 each time it transits the Seaway between Montreal and Lake Ontario, and vice-versa. The length of the Seaway is approximately 124 miles. I regret to hear the junior Member for Halifax (Mr. Regan) applauding, Mr. Speaker. This amounts to a toll of $100 per mile.
Out of every $100 collected from tolls, $29 is paid to the United States in U.S. funds. These funds are coming from Canadian vessels. To my mind this is a humiliating position for a country which built and operated an all-Canadian Seaway from Montreal to Lake Erie on a virtually toll free basis for 111 years. Our main interest as Canadians, Mr. Speaker, should be to bring about abolition of all tolls on Canadian inland waterways in accordance with the long-standing Canadian policy of toll free navigational facilities, which has served us so well in the past. The continued existence of tolls on what was once an all-Canadian and virtually toll free Seaway constitutes a dangerous precedent for the extension of the principle of trying to recover the capital costs of other vital water transportation facilities, both coastal and inland, in this fashion.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
Thus it is my sincere belief that Canada should restore the St. Lawrence Seaway from Montreal to Lake Erie to its all-Canadian character by constructing a lock at Cornwall, Ontario, and revert to our historical policy of toll free inland waterways which still applies to our coastal waterways. We face a battle to prevent the usefulness of the whole St. Lawrence waterway from being curtailed by the actions of those who have always been opposed to its existence and who now have greater reason than ever to fear and resent its success.
It is interesting to note that the Seaway opened this year on April 8, and I should like to quote from an article which appeared in the Ottawa Journal on that date, as follows:
The St. Lawrence Seaway opens today for its seventh and probably most profitable season-
I suggest that we have a hard battle to fight against very powerful and persistent
DEBATES	225
The Address-Mr. Macaluso enemies both in the United States and at home. This was described in Mr. Chevrier's book. I regret that the hon. Members for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Basford) and Halifax (Mr. Regan) take such a regionalistic outlook to this very important problem.
Major opposition to a toll free Seaway from Montreal to Lake Ontario has been based on the premise that exemption from tolls is equivalent to a subsidy. Let me name some of these very revealing titles. The National Association for Non-Subsidized Seaways; the Maryland Committee for Non-Subsidized Seaways; the New York-New Jersey Committee for a Self-Supporting Seaway; the United States North Atlantic, Gulf and Caribbean ports, as well as the Association of American Railroads, all are long-standing opponents of the Seaway.
Yet strangely none of the above mentioned bodies, or other opponents of the Seaway, are on record as being opposed to the maintenance at public expense, on a toll free basis, of channels capable of accommodating deep sea ships in such United States rivers as the Hudson to Albany, New York; the Delaware to Trenton, New Jersey; the Mississippi to Baton Rouge, Louisiana; the Columbia to Dalles, Oregon; and the Sacramento to Sacramento, California. None of those rivers is of such importance to the economy of the United States as the St. Lawrence is to that of Canada, yet in all of North America only the St. Lawrence from Montreal to Lake Ontario is subject to tolls.
In the light of our dependence upon exports for the level of our over-all business activity it is difficult to understand why this discrimination should be tolerated by Canadians. The St. Lawrence Seaway not only provides access to overseas markets for Canadian grain and other natural products, and for a growing export of manufactured goods, but also provides access to the extensive and growing United States markets in the Great Lakes area for forest and mineral products from Quebec and the Maritimes. This means that the Seaway makes a very vital contribution to the solution of our vexing balance of payments problem.
Many, many ports in the U.S. are now proceeding with channel and harbour deepening and placing themselves in a position to handle ships of a size quite beyond any currently contemplated capacity of the St. Lawrence Seaway, all of which are, and will remain, toll free. The efforts of U.S. North Atlantic ports to meet Seaway as well
April 12, 1965

The Address-Mr. Macaluso as other forms of competition at public expense on a toll free basis should be of real concern to we Canadians whose interest in our inland waterways is vital.
We must remember that the United States really showed surprisingly little interest in the navigation of the St. Lawrence River during all the years when Canadians were striving for ever greater improvement of their own transportation facilities on that water highway. It was, of course, very natural for Canadians to press for the construction of a seaway in the face of United States indifference of obstruction, because the St. Lawrence waterway gives us our principal access to the Great Lakes. Without such access Canada would not have become the dynamic, prosperous and progressive country which it is today.
Mr. Speaker, the ignorance which has existed and which in large measure unfortunately still exists as to the economic and social significance of the Seaway and the Welland ship canal is really deplorable. This ignorance is more remarkable in that Canada has spent many hundreds of millions of our hard earned dollars on aids to navigation, dredging, canal building and harbour construction. Therefore there is still far too little realization on the part of Canadians generally as to the vital importance of the Seaway and the Welland ship canal to the future progress and continued prosperity of this country.
This perhaps explains one of the difficulties we face in fighting the battle against tolls on inland waterways. While we search desperately for a Canadian national identity, we persist in ignoring the Biblical advice "by their fruits shall ye know them"; and judging by the fruits of Canadians we are really a great people, despite our relatively small numbers. In almost any other country but Canada the whole St. Lawrence waterway would be a source of such immense national pride as to make its future absolutely secure from inimical action from any quarter.
The present Welland ship canal was completed in 1932, and it is still, in almost every particular, the most outstanding man made water transport facility in the world. Certainly none other performs a more outstanding service for any national economy, and none approaches its spectacular feat of lifting 700-foot ships, weighing with their cargoes up to 45,000 tons, 326 feet up an escarpment, the difference in height between Lake Ontario and Lake Erie. The Welland ship

canal is unquestionably one of the greatest existing tributes to Canadian ability, Canadian courage and Canadian vision. It would probably be easier to bring home to Canadians the contributions the Seaway and the Welland ship canal have made and are capable of making to our present prosperity and future progress if they both had been the subject of less criticism by those with a vested interest in other forms of transportation.
This brings to mind the brief submitted to the Government by the National Legislative Committee of the International Railway Brotherhoods of March 11, 1965. I should like to quote from page 6 of that brief as follows:
It is the opinion of this Committee that the best interests of the people of Canada will be served if Seaway tolls are brought to a level that will meet current operating costs and the financial obligations contemplated in the Seaway Act. Thus the St. Lawrence Seaway will find its proper place in the over-all transportation system through competitive operation and not by way of subsidization.
The Government of Canada should oppose any scheme designed to lower present inadequate Seaway tolls or extend the 50 year amortization period predicated by the Seaway Act.
I have only one statement in respect of that brief and that is that in my opinion it is absurd. I regret that the Minister of Transport at the time the brief was submitted seemed to indicate that he might be in agreement with the submission. I certainly want to bring this situation to the attention of the Minister at this time, and I hope I can change his point of view.
Those who have been persistently and vociferously opposed to the development and use of the St. Lawrence and our other inland waterways and who seek to limit their use do, it seems to me, take a very shortsighted attitude. In the final analysis all our forms of transportation depend for their own progress and prosperity upon the progress and prosperity of the whole Canadian economy. Most of the bulk cargoes handled through our inland waterways are carried at some point, very often for considerable distances, by rail or other forms of transportation. Canadian manufactured products, even those destined for ultimate shipment to overseas markets, are very largely transported by rail or truck. Therefore it seems to me there is very considerable identity of interest between all forms of transportation in this country.
History has already amply demonstrated that our inland waterways are a priceless asset to the Canadian economy and, as such, have played a great part in our industrial
April 12, 1965

and social progress. Why then should inland transportation, which makes such a valuable addition to national employment and national wealth be discriminated against in this fashion? Why not revert to our traditional policy of toll free inland waterways?
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
A very considerable tonnage of Canadian iron ore already finds its way to United States Atlantic ports from the lower St. Lawrence in ships far too large to transit either the St. Lawrence Seaway or the Welland ship canal. Those large vessels and their cargoes contribute no revenues-I repeat, Mr. Speaker, no revenues-to any part of the Seaway. If such off-shore traffic increases at the expense of Seaway bulk traffic throughput, then trying to recover the capital costs of the Seaway and Welland ship canal through tolls is bound to create more and more difficulties for those who must rely upon our inland waterways for their fuel and raw materials. These large U.S. carriers are able to take iron ore and other bulk materials to ports all over the world and deliver them to plants whose finished products compete with those produced by Canadian industries dependant upon much smaller carriers which are capable of using the Seaway and the Welland ship canal.
In the light of these developments and others that are likely to take place, the Government should seriously consider whether we should bring the Welland ship canal locks up to the standard of the new United States locks now being constructed, at federal expense, at the Sault, Michigan. It would seem to me to be somewhat shortsighted to build twin locks in the Welland ship canal now only to the dimensions of those already existing. It is clear that this will not exactly help to cope with the problem in the future. In fact it is estimated by the experts that even with the twinning of these locks they will be saturated within a few years after completion. It cannot be too often emphasized and brought home to the people of Canada that if the existing level of tolls on the St. Lawrence Seaway is raised, the whole future of our Seaway is likely to be placed in serious jeopardy.
In September, 1957 the Mayor of Milwaukee wrote a letter to the United States St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation in which he expressed the belief that the objective of the National Committee for a Non-Subsidized Seaway was, to quote him, "to set the tolls so high that the Seaway will
The Address-Mr. Macaluso probably not be used at all". We in Canada, Mr. Speaker, are not the only ones fighting the battle against tolls. There are many interests in the United States which are also doing so, but it must be agreed that the opponents of the Seaway are very powerful interests who command a lot of votes in the United States.
Closer to home, the Steel Company of Canada and Dominion Foundries and Steel, who are situated in the city of Hamilton, and some U.S. steel interests have hundreds of millions of dollars invested in the Wabush mines in Newfoundland and in its harbour works and railway lines and the pelletizing plant at Pointe Noir, Quebec. These projects have contributed substantially to employment and to the growth and prosperity of the lower St. Lawrence valley and Newfoundland. These great developments, especially Wabush mines, were set in motion in 1956, and were predicated upon the assumption that the St. Lawrence Seaway would continuously provide low cost water transportation to our Great Lakes area. Low cost water transportation, Mr. Speaker, is vital and essential to these steel complexes.
Back in 1951 the Canadian Government agreed to bow to the wishes of what Hon. Lionel Chevrier described as "tremendously powerful United States business interests" and agreed to make the Seaway self-liquidating within 50 years through tolls. This was a unique departure from our traditional policy of paying for public works out of the consolidated revenue fund, but our government to do so was the price that Canada was asked to pay for United States collaboration in the construction of the Seaway. The large and wealthy United States, Mr. Speaker, only constructed two of the seven Seaway locks and a short canal to connect them at a cost of less than $132 million. This was the same as the cost to Canada of building the Welland ship canal between 1913 and 1932, when our wealth and population were far lower than today. The over-all cost to Canada with regard to the present Seaway was about $500 million.
I think we made a very bad bargain when we bowed to United States pressure. I believe we should have gone ahead alone. At that time the House supported unanimously a resolution to go ahead with the Seaway, and it is recorded in Mr. Chevrier's book on the Seaway that there was great disappointment when the United States finally decided to go into the construction of the navigational end of the Seaway. The House was unanimous
April 12, 1965

The Address-Mr. Macaluso
because it was stated that "everybody in the House recognized that if it were beneficial to the whole nation it would ultimately be beneficial to the separate parts of Canada."
It is because I believe that Seaway tolls are against the public interest of Canada that I make no secret of my belief that they should be abolished, and Canada should build an all-Canadian seaway. I think it was visionary at that time that the Canadian Government did build the abutments at Cornwall to provide for this being done, although this was opposed at that time by the United States interests. I realize only too well that the abolition of tolls is not an easy objective to achieve, and it will only be achieved if Canadians can be made to realize the importance of the Seaway to our national economic prosperity and social progress.
The continued existence of tolls on the St. Lawrence Seaway is an invitation for the imposition of similar charges on the Welland ship canal, the Sault locks and the river channels connecting Lakes Superior, Huron, Michigan and Erie. Some eight or nine years ago the Hoover Commission in the United States recommended such user charges on all such facilities in the United States, and President Johnson in his budget message to Congress in January, 1965 recommended the imposition of such tolls on United States inland waterways. Imagine if you can what the situation would be if tolls had to be paid for the use of inland waterway facilities on all grain shipped from the Lakehead to markets in Europe, and on all iron ore cargoes upbound from the lower St. Lawrence. Tolls are a hindrance to export trade and I wish to say-

Mr. Speaker, after consultation with the House Leaders of the other parties, a consensus was reached whereby the House would continue to sit during the dinner hour tonight; it would sit continuously tomorrow after it convened at eleven o'clock, until the completion of the Address in Reply tomorrow night. When the vote is taken on the Address in Reply tomorrow night, that will be the conclusion of the proceedings.
The Government undertook that it would not introduce any other legislation except two items on today's order paper, Government Notices of Motion Nos. 5 and 6, which merely give legislative effect to those items in the supplementary estimates which had to do with the civil service and mounted police pensions and the extension of the date for rebates under a tax act. No legislation, other than those two items, will be presented.
On the adjournment of the House tomorrow night the Government would move it stand adjourned until Monday, April 26, at 2.30 p.m.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as is the custom in this House, my first words must be words of congratulation to the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. The hon. Member for St. John's West and the hon. Member for St. Maurice-Lafleche did a noble job with the very sketchy material with which they had to work.
The Speech from the Throne, Mr. Speaker, reminds me of a Mexican game-I forget the name-in which they have a paper bag full of goodies at Christmas time. The participants in the game bang it around until they have broken it and out fall all the candies and goodies. The Prime Minister and his cabinet remind me of this game. They have broken this bag and out have fallen the candies and goodies, the absolute sop for the Canadian electorate.
The Liberal Party came to power almost two years ago with a number of slogans, such as "The Liberals have all the answers." A reading of the Speech from the Throne must have caused great disappointment to Canadians and to the backbenchers on the other side. It must have been disillusioning to the thousands who supported the brave words "60 days of decision", and "a time to test the strong, excite the daring and give new promise to the timid". Over the last two years-it will be two years on April 23 since this Government took office-all we have had have been the affairs which have hit the Government and the Members of the Cabinet, and which have aroused great disillusionment and confusion in the minds of Canadians throughout the country.
We have had, instead of a time to test the strong, a time to test the credulity of Cana-22620-16
DEBATES	229
The Address-Mr. Nielsen dians, in that the Prime Minister would allow the conditions to exist which were the subject of the amendment voted upon last Friday. Instead of a new promise for the timid we have had despair for the hopeful thousands. This Government was going to bring a fresh new breeze to the Canadian political scene, but we have had something that has been certainly something less than fresh. It was not long ago that Canadians heard this stirring battle call of the Liberal party, "Let us get Canada moving again". They said we were in the economic doldrums and criticized us severely for the action which was taken in pegging the Canadian dollar. However, we have a perfect example of the policy of retreat and indecision followed by this Government in the answer of the Minister of Finance today when he flatly said that the present rate, that is the 92J cent dollar, was quite acceptable and they were quite happy with it.
So, instead of these brave promises and new words, we have been given a Speech from the Throne in which all we have is the warmed over leftovers from the last session. We have sections that have been blatantly plagiarized from the Kennedy and Johnson administrations in the United States. I am sure hon. members who saw that program on the C.B.C. last night would have had a laugh or two at the conversation between the Prime Minister and the President. Then to wind up the whole thing we have the amazing, wholesale borrowing from the N.D.P., so much so that one commentator was led to say in a television and radio broadcast that after this Speech from the Throne, all the N.D.P. had left in their platform was anti-Americanism.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
What has happened to all those brave words? Where have all those promises gone? Where is this brave new world that was going to be ushered in for Canadians by the Liberal Party? From 1960 to 1963 we have had the Madison Avenue hucksters forming all the catch words, with all the slogans of the Kennedy campaign being parroted by the Prime Minister, the leader of the Liberal Party. For the past year or more the advertising specialists, to whose Edgar Bergen the Prime Minister plays Charlie McCarthy, have been putting the slogans of the Johnson administration directly into his mouth.
Down there across the 49th parallel they have the "great society". Here we have got
April 12, 1965

The Address-Mr. Nielsen
the "good society". South of the border they have a war on poverty, and so the Liberals declare a war on poverty here. The Americans have a peace corps, and all of a sudden we have a youth corps. And so it goes. I daresay soon we will be having barbecues at 24 Sussex Street. It is a degrading spectacle for the Prime Minister of this country.
There have been moments in his administration when free from the foolish and vacuous image making of his public relations men-and even these have been failing him, according to one prominent member of the Press Gallery whose notable achievement was the publication of another book before this government took over-when we have been able to see the Prime Minister at his best; and we can be forgiven sometimes for wanting to ask, in the vacillations that have occurred between all the other images attempted by the Prime Minister, "Will the real Lester B. Pearson stand up and be identified"?

There isn't a real one, a colleague of mine says. I have heard people, speaking about disillusionment and confusion across the country, say "We would not be in the terrible mess in Ottawa if Pearson were alive."
It is perfectly understandable if Canadians have no confidence in the present Government. They are unable to act decisively. They are unable to act imaginatively in the area of policy, whether it is affecting the economy, labour, immigration, agriculture, or indeed in an area that vitally interests all of us, the area of justice; and in an area which vitally concerns me, my colleague from the Northwest Territories and a good many others on this side of the house, the area of northern development.
Since the change of government there has not been a single new development project undertaken above the 60th parallel. Why? Is it because there exists that fundamental difference between the approach of the Liberals and the approach of the Conservatives in these matters? How can we expect government investment to develop our northern frontiers when we have this grab bag of eyecatching goodies falling out of the paper target the Prime Minister breaks blindly with his pole, as they do during a Mexican Christmas celebration?
The Prime Minister in his speech last Tuesday dealt with this problem in a way that will shock many Canadians. When a

housecleaning is clearly in order he resorts to legalisms and to hair splitting, in which all the Cabinet Ministers indulge on almost every occasion when questions are put to them intended to elicit proper information. A man must be en route to the courts before prime ministerial notice is taken of his behaviour.
Prudence and good judgment, discretion in the choice of one's personal associations, probity in one's business transactions-none of this matters, apparently. The Prime Minister has made his decision: there will be no clean up in his cabinet, and we are stuck with it until the government is changed. There will be other opportunities to deal with this question of integrity in high places, and no one will find those on this side of the house loath to take advantage of those opportunities.
Canadians do not have to look far to find the reason for this lack of initiative, the lack of originality in the Speech from the Throne, or to find why the Government of this country has become, as one respected overseas publication has put it, "a rudderless mess." The Cabinet is in disarray because of the pressures exerted not only by a public outcry for a public hearing but by an outcry from all the opposition parties combined. The Cabinet is beset by every manner of division.

How well we remember the non-confidence motion, moved by the then Leader of the Opposition in February, 1963, referring to divisions in the Cabinet.
The present Cabinet, this present rudderless mess, has more holes in it-I did not say leaks-than any ship of state in this century. I could say it has more leaks in it than in the Progressive Conservative Party caucus, and that is saying something.

Almost a year ago a responsible correspondent, a columnist of the Montreal Star, Mr. W. A. Wilson put it this way:
The underlying problem.. .seems to be that Mr. Pearson has so far failed to weld his Cabinet into a team-despite the 1962 election slogan touting the "Pearson team." Members of a team do not normally scupper their colleagues in Mr. Tremblay's
April 12, 1965

reckless fashion nor embarrass important causes as Miss LaMarsh did through her electioneering. It would be unjust to suggest that these are disloyal people but in a very practical way they are lacking in true loyalty to the ministry to which they belong because they fail to weigh their private inclinations against the public good.
Well, that failure is still with the Prime Minister, but we understand his failure better now. You can't build a team, and even he can't build a team, with nothing to work with.
As I watched this strife-torn Cabinet day after day my eyes often wandered beyond the treasury benches to all that talent on the backbenches, all those capable and intelligent backbenchers on the other side both men and women, waiting for their turn, a turn that will never come because the Liberal old guard is still holding the reins. The old guard of that party has triumphed, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister is their captive and their advocate.
What a sense of frustration must overcome all those ambitious Members behind the treasury benches. I think of one in particular, the hon. Member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene). Here is a Member who looks on with envy each day this house sits, when he observes the conduct and the machinations of those who occupy the treasury benches today. He thinks to himself "How much better I could do it if I were the leader, the Prime Minister."

[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
One need look no further than the treasury benches to witness examples of frustration. The Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), who I understand has gone on an extended vacation, has been ready, willing and able to take the initiative in cleaning up the party, especially in his own Province, even though he would be facing a herculean task in that regard. But he has been kept down. He has been smothered by the Minister of Justice, by the Secretary of State, by the Postmaster General, and finally by the Prime Minister himself. I think 22620-165
The Address-Mr. Nielsen the Minister of Transport is perhaps beyond ambition for leadership these days.
The Brandon Sun put it this way almost a year ago; conditions have not changed and I quote from that publication:
Young, forceful, frank and politically appealing, he is an avowed member of the Liberal Party's left wing who, it has been suggested had hitherto been held down in the party ranks by more reactionary elements.
A more recent comment came on March 20 of this year in La Presse under the by-line of Pierre O'Neil, who described graphically and at length the complete fragmentation of the Liberal Cabinet. I have a translation of the article here. It is lengthy and I do not intend to read it all, but the subheading reads:
Maurice Lamontagne is on the brink of resignation; Maurice Sauve is 'on the outs' with the Prime Minister; only the Minister of Justice, Guy Favreau, retains a bit of enthusiasm.
What a description. The article says:
The Quebec wing of the Pearson Cabinet is in full rout. Mr. Maurice Lamontagne almost resigned recently. Mr. Maurice Sauve is 'on the outs' with the Prime Minister who has turned a deaf ear toward him. Mr. Guy Favreau, the Minister of Justice is the only one of the three Quebec generals to keep some enthusiasm despite the extremely hard blows that he has taken recently.
The caucus, it goes without saying, is also tossed about by the tempest. The ship is going around in circles, not knowing in whom to repose its trust.
People are familiar with the old story of politicians going around in circles. The Prime Minister of this country is as capable of doing so as is the Secretary of State for External Affairs. That is all he does; he goes round in circles and stands foursquare for everything. The article goes on:
In this climate is born the rumour insisting that Mr. Lucien Cardin is gaining stature in cabinet deliberations and that he will be in his turn an important Quebec spokesman.
It is not easy to evaluate all that has happened recently which has revealed this crisis. It is still less easy to predict where all this will lead the Cabinet, and the caucus. Above all it is not easy to know how the Federal Liberal Party in Quebec will extricate itself from these convulsions.
We all know the end product of convulsions.
The case of Mr. Lamontagne is typical.
As for the tensions between Messrs. Favreau and Sauve, they resulted from their different conceptions of what should be done in Quebec to reinforce the party and to make it responsive to the important changes which have happened these past years in the Quebec political society.
The Secretary of State is just recovering from the hard blows which have been struck him in the House on the subject of the famous furniture

Members should withhold their applause until they hear what Mr. Fraser Kelly of the Telegram has to say about this hon. gentleman:
The switch of controversial Rene Tremblay from Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has sparked bitter resentment among Canadian postal workers.
The implications are crystal clear. In the Canadian cabinet the portfolio of Postmaster General is the ultimate disgrace, the Outer Siberia, cries an editorial in the Canadian Postal Worker, a civil service publication.
We, in public estimation, are so low on the totem pole that we have sunk into the mire. We are fit only to be headed by some incompetent.
Under a thick red headline stating We Protest, the editorial asks isn't it time that a cabinet be thought of as a team of experts.. .not a party grab-bag with juicy plums for some and bitter quince for one unfortunate other.
The news story in the Telegram continues, quoting the Canadian Postal Worker as follows:
To those of us who have considered the keeping open of the lines of communication a worthy calling, to those of us who have taken pride in the handling of the Royal Mail, the implications of the situation have come as a blow.
A foul wet rag across the face could have carried no greater impact.
That is what the employees of the Minister's Department feel about this Minister. So one need not wonder why the Canadian public came to the same conclusion.
How well we remember the cries when the former Government was in office that Canada's reputation had suffered abroad. I wonder whether hon. gentlemen opposite have been reading the overseas press lately about the aura of uncertainty that surrounds the Cabinet, about scandal and the lack of leadership in Canada. That is what these publications are saying. Have they heard about the Gallup poll in Great Britain which showed that the British people regarded the United States as their number one friend, with Australia number two and Canada third? That is a condition which did not exist when the Conservatives were in office.

DEBATES	April 12. 1965
While this fumbling and bumbling is going on over there, serious situations are arising and the Government is failing to deal with them.
We heard the Prime Minister's new politics described in January of 1964 in the course of a national bilingual television broadcast. Well, having seen them in action on the Canadian political scene, I say we have had enough of these new politics. He has recently been touring the country whimpering and whining about the Opposition, saying we are obstructing, filibustering and preventing his new politics from being implemented. This is the same right hon. gentleman who, when he was Leader of the Opposition in September, 1962, speaking to the Young Liberals in Toronto, used some of the most disgraceful language I have heard any person use against a Prime Minister of this country, referring to falsehood, gross deception and deceit. Then we have Cabinet Ministers opposite like the Minister of Justice who complain and whimper when somebody else says a statement is false. Where do we go in Canada? The conduct of the Cabinet is not such as to warrant confidence either at home or abroad.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
The Minister of Health and Welfare-I am sorry she is not in the house today-has indulged in hobbies from the anti-smoking campaign, which is getting nowhere, to the defence of some, if not all, of the members of her sex as is reported in the Toronto Star of November 5, 1964. I quote from that article.
Winnipeg-Health Minister Judy LaMarsh yesterday criticized Opposition Leader Diefenbaker, Manitoba Premier Duff Roblin and people who question the intelligence of large bosomed women. Miss LaMarsh at a press conference was asked about an American scientist who recently said that small bosomed women have the highest intelligence quotients.
Then the paper quotes the hon. Lady as saying:
"A bosom size doesn't prove a damn thing about my brains".
I am happy that the hon. Lady was so frank with the press. A year ago it was reported that the Minister had threatened to resign because she was being excluded from secret consultations between those at the federal level and those at the Quebec level concerning the design of the pension plan. The Montreal Gazette had this to say:
The gesture is said to have been made in protest over the primary responsibility for Canada Pen-

sion Plan planning transferred out of her hands, and over the Federal Government's decision to adopt a new pension scheme embodying many of the features of the Quebec pension legislation. Miss LaMarsh was not a key figure at the Quebec conference, at which federal plans underwent a drastic change.
We all know, Mr. Speaker, which Minister in the Cabinet carried the bill through this House, and it was not the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
The Minister's troubles are not confined only to pensions, but I do not want to elaborate any further with respect to her troubles except to say, in connection with this brave new world of politics that the Prime Minister is ushering in, that according to the Vancouver Province for December 5 the Minister is reported to have said:
"Sit down, shut up and let the matter come to a vote", yelled Health Minister Judy LaMarsh to Tory M.P. Deane Gundlock in Parliament the other day, and no doubt the suffragettes of yore revolved in their graves.

Judy LaMarsh counsels tact in debating Canada's future.
That is her idea of tact, Mr. Speaker. The Secretary of State for External Affairs-I see only two Cabinet Ministers in the house at the moment, and they are probably the only two who have no leadership ambitions on that side-who retired from politics long ago, does not get mixed up in anything so blase as party wrangling and politics nowadays. That clearly sets out that a report which has been submitted to the House by a committee established during a previous session can be brought in at a following session for approval or on a motion for concurrence, providing the Government is willing to take that step. It is my opinion that I, as Chairman of one of the subcommittees and the Member who moved concurrence in the reports numbered 18 and 19 on behalf of the whole Committee, could make such a motion but, of course, it would be buried along with a great number of other private members' motions. If the Government was serious and intended to change some of the rules of this House in order that we can complete the tremendous volume of business with a certain degree of order and dispatch, it could revive these two Committee reports and have them debated and, I would hope, subsequently passed during this third session of the twenty sixth parliament.
If the Government was ready and willing to do this, Mr. Speaker, it could appoint a day, as is set out clearly in citation 320, for the purpose of passing these two reports. If the conditions and recommendations contained in reports Nos. 18 and 19 are acceptable to the Government, surely this would be a far better way of bringing about these reforms than by bringing forward a completely new Government motion. I say that because of the obvious fact that these reports were developed, worked out, compromised, written and rewritten by a Committee made up of members of all five political parties in this House. Surely that, would be more acceptable to this House than a new Government motion which would almost automatically receive the opposition of many Members in the Opposition.
Reports Nos. 18 and 19 deal with changes to Standing Order No. 65, to realign the Standing Committees of this House, and with Standing Order No. 56, which deals with the limitation of time in debating the main estimates in this House. These involve major reforms which have received support from at least some Members of all the parties in this House. Therefore it seems to me that it would be highly desirable for the Government to take the course open to them under citation 320 of Beauchesne.
The Members of the Special Committee on Procedure and Organization spent many weeks, in fact several months, meeting several times each week studying these reforms and drafting these reports. The committee took into account the various opinions and sugges-
The Address-Mr. Olson tions in writing the reports and arriving at compromises so they would at least in some measure meet the approval of Members from all parties. I hope the Government will take this course of action which is open to it. I am not suggesting that it will be going far enough in this regard, but this will at least permit the establishment of standing committees of this House in such a way that they will be in a position to receive and deal with all the estimates of the Departments of Government.
Standing Order No. 65, as it is now constructed, does not in effect allow all estimates of all Departments to be referred. The old committee on estimates could perhaps be a catch-all committee to deal with those estimates which cannot appropriately be referred to specific committees. That is not what we intended, nor is it the way most Members of this House feel these estimates should be referred to committees.
Mr. Speaker, for these reasons I make the very positive suggestion to the Prime Minister and the President of the Privy Council that a major step forward toward the modernization of our rules could be taken by following the course open under citation 320. The reports of the Committee are now before us. They have already been approved by the Members of the Committee on Procedure and Organization, and it would be very easy for the Government to reinstitute them for consideration at this Session.
The other subject to which I wish to refer is that covered by this part of the Throne Speech:
My Government is developing new policies to enable farmers generally to achieve larger and more reliable incomes so that their living and working standards will be comparable to those enjoyed in other sectors of our economy.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
I suggest it is about time, Mr. Speaker, that a concerted effort was made by the federal Government to do something about the price structure for the primary producers of food, or the primary producers of groceries, as the Minister of Agriculture has said on a number of occasions. I do not wish to downgrade in any way the very useful amendments that have been made to the Farm Credit Act, the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the new Farm Machinery Syndicates Loans Act, but we have reached the end of what we can do to assist farmers by increasing the maximum amounts of credit available. In fact, in my opinion we have already gone

April 12, 1965
The Address-Mr. Olson too far in many cases, in that there are extensions of credit to farmers in various parts of Canada far beyond their ability to repay the money within a reasonable length of time.
I suggest further that these extensions of farm credit, which are burying farmers deeper and deeper in debt, gloss over the real problem, which is the whole structure of the prices that farmers receive for the goods they produce. The new dairy policy announced a few days ago by the Minister of Agriculture is useful. It at least sets a pattern of first of all increasing and then holding up the price of milk used for manufacturing purposes, and this is in addition to the butter support price which has been in effect for a number of years. But this is only one sector of primary production in the field of agriculture, and I simply say that it is a step in the right direction.
I am not going to refer to a lot of statistics, Mr. Speaker, but it has been said that 70 per cent of the farmers of Canada have incomes of less than $2,500. This should illustrate forcefully that the industry in general is badly in need of some revitalization. A survey by the Ontario Federation of Labour showed that 27 per cent of Ontario's farm families or 131,000 people are in a state of abject poverty with net incomes of $600 for a family of four. Sixteen per cent of Ontario's farm families or 72,000 people are living at a subsistence level with incomes between $600 and $1,250. Twenty two per cent of Ontario's farm families, with incomes between $1,250 and $2,250, lack the necessities of life.
Dr. Travis Manning, head of the Department of Agricultural Economics of the University of Alberta, in a survey based on figures from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, shows that in Alberta only 3 per cent of the farms have gross sales of over $25,000, while 11 per cent have gross sales between $10,000 and $24,000, 22 per cent have gross sales between $5,000 and $9,999, and 64 per cent have gross sales of less than $5,000. These figures illustrate that relatively few farms have gross sales sufficient to assure an adequate income.
Very recently there was a decline in the price of Canadian wheat because of a lowering of the price in the international market. A recent issue of the Western Producer, which is published in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, had this to say about the situation:
Faced with the stark fact of declining prices and the strongest competitive conditions they have encountered for many years, western Canadian

producers are worried. Their worries are justified, as we have noted, for they are literally the only producers in the world whose governments in the past have expected them to weather on their own the storms of declining prices in the export market.
I am not one of those Members, Mr. Speaker, who think that all sectors of the Canadian economy should run to the Government every time they are in a little difficulty. I think I am perhaps as much of a free enterpriser by nature as any Member of the House. But, Mr. Speaker, the whole price structure of Canadian farm products is based on the surplus and dumping prices in the international market of all other countries in the world. The price that our own people pay for wheat is exactly the same as the lowest price that is available anywhere in the world. This also applies to sugar and to many other farm products.
There is no other developed nation that does not make some special arrangement for insulating their own domestic food market from the dumping prices of other countries in the international market. The Minister of Agriculture, for example, has said that in Great Britain 7.5 per cent of the national budget is used to maintain and support the price structure of the farm products of that country. In the United States, Denmark, Sweden, Norway and France 8.2 per cent of the national budgets are used to maintain and support the prices of agricultural products grown in those countries. In Canada the figure is 3 per cent.
I might point out that this becomes even more significant when you realize that in the United States and Great Britain, for example, the percentage of their contributions to the armament of the western world is also substantially higher than that of Canada. I suggest that if we look at some of the statistics respecting the change in the prices that farmers receive for what they grow in relation to the cost of what they have to buy, and in relation to the increased incomes of people in almost every other sector, the picture becomes even more alarming and adds further justification to the fact that some concerted effort should be made now by the Federal Government to, as they say in the Speech from the Throne, "achieve larger and more reliable incomes" for farmers.
For example, on a number of occasions we have heard the Minister of Agriculture say that in 1964 farmers had a higher total gross income than at any other time in history. I think he mentioned a figure of approxmiately $3.4 billion. That may be fine on a basis of
April 12, 1965	COMMONS
gross returns, but when you place that alongside the increased cost of production and the fact that some of the sales were out of inventory, it does not look quite so good. When I refer to sales out of inventory I want to make it abundantly clear that a large part of the money that went into the total gross sales came from wheat that was sold in 1964 but was actually produced in 1963.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
The Dominion Bureau of Statistics, in a publication issued in March, 1965, deals with farm net income for 1964 and gives figures for the net income of farm operators from farming operations for the years 1962 to 1964. In 1962 this figure was $1,627 million. That was net income, not gross income. In 1963 this had risen to $1,654 million. By 1964, Mr. Speaker, it had dropped down to $1,432 million. So, Mr. Speaker, in spite of 1964 being the year with the highest gross farm income, there was a decline of over $200 million in net farm income as compared with the previous year. This is not satisfactory any more.
Another point I should like to make is this, especially when we are talking about subsidies. I asked the then Minister of National Revenue in July, 1963 for a complete breakdown of subsidies paid to agriculture producers. If you look over this list you will find that out of the $71 million paid out during the year ending March 31, 1963, $42 million was paid under the butter support program. I wonder if it is fair to call this butter price support program a farm subsidy. It seems to me it would be just as fair to call it a consumer subsidy. We know that the Government is in fact subsidizing the price of butter to the Canadian consumer to the tune of 12 cents a pound. The subsidy is paid through the Department of Agriculture, but it is certainly of direct benefit to the consumer of butter in Canada. If you deduct that consumer subsidy it leaves the total Canadian Government support for farm produce in all sectors at less than $30 million for that year.
I have another publication before me called the Economic Analyst, published in August, 1964, by the Department of Agriculture. This publication shows that in April, 1964, the latest month for which figures were available, the price index, that is all farm prices for agricultural products, has risen to 245.8 based on 100 equalling the period from 1935 to 1939. During the same month the prices of commodities and services used by farmers had risen to 309.9. You have to go back to 1948 before you can find a period when the average
DEBATES	237
The Address-Mr. Temple of prices received by farmers was less than it was last year. There were one or two years, 1954, 1955 and 1956, when it was approximately the same as the index for April, 1964, but to find a substantially lower amount you have to go back before 1948, some 17 years ago.
In spite of the fact that there has been no substantial increase in the prices farmers have received for their goods and services, particularly for the primary goods they produce, namely food, there has been almost a doubling in the cost of those things which are required by farmers, that is commodities and services. I hope, therefore, there is a determination on the part of Government, as indicated in the Speech from the Throne, to do something finally to upgrade the whole price structure and provide it with some reliability. Credit is no longer the answer. We have now to provide our farmers with an opportunity of repaying some of the credit extended to them during the past few years.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not care who gets the credit for it. I give the Progressive Conservatives full marks for all the things they did that were beneficial and useful to the farmer. I give also, to the Liberals, full credit for all the things they did that were beneficial to the agricultural sector of our economy. But really none of the policies have been able to get at the root of the problem, that is this competition from the dumping of surplus products from other nations in the world. As I said at the outset, other countries in the world have insulated their domestic market against these surplus pricing arrangements.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I hope there will be a concentration of the effort of all parties, of all members of all parties, to get on with correcting this problem which is so old, and I am not concerned about who gets credit for it.
