April 12, 1985

The Address-Mr. Temple
It would be nice, Mr. Speaker, il we could compliment everyone in this House all the time, everyone in Canada and everyone on the international scene. Of course this is not possible. We have a great many troubles in the world today, and on the international scene certainly not the least of them is Viet Nam. In the past there has been a tendency to say that the United States should stop acting as international policeman and should pull out of South Viet Nam. It would be very nice if the need were not there for an international policeman. However, the facts of international life today are such that we, as Canadians, are very fortunate in having a friendly ally such as the United States willing to take on the responsibilities it has assumed for international affairs.
When people say that the United States should get out of Viet Nam or get out of this country or that country, I suppose what they are saying is, let these people determine for themselves; these people can and will determine things for themselves. This would be all well and good if these people were allowed to follow the process of self-determination. We do not need to look very far. Let us look at Poland. Did the people of Poland have the right of self-determination? No. Did the people of Hungary, after the war, have the right of self-determination? Again the answer is no. The people of Rumania; did they have that right, or the people of Bulgaria? Of course the people of Czechoslovakia in 1948 were not given the right or opportunity to determine their own course, because their democratic government was overthrown by a coup by a minority party. Well, if the United States were to pull out of South Viet Nam without making provision for an absolutely free self-determination by the people of South Viet Nam, then the same old pattern would repeat itself.
[DOT] (3.40 p.m.)
I welcome, as I am sure all do, the detente in Western Europe, although the events of the past week in Berlin make me rather wonder if this is going to be a continuing detente. We have welcomed it during the last two years, and it is not time yet for us to let our defences down. In my opinion it is always best to bargain from a position of strength.
I hope that this can be brought about in South Viet Nam so the South Vietnamese will have the right of really free self-determination. Of course I welcome also what was announced by the President of the United

States last week, that the United States is willing to put in and will put in up to $1 billion of economic aid in that troubled area. I also compliment our Government very much for going along with that and saying Canada will share part of that burden.
If, Mr. Speaker, the United States pulls out without having brought about these negotiations, if it pulls out its military forces from South Viet Nam, what will happen? It will be like a game of dominoes; the whole thing will collapse. I suggest Laos will be next, and Cambodia. Then will go Thailand and no doubt Burma. Then will come Malaysia, but it is hoped it can be contained there. It is less than 20 years ago that the war in the Pacific came to an end. That war was fought, as I understand and believe it, to stop the spread of another type of imperialism throughout the Pacific. So let us not let that happen again.
I was particularly annoyed and upset a week ago Sunday night at a program called "This Hour Has Seven Days." Mr. Speaker, Voltaire said that a man has a perfect right to say what he believes in, no matter how much one may disagree with him, and I subscribe to that. But if this program has the right to say what it does surely I, as a Member of Parliament have the right to say what I am going to say about it. It depicted the American in South Viet Nam as a stupid, sadistic moron who did not know anything except torture and war, and disregarded everything else. I take very strong exception to that program which I consider had either no taste or certainly was in very bad taste.
In my opinion the Minister of Justice is to be highly complimented and congratulated for the decision to introduce legislation that will provide an Ombudsman for Canada. Having read the Minister's speeches on this subject for the past several weeks, I understand it will be the task of the Ombudsman to protect the rights of the individual Canadian. This is terribly, terribly important. What distinguishes us from other, non-democratic governments is our basic desire to protect the individual and the individual's rights. Therefore I say the Minister is to be complimented on this decision.
Something which I am not so happy about is a bill introduced in a provincial legislature during the last few days concerning wire tapping. It is called a bill to prevent wire tapping, but instead of being a bill to prevent wire tapping it gives the authorities the opportunity to obtain an order from a federal judge, if they are able to give him evidence that they have reasonable grounds to suspect
April 12, 1965	COMMONS
somebody may be committing or conspiring to commit a crime. Any hon. Member who is a lawyer, and a good many hon. Members who are not, will realize it is not too difficult to present a case to a judge showing you have reasonable grounds to suspect something, and thus be able to get an order. The part I especially do not like, apart from the very fact of wire tapping itself, is that the bill provides for a secret order that can go on month to month, and in fact provides it is an offence for anyone to disclose publicly that such an order has been obtained. Making such information public is to be punishable by a fine and/or imprisonment.
I made my maiden speech in this House two years ago, and in closing stated I was very concerned that the liberty and freedom of the individual be retained, and that it not be whittled away. There has been no change in my feelings since then, nor will there be in the future. I realize of course that this is becoming a more and more complex civilization and society. I also realize the dangers of organized crime; but I believe this provincial legislation is an attempt to reach a proper end by improper means. We are trying to protect society and the individual in the wrong way. What is in effect being done -not by this House, thank goodness-is a whittling away of the liberties of the individual.

I would also like to congratulate the Government for including a statement in the Throne Speech that there will be a free debate on capital punishment. At the outset, Mr. Speaker, I must say I am in favour of the abolition of capital punishment. It used to be in the days when Babylon was at the height of its power and grandeur that the old maxim of "an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth" was generally accepted. We would have thought that over the years we would have grown away from that, but instead of that adage being accepted or not being accepted, as we went along things became worse.
When Rome was at the height of its power, a good many hundreds of years after Baby-
DEBATES	239
The Address-Mr. Temple Ion, the crime of parricide was punished by sewing the condemned in a sack with a dog, a cock, a viper and an ape, and throwing them all into the sea.
Then we come to the eighth century in England and one would think we should have been progressing, but I doubt that very much so because there they had ordeals by fire and water. In ordeal by fire the accused carried a red hot iron around in his hand for a certain length of time. In ordeal by water you placed your arm up to your wrist or elbow in boiling water for a period of some minutes. The hand was then bandaged and kept bound for three days-I suppose they had no antiseptics-and after they removed the bandage, if your hand or arm had not healed you were guilty. The crown attorneys of that time must have had a real field day.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
We now come to the time of the Puritans in the seventeenth century. In England in 1650 a law was passed by parliament making adultery punishable by death, and this savage sentence was actually carried out in two or three cases. But then it became a fact that even Puritans would not convict for this, and the law was repealed. I think it was rather remarkable that the law was repealed so quickly, because usually a criminal law is not repealed until many years after it has gone into disuse and is not looked upon with favour by the public. The people in the England of the sixteenth, seventeenth or eighteenth centuries were not more stupid than the people who live in England and Canada today, but there was a tradition in force there, and this tradition could not keep up with the facts. Mr. Speaker, because something is widely believed does not necessarily mean that it is true. Prior to the time of William Harvey in the seventeenth century people thought the arteries were filled with air, and that there was no such thing as the circulation of the blood. Even after he had proved his theory of blood circulation people condemned him and said he was a heretic.
In the eighteenth century no less than 240 different offences were punishable by death in England. I am sure the Government of that day was trying to cut down the number of crimes of all types. Between 1525 and 1550 it is reported that 72,000 people were executed in England. But crimes of violence did not cease; on the contrary, they increased. They got worse. Gradually people began to realize that it is not possible to have a completely harsh outlook on life and then expect people to act in a refined, decent and honest way.
April 12, 1965

The Address-Mr. Temple
This is my point. I do not believe capital punishment is any deterrent to murder. I will not take the time of the House now by going into statistics; we shall have an opportunity to do that at a later date. But I am unable to find any states or countries where the abolition of capital punishment has led to an increase in the ratio of crimes. I am not saying it leads to a decrease; I am saying it has no effect at all.
What we are doing when we put someone to death at a definite hour on a certain appointed day is this. We are debasing all of ourselves, all of society. When we put a man to death that is what we are doing; we are shaming and degrading ourselves. If it were not so why do we do it so furtively, at midnight behind closed walls? If there is to be a real deterrent effect, bring these things out into the open and let us have a real circus; sell the beer and the hot dogs and have people jumping around waving flags, whatever they might be, and let the condemned man say his last words.

I appreciate this opportunity to take part in the debate. I preface my remarks by saying to the Speaker, the Deputy Speaker and to the Acting Speaker (Mr. Batten) that I hope you will all continue to enjoy the good health you have enjoyed during the marathon session just completed, and that you will continue to show the patience of Job and the judgment of Solomon during the months to come, as you have during the gloomy events of the last 14 months.
I should like to congratulate, too, the Mover and Seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. Though young in years they have displayed a rare maturity of judgment without having lost the idealism of youth. Young men of that calibre will go far in the service of their country.
We have had a Government which has been at the helm of the ship of state for almost two years, longer than it had ever expected. During that time it has presented three Speeches from the Throne. This is the third, and like all such speeches it gives some indication of the Government's plans for the coming session. The present Speech is longer by far than its two predecessors. It contains no less than 58 items of business as far as I have been able to determine, and this from a Government which has been suffering from a bankruptcy of ideas. I believe it is still suffering from a bankruptcy of ideas, but 58 items of business represent quite an order.
Some of these items in the Speech from the Throne are worthy of consideration. Some are original and others have been borrowed from other parties. Together they make up this wonderful bag of gimmicks, tricks and promises which the Government dangles in front of the Canadian people. When the hon. Member for Villeneuve was asked to comment on the Speech from the Throne the day it was delivered he said, over the C.B.C., that there were so many promises in it that we would have to work for the next two years, so there would be no election before that time. In the light of the methods this Government has used in planning its legislative program it might take even longer
April 12, 1965
than that unless, as I believe, the Government has in mind giving us merely an election manifesto hoping that opposition parties will get together and give it the boot. Then they can go before the electorate and say "Look at all the goodies we had to offer you; now we cannot provide them because the wicked Opposition would not let us proceed." [DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I feel this House should give the Government an opportunity to carry out these plans for this Session regardless of how long it takes. After all, we have had one record breaking Session, and we could have another. They came into office on several election slogans and promises.
Let me bring you back, Mr. Speaker, to 1962 and 1963 and the 60 days of decision. Yes, in 60 days there were going to be visible improvements in all facets of the Canadian economy. Divide and rule was another method used, making different promises in the west from those in Central Canada and Eastern Canada. But the main platform was that the wicked Tories were driving the country into bankruptcy by devaluating the dollar. We all remember this, and I think the Government can stand to be reminded on this score. Today that "Diefendollar" seems to be pretty sound currency for the troubled Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon).
Another favourite expression used by the Pearson team was "Get the economy moving". What was the state of the economy during the Conservative administration? On this subject I am going to quote an authority, a Minister of the Crown, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh), whose opinions at rare times are worth repeating. On April 5, 1965 she spoke to the Women's Club of Montreal, and according to the Ottawa Journal had this to say:
I feel that we can now say with pride that we have lived up to this our most important promise. .. the usual economic downturn has been avoided in the current business cycle and Canada is now in its fifth year of almost unbroken economic development.
To anyone who can even count on his toes the Minister stated that the economy had been rising for the past five years. This statement was made in 1965, so the economy started to go upwards in 1960, a time when the Liberals were far, far away from even becoming the government of this nation. Is that not an admission that this slogan or cry of "Get our economy moving" was just
The Address-Mr. Mandziuk an election gimmick, something to try and fool the people?
I will quote no other authority than the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), who the Gazette for March 13, 1964 quotes as follows:
Finance Minister Gordon says he detects no signs of weakening in the current economic upswing which now has lasted three full years.
So that in 1964 it had already lasted three full years. Therefore it was in full swing in 1961. Where were the Liberals in 1961? They were in the wilderness and they are in the wilderness today.
We have had admissions from the Minister of Finance that the devalued dollar is a perfectly sound currency, and we all know how the "Diefendollar" has carried right through the country both in the West and in the East. I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) himself went on a buying spree in a grocery store just to show how much more the groceries would cost if the wicked Tories got into power. But today the Government say everything is fine. In this regard I should like to refer to an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Journal shortly after the Liberals took office. It is headlined "A house left in good order". I should like to put some of this editorial on record because I think the House should be reminded of what happened. This editorial sums up the condition of the nation when the Liberals took over, economically, financially and otherwise:
He left-
"He" is the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker).
-Mr. Pearson a country whose national production in 1962 had climbed 8 per cent to a peak of $40.4 billion-the greatest increase achieved by any western country, and the biggest income ever earned in history by a country with a population of 20 million people.
He left him with a country which, after years of trade deficits, had at last achieved a favourable trade balance.
He left him with a country which, on the testimony of President Kennedy-
That is the late President Kennedy.
-had achieved a greater price stability than any other western industrial nation.
He left him with a country whose reserves of gold and U.S. currency had been brought to $2,700,000,000-the greatest reached in years.. .
In short, Mr. Diefenbaker left Mr. Pearson with a country whose people were producing more, selling more, earning more and saving more than ever before in their history.
I should like to see the Government challenge that record instead of spreading stories about getting the economy moving. If they

I should like to return to the Speech from the Throne which, on careful analysis, gains more prominence by what it does not say than by what it does say; and as I have said already it tries to say plenty. In this, as in the first two Speeches from the Throne, the farmer is a forgotten man. I am not speaking of the farmers of the West but of all farmers in Canada. Whether we admit it or not, agriculture is still one of the most important industries in Canada. But the farmer is a forgotten man.
I would remind this Government which lacks ideas, this Liberal Party which, when in Opposition, all it ever did was to remind the Conservative Party about our election promises-which we did carry out-of what the facts are. I have authority for this in the person of Peter Newman, one of their best apostles in the press, who admitted to Maclean's magazine that the Diefenbaker government carried out practically all its election promises.

Perhaps gross incomes are up, but what has happened to net incomes, that is what I want to know. Has the Minister of Agriculture ever worked out what net incomes are after the farmers have paid out their expenses? It is my understanding that the farmers are even more firmly held by the cost price squeeze. According to the Minister of Agriculture the farmer is not important. He is a forgotten man as far as this Government is concerned. He is the man responsible for providing food for the world. He does not observe a 40-hour week. What has happened to the price of eggs during the last two years? Those gentlemen who now sit in the front benches on the other side of this House, when in opposition promised regional price support. They promised the poultry farmers price support on eggs. Last Christmas when I was back in my constituency the farmers there were selling eggs for as low as 12 cents a dozen. That does not mean that the consumer was paying any less for them. The consumer was paying the same price for eggs and someone else was receiving the benefits of the price spread. Apparently that is of no concern to this Government.
The Canadian consumers of agricultural products asked for a royal commission to be set up to investigate the price structure on eggs. What answer did that organization receive? I do not think it received any answer.
What has happened to the price of beef to producers? In 1963 after the Liberal Government took office the price of beef to producers dropped. In 1964 this price dropped on an average of five cents per pound. One can imagine the effect of that price drop on a thousand pound steer, particularly to a small producer. Mr. Speaker, at the outset of these remarks, I should like, according to practice, to offer my congratulations to the mover, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin) and to the seconder, the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien) of the address in reply, who discharged their task conscientiously and who carried out properly their duty which is to put forward the views of the government.
As for me, not being a member of the Liberal party, I might be allowed to differ as to the goals and objectives pursued by the policies set forth in the speech from the throne and also as to the means proposed by those two government spokesmen.
I should also like to refer to a certain part of the speech made by the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche when he discussed the exodus of the graduates from Quebec technical institutes.
The exodus of our young graduate technicians, well prepared for a technical career, was a tragic thing. May I point out, he said, that in 1961, while I was teaching graduates at the Technological Institute of Shawinigan, ten students only out of 100 intended to remain on the local labour market.
Such a statement, Mr. Speaker, means that the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche, as teacher at the Shawinigan Technological Institute, must assume his share of responsibility for such a situation.
It was not the fault of the students and graduate technicians if they ended their stud-

DEBATES	April 12, 1965
ies with a stock of knowledge that did not enable them to find employment in their own working area.
They cannot be blamed for the programs not being adapted to the conditions of the local labour market. It is not their fault if the Shawinigan Technological Institute did not train young metallurgical technicians for the aluminum plants at Shawinigan; they cannot be blamed if the programs did not train technicians for the chemical industries in Shawinigan; they can neither be blamed if the Shawinigan Technological Institute did not train technicians for the pulp and paper industries in Shawinigan, Grand'Mere and La Tuque.
The fault cannot be placed on the shoulders of the graduates of that institute, but on those whose duty it was to train competent technicians the district required and prepare programs suitable for the working and employment conditions in the Shawinigan district.
The responsibility rests with those whose duty it was to prepare those programs, namely the directors of those institutes, the authorities in charge of specialized education in the province of Quebec and the whole teaching body to which belonged the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche; they were the ones who should have advised those in charge of preparing the programs.
In this regard I must say, Mr. Speaker, that the results of a survey of professional and technical teaching in the province of Quebec show that the teachers themselves- most of whom were former graduates of those technological institutes who had never visited a plant and, therefore, could not know the needs of industry-were incompetent and inefficient at training qualified technicians capable of meeting the needs of industry in their respective districts.
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne makes a great play about the fact that Canada must wage war against poverty and makes it clear to us that we must get behind such a fight.
It is as if we were asked, Mr. Speaker, to take a stand against alcoholism, crime or sin.
Everybody is against poverty. Everybody wants to do away with it. Everybody, the Creditistes to begin with, wants for our families and their members a decent living. Everyone wants for our people reasonable and paying salaries and wages. Everyone wants education and training to be made available to our youth, in keeping with the
April 12. 1965	COMMONS
economic and cultural needs of our times. Everybody would like to see want and illness disappear from our homes.
Everybody would like farmers to earn a decent living on their farms.
We all agree about that. Everybody including members of all parties, will endorse the government proposal for an intensive fight against want, poverty, illness and ignorance.
But if we are all agreed about the necessity of removing poverty from our homes, and providing a decent living to all, we disagree about the means to attain this end.
Those who are steeped in materialism and collectivism and who would like to make the individual subservient to a party, a class or the state will try to deprive the individual of his most important asset, freedom, and put forward some measures to depersonalize the individual, to make him lose his dignity and forget the purposes of his existence.
On the contrary, those who believe that man, as stated in the American Declaration of Independence, has an inalienable right to life, freedom and the pursuit of happiness, should see to it that, as stated by John XXIII in Mater et Magistra, and I quote:
-precautionary activities of public authorities in the economic field, although widespread and penetrating, should be such that they not only avoid restricting the freedom of private citizens, but also increase it, so long as the basic rights of each individual person are preserved inviolate. Included among these is the right and duty of each individual normally to provide the necessities of life for himself and his dependants.
No step detrimental to the freedom of the individual should be taken to fight poverty of the individual or the family.
Any step taken to raise the intellectual and professional training level of young men and women or adults should respect their freedom, the freedom of their parents or the freedom of lower levels of government such as provincial or municipal governments or school boards, or organizations whose rights supersede those of the central state in the field of training and education.
Any step taken to improve health standards should not be imposed without respecting the freedom of the individual and the autonomy of the provinces in that area.
Any step taken to help farmers should not place them in a strait-jacket, remove or limit their right to ownership and should not replace the prior right of the provinces in this field.
No measure for the development of natural resources should run counter to the purposes

Now, the object of industrial organization is to produce as cheaply as possible the goods required to meet the consumers' needs. Industrial organization is not meant to provide employment, but goods and services. Consequently, when policies implemented by governments are aimed at and succeed in reversing the order of ends and means, such policies are bad, harmful, and have no place in a federal system like ours.
To conclude this part of my statement, the centralizing policy advocated in the speech from the throne-and which the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche described as a collectivist policy-ought to be rejected because it runs counter to the particular autonomies at the various government levels in this country.
It is not by adopting centralizing measures that the most complete development of the human being will be ensured, but through measures making the individual more and more free and able to free himself with the help of institutions of his own making.
However, there are certain goods or means which can only be made available to every member of society through state intervention: currency and credit.
The creation of money has always been a royal, a state prerogative. And it is due to a certain mental aberration that governments have waived their right of controlling money and credit.
In Canada and in Quebec nowadays, the creation of credit is left to the discretion of a small number of private individuals and organizations. Today in Canada, the creation of money has become the prerogative of some financiers who in this way happen to control the very lifeblood of social and economic organization.
As the Creditistes explained on several occasions, private citizens or organizations should not be allowed to create money and credit, because money and financial credit, which must reflect the real credit of the country, rightly belong to all those who contribute to the production of goods and services.
Therefore, if the community produces a certain amount of goods and services wanted by the consumers of whom that community is composed, the amount of money or credit placed at the disposal of the community must be equal to the amount of goods and services produced.
248	COMMONS DEBATES	April 12, 1965
The Address-Mr. Plourde
I will go further. In order to make possible the production of a certain amount of goods and services wanted by consumers, if the members of society as producers want and are able to produce this amount of goods and services, money and credit which make possible the creation of this amount of goods and services must be given to the community before hand. This is what is called "credit advances".
But if there are some classes of goods which are of a private character, the production of which is likely to produce benefits and profits and which, consequently, justify a payment of advanced or loaned credit, on the other hand there are other classes of goods which are mere services given by society to itself, mere services which do not produce benefits nor profits.
For instance schools, universities, hospitals, roads, highways, waterworks, streets, sidewalks are not private assets but public assets, because their purpose is to serve society as a whole; they cannot be monopolized in the hands of a few, and they are meant to provide for the well-being of society, to favour the weal and, consequently, to serve all human beings.
Since public capital must not bring in dividends and profits, since public capital is only used for the production of goods intended for the community as a whole, it is obvious that this capital must be made available to the community interest free.
This is, therefore, the efficient part the Bank of Canada must play in this field. Therefore, the government must deny private institutions the power to create credit and give back this power to the only agency fit to create credit free of charge for the community as a whole.
That is why we say that the Bank of Canada should make available to the federal and provincial governments, to the municipalities and the school boards under their jurisdiction the money they need to finance universities, schools, libraries, waterworks, sewers, highways, streets, sidewalks, hospitals, recreational centres, etc.-we could continue this enumeration till tomorrow morning-as long as these public capital investments are materially possible and there are needs to be met.
Now, there are in Canada hundreds of thousands of unemployed; there are plants which are not operating at full capacity; there are plenty of raw materials and other materials.

The needs are there also. The medical schools of the University of Montreal and Laval University, in Quebec City, had to refuse 600 young people who had prepared for 15 years to become doctors; the agricultural school of Ste Anne de la Pocatiere, in the province of Quebec, had to refuse many rural youths who wished to learn rational farming.
Why? Because these institutions lacked space, and money to provide more space. We need a humane and orderly economy. A government convinced of its responsibilities toward society would endeavour to provide the necessary public capital to meet these needs.
Such a policy, providing public capital without interest, would bring about certain results.
It would allow, for instance, a reduction in the ever-increasing costs of the public debts of our different governments. The reduction of interest payments on public debts would enable governments to reduce taxes, and thus increase the purchasing power of families and of individuals.
That is why we, of the Ralliement creditiste, are calling for legislation which will permit the provinces to use their real credit as they please, according to the needs of their citizens so that the wholesome and useful things which could benefit the people may be made available to them.
There is another thing the Ralliement Creditiste calls for, and it is to allow the provinces to control their own trade.
Mr. Speaker, the members of the Ralliement Creditiste are not the only ones to regret the evil effects of the control of trade on the part of the federal state. Here are two examples:
At the federal-provincial conference of November 1963, the premier of British Columbia, Mr. Bennett, said:
British Columbia urgently asks the Canadian government to revise as rapidly as possible the national tariffs. Measures conceived to protect manufacturing industries in central Canada at the expense of other provinces must be cancelled as soon as possible.
And he added:
Canada's tariff policy protects manufacturing industries in Quebec and Ontario. Consequently, the British Columbia consumers must pay a higher price for their consumer goods.
Another authorized spokesman for the prairie provinces, Mr. Charles Gibbins, president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, also stated the problem in the following terms
April 12. 1965



before the Canada-Japan Trade Council on October 15, 1964.
After noting the Canada wheat sales to Japan and the possibilities opened by Japan to western farm products, Mr. Gibbins stated that the high tariffs and the quotas laid down by Canada against imports of Japanese products impaired our grain exports. He added:
Only 8 per cent of Canadian imports of textiles come from Japan. Only 4 per cent of our imports of various goods come from the same source. In fact, Japan supplies only 2 per cent of our total imports.
And yet, Japan is requested to make sacrifices in order to enable some of our marginal industries to continue to deteriorate. That is expensive for us all. We pay more for those goods which we could buy from Japan if that country was given a reasonable access to Canadian markets. We place a most heavy burden on a very good customer, so much so that Japan must wonder how long it will be able to continue buying from us.
So, Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that the control of Ottawa on our international trade is not satisfactory.
Canada is too large geographically; its production is so diversified that tariff measures likely to help an area of Canada cannot but be to the disadvantage of another.
For instance, if easier access to Canadian markets were provided for Japanese textiles so as to reduce the cost of living in certain parts of Canada, the textile industries in Montreal, St. Gregoire de Montmorency, Drummondville, St. Hyacinthe, Granby, Magog and Sherbrooke, in the province of Quebec, would automatically bear the brunt of that new policy. Thousands of workers would be laid off and hundreds of families would suffer hardship.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, the Ralliement Creditiste is justified in demanding that the provinces have control over local and external trade. It is not that Quebec seeks to put up tariff barriers between itself and the other Canadian provinces, because it could make with them trade agreements similar to those prevailing between members of the European community, the common market.
However, Quebec could have more effective control over its import and export trade with foreign countries. It would thus be in a better position to meet more adequately the needs of its population, taking into account the goods and services with which it could provide that population through its production and its trade with other countries.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the Ralliement Creditiste will keep asking for a federal-provincial conference to amend the Canadian

Consequently, I want to move an amendment.

Mr. Speaker, it is customary for a member taking part in the debate on the speech from the throne to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address. The speech from the throne gives the people of Canada an idea of the legislative program to be submitted to both houses in the days ahead.
Our two colleagues, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin) and the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien), were worthy of the confidence placed in them and everybody appreciated the moderation and seriousness of their speeches. They succeeded in emphasizing the truly national democratic spirit of the government of our country.
They have stressed the social aspect which we will be considering and they should be commended for having placed the higher interests of the nation above cheap politics. In doing so, Mr. Speaker, they represented with
[Mr. Plourde.l
dignity their voters; they represented with dignity this great Canadian who is our leader, the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Pearson); they represented with dignity the holder of the Nobel prize for peace; they represented with dignity the one who, because of his courage and his indomitable willpower, personified the soul of our people in a flag and who, tomorrow, by means of our own national anthem, will tell the whole world:
O Canada, terre de nos aieux
Ton front est ceint de fleurons glorieux
It is also customary, in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, to pay tribute to one's constituents. I would be remiss in not doing so and in not thanking publicly all those who gave me the largest majority of anybody in this house. Therefore, my most sincere thanks to the electors of the third largest riding in Canada, whose various classes of people are truly representative of the aspirations of every group in this country, be it that of the farmers, the city workers, the manufacturers, the businessmen or the professionals. It is my duty to thank them and, as their member, not to forget that, as the seconder of the address pointed out, before being a Liberal, I must stand for national unity, for this strength of which Sir Wilfrid Laurier said, at the beginning of this century:
Thanks to the goodwill and the enlightened patriotism of everyone, the twentieth century will belong to Canada.
This prophesy of a great statesman has come true, but this wonderful reality could become still more actual if it were possible to forget, or rather settle our differences; if the rights of minorities were respected and if an attempt were made to find a form of agreement among the provinces which would enable everyone of them to play its full part to enhance the fame and the greatness of our country.
In the last few years, the advantages of cooperative federalism have been felt. Certain people, steeped much more in petty politics than in true and sincere patriotism, have decried that theory, but its results are there to prove its worth.
Following Federal-Provincial meetings, compromises satisfactory to each party were reached, and immediately the beneficial results of those discussions, of this co-operation with the federal government, were felt. It was realized that all were equal partners, that what could be obtained was not a mere handout, but a right recognized to everyone.
April 12. 1965
With a thorough understanding of its role, the present Liberal government proved that it was worthy of its past achievements. It pursued its social assistance program without paying attention to the malicious remarks of those whose only ambition is to return to office, even if in so doing they smear and blacken reputations. It forged ahead, and today as in the past, it advocates a comprehensive social program.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) sees in it worn-out measures borrowed from other countries. But what does it matter, Mr. Speaker, if those worn-out measures can erase poverty from our country, if those measures borrowed from other countries can produce the wonderful results achieved by the American peace corps, dreamt about by one of the greatest figures of our times, the late President Kennedy of the United States.
After the Prime Minister's masterful speech last Tuesday, after his clear and precise outline of the steps that should be taken to fight poverty, needless for me to repeat what he said and what others, ministers as well as members said also when they dealt with help for the sick, for those who are obliged to change jobs because of automation, for the farmers in eastern as well as western Canada, who talked about the creation of a Canadian dairy commission, a public assistance program at the federal level, and help for those who cannot benefit from the Canada pension plan. They knew how to explain the government's views, show the social scope of those measures and the benefits that will be derived therefrom when they have been passed by parliament. There is no need for me to do that.
However, I would like to stress one point which struck me and which meets so well one of today's most pressing needs, namely help for young people.
Provincial governments, through their department of welfare, do a lot and those which, like the government of Quebec, have a department of education allocate huge sums of money for the education of our young people; parish organizations set up recreation centres because it is a well-known fact that a clear mind needs a healthy body. Everyone is agreed that we must allow our young people to assert themselves, that we must allow them to spend their energies for the good cause, that we must prepare them for the role which will be theirs tomorrow. Therefore, the federal government, without inter-
The Address-Mr. Rochon fering with any provincial right, intends to introduce legislation to help them.
Mr. Speaker, I represent one of the most heavily populated constituencies in Canada; several of the great teaching institutions of the city of Montreal and its northern suburbs are located there-teachers' colleges, classical colleges, high schools as well as grade schools. Thousands of young people study there. Therefore, you will understand why I welcomed the announcement in regard to the establishment of a company of young Canadians, through which the energies and talents of youth can be enlisted in social and economic projects, both in Canada and abroad.
I have applauded this beautiful and noble deed on the part of this government. On reflection, an idea flashed through my mind; I thought of another deed that would be equally beautiful, great and noble. Why would not these talented young people channel their energy toward a social achievement which might take the form of an investigation to eliminate an evil that poisons the soul of our youth, cripples and numbs too many of these young brains who could do so much tomorrow when the time comes for them to take over.
You realize, Mr. Speaker, that I am referring to certain radio and T.V. programs, to certain publications through which immorality and sexuality find the doors of our homes wide open.
However, I would not want to make a blanket condemnation-and nobody would take me seriously, if I did-because to condemn these marvellous media of popular education such as radio and T.V., would be condemning everything that modern science and human genius have achieved that is beautiful and great in this world. I would not think of it.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Everybody realizes that in this atomic and space travel age, one needs much more training than in the past and that to keep up with progress, one has to be familiar with modern techniques and methods of self-improvement. Apart from schools and teachers, where could we find, to provide us with such methods and techniques-to open up our minds to the unlimited horizons of the world-anything better than radio and television? However, as anyone may have noticed, what should be used only for the good of humanity can one day become a pernicious instrument and be put to work for evil purposes. As I said a while ago, Mr. Speaker, that is where I felt educated young people could exert a healthy influence.

April 12, 1965

The Address-Mr. Rochon After investigation, they could examine the problem and suggest the most efficient ways of eliminating this evil. What a fine social undertaking and what noble action on the part of the government who would bring this about.
Our young people are not bad, far from it; they have to be guided; their enthusiasm must be directed toward a just cause; they are imbued with ideals; we could spare them difficulties and give them the opportunity to assert themselves in allowing others of their own age to devote their energy and their talent to their service. This is a thought that occurred to me. Why would it not come through?
May I, Mr. Speaker, deal with a question of current interest? The quiet revolution going on in the province of Quebec, which, in 1867, agreed to become a partner in confederation, accepted its responsibilities but expected its rights to be respected.
During the last debate on the address in reply, in February 1964, I dealt at great length with that matter; I recall the statement made in the house in 1865 by one of the fathers of confederation, Sir Georges Eltienne Cartier, and I quote:
The delegates who will go to England will not accept any decision from the imperial government unless it is one based on the resolutions passed by this house and they will bring back no others.
And apart from guaranteeing the preservation of our language and our faith, the main resolutions also guaranteed Quebeckers that they would be considered equal partners who would take a full part like their Englishspeaking fellow citizens, in the country's economic, social culture and political development. The federal system did much for the emancipation of our country. We are now a great nation which is listened to and respected. Every province had a share in it, Quebec as well as the others, but unfortunately, Canada was too long considered as an Anglo-Saxon country, which has obliged us, from Quebec, to fight for survival.
For too long they have forgotten to treat us as equals, for too long they have forgotten that we were partners, so much so that we felt and unfortunately we still feel too often, that we are strangers in our own country. It is true that we had to fight for our survival, but those days are gone now. The province of Quebec became conscious of its value, and particularly of the part it can play within confederation, and this government, more than any other, endeavoured to make it clear

to Quebec. It endeavoured to direct its action towards the union of all men of good will and, as one of our historians said last year:
Let us recognize that the Prime Minister of Canada has a fine quality; as a diplomat, as a Canadian who thinks of national unity before everything else, he strives to make it clear that throughout discussions among the different groups of people, Canadians should show themselves more realistic and less emotional.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)

If we would only be willing to forget our differences of opinion and try to join in our efforts, how much more beautiful and great a nation we could build.
And, as a professor of McGill University stated, in his report to the Laurendeau-Dun-ton Commission, "English speaking as well as French speaking are faced with a problem of national unity", which should be resolved so that all inferiority complexes would disappear into Canadianism. And, according to that professor, the majority of our English speaking compatriots are doing their utmost to understand French Canada.
If Quebec seems, at times, to be the only Province changing in recent years, we should remember that industrialization in all the English speaking Provinces, as well as in Quebec, has totally changed the face of our country. So, instead of losing precious time in sterile discussions, instead of trying to destroy one another, why not try to understand each other and reach our goal-a great Canada-a great nation.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Cashin for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a convention of the House on occasions such as this to pay tribute to the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply. Although it is a conventional expression of tribute, yet in the years I have been here I have never known it to be merely conventional. It has been well earned on every occasion, and certainly this applies to the mover and seconder of the Address on this particular occasion. They carried themselves excellently. They did a very good job. They were a credit to themselves, to their party and to the House, and I want to express my own congratulations to them on having performed a very difficult task.
Dealing with the Speech from the Throne in the very few minutes which are allotted to one, some 30 in this debate, it is impossible to cover many of the points with which one would like to deal. The Liberal Party in its election campaign of a year ago used a comic book, which had various sections with instructions, such as "colour them green." I think, Mr. Speaker, they must feel everybody in Canada is green if they accept all the statements contained in the Speech from the Throne.
253
The Address-Mr. Nowlan
Many years ago Marie Antoinette when she could not understand why people did not have bread, said, "Well, let them eat cake." In this case the cake would not be of the Government's making. The frosting would not be of the Government's composition but the results, if and when the Speech from the Throne is implemented, will in the great majority of cases be a numerous multiplicity of Dominion-Provincial conferences, and this is something on which I wish to comment.
Take the war on poverty, that grandiloquent phrase borrowed from President Johnson, the new manpower policies, the changes in ARDA, the Canada assistance plan, medicare, the agricultural policies and the constitutional question-as, if, and when dealt with-will all result in a very large number of Dominion-Provincial conferences; indeed will depend upon an interminable series of these conferences.
A Dominion-Provincial conference in itself is not a bad thing, but when you have a continuation of them to the extent that they enter upon practically the whole program which the government places before the House, it is a matter to which the House should pay more than passing attention.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I do not want to give any partisan criticism on matters such as this. I prefer to refer the House and you, Mr. Speaker, to a statement made by the non-Conservative partisan, Mr. Peter Newman of the Toronto Star, whose claim to fortune, if not fame was the publication of the book "Renegade In Power".
This is what he had to say with respect to Dominion-Provincial conferences. Dealing with this specific Speech from the Throne he writes:
The massive intrusion into the economy suggested by the Speech from the Throne, will require fiscal and constitutional powers that Ottawa does not possess. It is clear that the details of most of the proposals will have to be hammered out not in the open forum of Parliament, but in the cloistered privacy of Federal-Provincial conferences.
Later in the same article he goes on to say:
The Pearson Government has, as a matter of deliberate policy, down-graded the functions and the powers of the Federal Government. This being true, ail of the legislative initiative cannot remain in the hands of Ottawa, no matter what brave new world it conjured up in the Speech from the Throne. The Liberals simply cannot have it both ways.
If they want a description-I think one might want some light reading, some amusing reading and, I think authoritative reading
April 12, 1965

The Address-Mr. Nowlan about Dominion-Provincial conferences-I refer hon. Members to an article in the Montreal Star by one Mr. Leslie Roberts. This appeared on April 3. Mr. Roberts, as I think all of us know, is an active apologist for the Liberal Government. He knows the desires, the aspirations and the hopes of the Government. He has written and spoken for them in election campaigns and he writes for them in every article of his which appears in the press, directly or indirectly. In this particular article he was dealing with the political future of the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve). He was suggesting something of the future which might lie ahead of him and he based his prophecy on action the hon. gentleman took following the Dominion-Provincial conference which was held in Quebec last April, out of which grew the Canada Pension Plan. He described in some detail all that went on following that conference. He referred to it as a disaster of stunning proportions and he said:
Through the early days in April, nobody in Ottawa seemed to know what to do next. People wrote notes, memoranda and briefs, and in Quebec, Lesage alternated between tempestuous rage and silent sulks.
Then the Minister of Forestry persuaded the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) to allow him to take matters into his own hands. The hon. Gentleman, accompanied by that brain-truster Tom Kent, went to the Prime Minister late one afternoon and said: We are heading for an unmitigated disaster and something must be done about it; will you authorize us to go to Quebec and see what we can do? So they went to Quebec. They met a prominent civil servant in the Government of that Province. Then there are details here with which I will not bore the house-how they registered at the Chateau Frontenac under assumed names, and so on. It has all the trimmings of plot and counterplot. Only the late Ian Fleming, creator of James Bond, agent No. 007, came near to matching what Mr. Roberts writes as to the activities of these gentlemen at this time. According to his article, conferences were held in a small hotel in Eastview. The Minister of Forestry and Mr. Kent conducted discussions in a men's room off the lobby. Out of these conferences and negotiations in men's rooms and hotel rooms, and under assumed names, grew the massive Canada Pension Plan.
That is the picture according to Mr. Roberts. It shows how Parliament can be denigrated in Dominion-Provincial conferences. If these policies are continued, if there is to be a
[Mr. Nowlan.)
multiplicity of Dominion-Provincial conferences, this House becomes a mere sounding board and Members of the House of Commons will certainly become nothing more than echoes of what is decided outside this Chamber, sometimes without even discussion between the various Departments.
Walter Stewart of the Toronto Star Weekly in a broadcast yesterday dealing with Dominion-Provincial conferences pointed out the menace presented by a multiplicity of conferences such as the Government proposes. He said that Government without representation is bad, but that Government without responsibility is much worse. I suggest to you, sir, that our whole system of responsible Government will not only be denigrated but will be so eroded and weakened that Parliament as a whole will have no more control of the public affairs of this country and that the Government will become only a sounding board for what is said at these Dominion-Provincial conferences.
John Meyer, financial editor of the Montreal Gazette said in one of his columns the other day, commenting on this subject of a war on poverty, that the idea was not original. I happened to be looking back the other day on some of the speeches made following the end of the second world war, and it is interesting to note the extent to which that is true. Mr. Meyer points out, in drawing a parallel between what was done then and what is proposed today, that when massive welfare programs were introduced following the Second World War the people of Canada were told at that time that these policies would end poverty; they were to end poverty and abolish it in this country. The fact that today after 20 years we find the Government of the day declaring a war on poverty would suggest that we did not eradicate it by those measures which were brought in at that time.
Poverty, I suggest, is not the result of any single factor. It is a combination of various element affecting different individuals in different ways. It is lack of health, lack of opportunity, lack of ambition, leading, in the end, to discouragement. Primarily perhaps it is lack of education. All these factors enter into poverty, and you do not eliminate poverty by moving people into better housing accommodation. This has been shown in the past. Very often people have been moved from poor housing conditions into better accommodation, but after four or five years the newer houses were in as bad shape as the ones they left. Neither do you cure poverty by pensions or handouts. Poverty is cured, I
April 12. 1965

suggest, in two ways; first by improving the educational system of the country, providing an education at least for our youth so that they can go forward confidently to earn a living in a new world; and second, by providing employment for the people. These two factors are the main factors to be considered in a war on poverty.
Several hon. Members have referred to the report of the Economic Council, Economic Goals for 1970. I was glad to hear this and I suggest it should be required reading for every Member of the House of Commons and, so far as possible, for Canadians generally. It sets very high goals for us and it says they can be attained. It says they have to be attained if we are to provide employment and even hold our own, let alone move ahead. It says this can only be done on the basis of a well trained labour force and population generally, and by an efficient productive system.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
I suggest that the most important problem which this nation and this Parliament is facing today is that of education. It is a problem which is scarcely mentioned, except indirectly, in the Speech from the Throne. If we are to attain the goals which the Economic Council holds out for us, we must improve our educational system, a system which weighs heavily on the Municipalities, on the Provinces and on the Federal Government. It may be in the years to come that the increasing burdens which have almost bankrupted many of the Municipalities will be eased to some extent. The population explosion has just about run its course. Our youngsters in the primary and secondary schools may not need more school buildings but the cost of providing teachers and servicing the debt, however, will be with us.
The Economic Council of Canada foresees that the cost of education will increase from its present level of $2,140 million in 1963 to $3,180 million in 1970, which shows a yearly increase of 5.3 per cent. This is over-all educational cost. In the field of university education the Council envisages an increase of 16.4 per cent each year from now until 1970. I say to you that the most important problem facing the country today is not the provision of bigger and better pensions, not the providing of medicare and various other matters, all of which are good in themselves; unless we deal realistically with the educational problem with which the country is faced, then we are not going to conquer 22620-171
The Address-Mr. Nowlan poverty. We are not even going to hold our own and consequently our economy will falter. Instead of improving our social security measures and increasing pensions we are likely to find our economy faltering, because we cannot maintain our economic development which the Council says is necessary and increase our efficiency and improve our competitive position in a rapidly shrinking world.
I do not want to be tagged with the label of being opposed to social security, because I am not. I approve of social security. In this country we have tremendous social security programs which all of us would like to see expanded in accordance with our means and other priorities. But I say with all the seriousness at my command that the time has come when we should stop, look and listen in regard to these continually expanding social security programs and decide on some evaluation. This decision should be made in this Chamber, in this Parliament, here. We must evaluate the various programs and challenges which have been thrown to us, and this should be done before we embark on any war on poverty or before we step further with some of these social security programs.
I say that the decision must be made here and it is easy to see why. We have a Dominion-Provincial conference, say, on health. Certainly the Federal Minister of Health responsible for the development of the program, and the ten Provincial Ministers of Health responsible in their own respective fields, will all welcome the additional moneys which may be made available. The same is true with social security and other welfare measures. You will find you get the approval of the Ministers representing the Provinces and the Minister representing the Dominion Government in their own particular fields; and when the matter is brought to this Parliament, then we are told that perhaps we are right in our criticisms and that the matter should have been deferred, that perhaps the Government should not have gone ahead with it. But then the Government will say that this decision had been made by a joint Dominion-Provincial conference and there is nothing the Government can do about it. We will be confronted with that situation. I suggest once more that the first responsibility of Parliament is not to initiate more welfare measures but to evaluate the ones we already have. We should consider the ones which we feel are necessary and have been recommended. We should choose
April 12. 1965

The Address-Mr. Nowlan between them and have a concrete evaluation of them. All of this time we must bear in mind the overriding responsibility, in my opinion, of Canada going ahead with an ample and a proper educational system.
Having dealt generally with education I should like to refer to a specific problem in university education, because I have been talking generally. I think that the main burden of education will fall upon the universities. As I have said already, the municipalities have perhaps already met the challenge in the last few years, and through private capital facilities have provided schoolhouses and everything else. Further additions may not be required and it may well be that the municipalities will be able to hold their own.
In this regard I think particularly of my own province of Nova Scotia. I think, for example, of Acadia University. I have been associated with that university for many years and know it well. We have a large number of small universities in Nova Scotia. They are good universities, very good, but they are not state endowed, with the exception of the Nova Scotia Technical College and the Dalhousie medical and dental schools. All the rest of them depend upon gifts, meagre endowments, Government assistance such as we know it today, and unfortunately in many cases they suffer from continually increasing deficits. That is hardly the way a university should be financed. We have a peculiar and pressing problem in the Province of Nova Scotia in that almost 40 per cent-39 and something per cent-of the students attending universities there come from outside the Province of Nova Scotia.
There are various reasons for this, Mr. Speaker. To use an old cliche, we have to export our brains, and our graduates leave the Province. But when they are older they like to send their children back to their old university. In my case I have at least two sons with children whom they want to go back to Nova Scotia and attend Acadia University, and the same is true with a great majority of people from Nova Scotia. These colleges are small in these days of mass production factories-which are what some universities are-and these parents want their children to go to a small university. As I say, almost 40 per cent of our students are from without the province. Everybody knows how the grants are paid by the Federal Government to the universities; they are paid on a basis proportionate to the population of the Province. Nova Scotia is a Province

which geographically is small, is relatively small in population, and the student grant is based on the total population of that Province with no regard whatever to the student population of the Province. I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that that is not the proper way to administer these university grants.
I remember speaking to a distinguished gentleman who sat opposite me in this chamber at one time. He held a very distinguished position, and even at that time I had said something to this effect. He told me afterwards that he was inclined to agree with me, but that it was part of historical tradition that we had to maintain at least the appearance of provincial control; therefore the only way the Government could get these grants through the house, or the only way they thought they could get them through the House, and the only way they thought they could get the support of all the Provinces, was to keep it on a Provincial population basis. I did not agree with him on this point, and in fact the Government did not get the support of all the Provinces for quite a long while.

* (6:10 p.m.)
This is a problem for the Provinces as well. I know it is well known to all of us that the Province of Nova Scotia is concerned and it is making large grants to Nova Scotia Universities. The same situation is in existence in the Province of New Brunswick. These governments are wondering whether they should continue to give grants for the support of students coming from all over Canada, or whether they should be limited in some way to those students emanating from those Provinces.
I would refer hon. Members to the Canadian Universities Foundation, an organization which represents all universities in Canada. From 1961 to the end of 1963, despite the
April 12, 1965

fact that these universities were all coming to Ottawa and asking the Government for more money as a result of their claim that they had to have substantial increases in grants, they said that the problem as far as the universities of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick were concerned was more acute, and urged upon the Federal Government to grant $400,000 per year to Nova Scotia Universities and $200,000 per year to the University of New Brunswick before providing increased grants to any other universities. In view of this attitude taken by the other universities, one does not have to urge this upon the Government, but I do suggest that if there is any validity to these arguments that these grants must continue on the basis of provincial population, then this recommendation of that association should be considered.
I should like to refer to the Atlantic Development Board which was created to develop the national resources of the Atlantic Provinces. This Board is doing very good work. It was instituted by that Government of which I had the honour of being a Member, and it has received the support of the present Government. I would suggest to the Government that, if it cannot pay out these amounts of money because of the population formula, then it might accept the recommendation of the Canadian Universities Foundation and have the special grants to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick universities paid by the Atlantic Development Board. I would suggest to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), who has a special interest in this Board, that he give his attention to the suggestion that the Atlantic Development Board could in some way be made responsible for the development of the Universities of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Perhaps part of the substantial sums of money which have been made available to that Board could be used for the development of these universities. Perhaps in that way the Government could move away from the difficulties in respect of grants on the basis of population, and also get around any technical constitutional problems that might arise. I can think of no greater resource which we have than our young men and women.
The universities of Nova Scotia receive $183.19 per student in the way of a federal grant. This can be compared to $281 per student in the wealthy Province of Ontario. Of course that Province has a larger population,
The Address-Mr. Nowlan and a larger student population. These universities receive $281 per student, as compared to the $183.19 in Nova Scotia. I suggest there is something radically wrong when this system is allowed to continue to operate in this manner; I urge the Government and particularly the Minister to pay some attention, to the suggestion that the Atlantic Development Board make some of the money which it receives available in this way for the development of that important resource. That Board has received large sums of money and will receive more when it is required, and 1 think it should give very careful consideration! to the necessity for making grants to these universities.
Mr. Speaker, I am afraid my time is running out. I am not sure how much time I have left.

Thank you.
As I have suggested, I think the youth of our Province is its greatest resource. Since this Atlantic Development Board was created for the purpose of developing our resources, this is a matter with which it could deal quite adequately and efficiently.
There are other problems of a more local nature to which I intended to refer, but as my time is running short I should like to refer to at least one, and then resume my seat.
The problem to which I have reference is one which was referred to by the hon. Member for Halifax (Mr. Regan). A suggestion has been made which has created fears in the minds of the people of Nova Scotia and in the Maritimes generally, to the effect that possibly some day the C.P.R. will terminate its service across the Bay of Fundy. I do not think this alarm is justified. This C.P.R. service has been in existence for generation after generation and I have been assured by officials of the company that, while there may have to be adjustments made in the future, it will likely be maintained.
One prominent executive said to me the other day: When you read during one week of the Russians walking on the clouds, and the next week of the United States photographing the moon preparatory to landing on it, do you not think we would be very foolish to commit ourselves to the expenditure of $4 million to $5 million for something which we can anticipate may have to be changed in five or six years' time. All they
April 12, 1965

The Address-Mr. Novolan are asking for is a delay in the consideration of this problem. If that is the situation, that is one thing. If this is an intimation that the service might some day be discontinued, that is an entirely different thing. As the Minister of Transport suggested the other day in answer to questions raised by the Member for Saint John-Albert and myself the discontinuance of that service is impossible. No Provincial Government in Nova Scotia or New Brunswick, and no Federal Government of any Party, would permit such a thing to happen. It is too bad that undue concern has been raised in this regard, because at the moment all we can do is wait to see how the situation will be resolved.
In addition to that problem, Mr. Speaker, there is a problem in respect of the fishermen. Originally a new wharf was to be built. The Government intended to spend between $3 million and $4 million to build that wharf. All the plans had been prepared and everything was ready. The old wharf was to be used by the fishermen. Plans have been changed and the old wharf will have to remain in service for the C.P.R. for some time. Other adequate accommodation will have to be provided for the fishermen. This is absolutely essential, as I think anyone who has seen the scores and scores of boats tied up behind the spur wharf will agree. The ability these fishermen have in operating in and out from that wharf is a credit to them.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I do not wish to trespass on the rules of the House by taking up more than my allotted time, and I know that other Members here wish to speak. I should like to refer to only one other local matter, if I may.
There is a problem which exists in respect of providing adequate accommodation for fishermen, particularly in the western part of my constituency, having regard to communication between Brier Island, Long Island and the mainland. These islands have had access to the mainland by two motorboats and two scows. Travel accommodation in that area today is worse than it was 75 years ago, and I am not speaking in a political vein in any way. Seventy five years ago there was daily service provided between Brier Island, Long Island and Saint John.

That service, of course, went by the boards long ago.
A suggestion was made that a causeway could be built across this very narrow bit of water. The Government made an estimate of the cost, which was about twice as high as an estimate made by a Nova Scotia engineering firm. If a causeway could be built it would provide easy communication for cars and trucks. Thousands and thousands of tons of fish were transported in this area last year by boats and overloaded ancient scows. With the construction of a causeway there would be a tremendous development in the fishing industry and a tremendous impetus given to the transportation industry generally between those islands and the mainland. You would provide a deep-water harbour, which is very badly needed today. Even in the short time I have been here the motorboats used largely by the inshore fishermen have become very much larger and you have large draggers owned by young fishermen which cost $80,000, $90,000, $100,000 or $125,000. True, they have borrowed from the Fishermen's Loan Board. True, they have mortgaged their souls to pay for them. True, they go into debt. But where can these boats lie at night? There is hardly a deep-water harbour along that coast, and such harbours must be provided. This is one way in which that service can be performed. When the estimates come before us, which I trust will not be too long from now, we will be able to go into greater detail with respect to these matters and others which I had hoped to raise at this time, but have not been able to do so.
I appreciate the courtesy of the House in giving me a few moments additional time because I know I am trespassing on the time of others.
[DOT] (6:20 p,m.)
