speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of my participation in the debate is to present a proposal for federal aid to education designed to deal with the stunning educational crisis which faces Canada today. It is a crisis which, if not met with boldness and imagination by all levels of government, will have drastic effects on the future of Canada for generations to come.
Throughout the world there is perhaps no subject which is causing more concern among responsible people than education. In the modern technological world no nation can hope to survive if it fails to develop the talents of all its members to the highest possible
April 12, 1965

degree. The future industrial strength of Canada will depend, not just upon the actions of the few but rather on how successful we are in developing the abilities and skills of all our people.
We hear much talk today about scientific change and automation, and the extent to which they will change our lives and displace workers. There is absolutely no hope of meeting such problems without a firm understanding of the role of education and the massive amount of money and effort which will have to be devoted to it in the years ahead. On January 12 of this year President Lyndon Johnson recommended to the United States Congress the doubling of the federal budget for education, which he described as the number one business of America. He declared:
Nothing matters more to the future of our country. We must demand that our schools increase not only the quantity but the quality of our education. It is our primary weapon in the war against poverty and the principal tool for building a great society.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, the bill has already been passed and was signed by the President on Sunday night, a striking example of what can happen when a determined leader determines to move aggressively in an important field. What a contrast this represents to the attitude of this Government which in its legislative program does not even mention the subject and has even forgotten completely about its very modest program of 10,000 scholarships. Canadians could take greater comfort if the Government's program had contained a firm commitment to work in cooperation with the Provinces toward the goal of equal opportunity for all to education at every level. It is time, Mr. Speaker, that Ottawa stopped hiding behind the British North America Act and, without interfering in the provincial field of education, began giving the Provinces strong financial assistance in carrying the heavy burden of education costs.
Equality of opportunity has always been held up as one of the great ideals of democracy, but in Canada so far as education is concerned this ideal has been far from realized. The inequalities between province and province and between urban and rural centres are conspicuous. Children are growing up in some parts of Canada with only a fraction of the chance of the educational advantages enjoyed in other parts, and these differences are caused by the mere accident of geography.
The Address-Mr. Scott
It is a tragic state of affairs when the quality of education available to Canadians depends upon where they happen to live. Yet, Mr. Speaker, a poor education is a handicap that follows a person all the days of his life. There are today in Canada 1,017,869 men and women with no more than four years of formal schooling. They represent 9 per cent of all Canadians of working age. In rural Canada 64 per cent have attended only grade eight or less. I need hardly add that in the modern Canada most of these people will be chronically unemployed as long as they live, unless schemes can be developed to raise their educational level and provide them with skills with which to earn a living. Persons with not more than four years of formal schooling are simply not qualified for the skilled jobs that are becoming ever more important in our society.
One of the best indications of equality of opportunity is the amount of money that is spent yearly for each pupil. In 1961 the amounts spent in each Province ranged from $378 in Alberta and $373 in British Columbia to $141 in Newfoundland and $162 in Prince Edward Island. Thus, in dollars one Province spent almost three times as much per pupil as another.
Another yardstick to measure equality of opportunity is teacher qualifications. The proportion of teachers with university degrees varies from 47.4 per cent in one Province to only 7.7 per cent in another. Thus, five times as many teachers hold degrees in one Province as in another. Where is the equal opportunity here?
Another test to apply is the ability of a school system to hold its pupils. Among Canadian Provinces there is wide variation in the number of early dropouts. In one Province six out of ten children in a particular age group remain in school until they reach junior matriculation. In several other Provinces the corresponding figure is less than three out of ten.
These facts and many others which I could add destroy any illusion we might have cherished about equality of education opportunity in Canada. Yet on this vital subject all we receive from the Government is a thundering silence. How can we hope to think of ourselves as a unified nation when one part of the country is on such an obviously different level from the rest? It seems to me a major contribution to the goal of Canadian unity would be a commitment by the Government to make available the necessary funds to wipe

April 12, 1965
The Address-Mr. Scott out this discrimination and provide every Canadian with equal opportunity to develop to the limit of his educational ability.
In addition, economic gain would also result. Instead of just handing out subsidies and tax concessions to private industry to stimulate growth in certain areas, we suggest that economic growth would be more effectively stimulated by equalization grants and other methods aimed at upgrading the general level of education. Investment in human capital is the most promising strategy in a long range attempt to reduce inequalities in education and living standards.
So far, Mr. Speaker, I have referred to the lack of equal opportunity in Canada. I should like to turn now to the level of higher education, for it is here that the staggering proportions of our education crisis become startlingly clear.
Let us look for a moment at the depressing lack of facilities. In Ontario, despite the fact that we have a critical shortage of doctors and dentists, the University of Toronto rejected three out of every four students who wanted to enter dentistry. Four hundred and sixty six students applied, but the lack of facilities meant that only 128 could be accepted. At the Faculty of Medicine two out of every three applicants were rejected because of the lack of facilities. At the University of Western Ontario 200 medical students applied but there was space for only 60 and at the University of Ottawa 200 were eligible but there were places for only 78. This story could be repeated for other such institutions from coast to coast and represent an appalling waste of badly needed brainpower.
In Ontario the number of applicants trying to enter university will climb from
33,000	in 1963 to over 100,000 in 1970. In Canada as a whole it will rise from 141,000 in 1963 to nearly 290,000 six years later.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
What answer will we give to this wave of young people battering on the doors of our universities? How many additional hundreds of thousands would there be if we were to take a step which the New Democratic Party has advocated for years, namely free university education to all with the ability to absorb it? Yet, if we fail to meet this crisis, if we fail to provide the facilities, we deprive hundreds of thousands of Canadian youth of the chance to a better life than that enjoyed by their parents. By failing to meet

this crisis, we deprive Canada of the contribution that such trained people can make to our general prosperity.
If we are to provide all these facilities in the next ten years, we will require a capital outlay of $1.7 billion. This does not include the expenses of such things as heat, light, maintenance and salaries. Yet, Mr. Speaker, in 1963-64 our universities received only 60 per cent of the capital grants which they requested. We are not even meeting current needs, never mind preparing for the wave of students that will face us tomorrow and that will continue to enter our universities well into the late eighties. Even if we were prepared to make massive expenditures to provide these facilities, we will still face the staggering problem of professors, teachers and lecturers. In the year 1961-62 there were 2,100 on the staffs as teachers. By the year 1970 8.5 thousand will be needed.
However, Mr. Speaker, instead of taking positive steps to hold our teachers in the fields of science, engineering, medicine, etc., we seem determined to create conditions in Canada that will drive them to other countries. Most people are familiar with the term "brain drain". Let me provide a few examples. We are losing doctors, scientists and researchers at the rate of 1,500 per year. We train them and export them, then buy back the products of their brains. Between 1950 and 1960, we lost 1,864 scientists, 5,864 engineers, 3,956 teachers, 569 professors, 2,107 physicians, the latter at an average training cost of $25,000. We have 12 medical schools and the yearly loss of 250 is equal to the output of three of them. Unless this drain is halted we stand no chance at all of building up a sufficiently large staff of teachers to man our universities. The loss to our economy of such brains is incalculable. Why do they go, and what can we do about it?
Part of the reason, no doubt, is salaries. The average United States salary in these categories varies anywhere from $3,000 to $10,000 over the Canadian scale. However the salary issue is by no means the most important factor. The most important factor is recognition of their worth to the community and the provision of adequate facilities for research.
Research, Mr. Speaker, is basic to the lifeblood of higher education. Without it, the whole level of your educational system falls behind the rest of the world. Without it, universities become nothing but glorified high schools. Since industry draws on such basic
April 12. 1965

research, a lack of it means your industrial growth is slowed. In short, a continued program of extensive research is vital to higher education. The tragic lack of such facilities is the single biggest contribution to the "brain drain" to the United States.
The Medical Research Council received a grant of $6,900,000. This meets only 65 per cent of the applications it receives for research projects. We are so niggardly in this field that many of these applicants could not carry on without grants from the United States. Four of our Canadian universities constructing basic science buildings will have to apply to the United States for grants because we have no mechanism for capital grants for equipment. For every dollar we spend per scientist Britain spends $3 and the United States $10 to $15.
In 1963 the total medical research grant for 12 universities was $4,800,000. In the United States, for 78 universities the grant was $900 million. By comparison, our grant should have been $100 million. Is it any wonder that we are failing to hold these people in Canada? Can anyone blame them for going where their talents are recognized and they are given the opportunity to develop their genius? One cannot help but concur in the view of Dr. D. V. Bates, the Assistant Dean of Graduate Studies in Research at McGill Medical Faculty, when he said:
The Canadian Government has been worse served in its scientific research advice in the last six or seven years than any other western government.
Another source of teachers is our graduates. If time permitted, I could detail our niggardly system of graduate bursaries, which results in our graduate system being about the worst in the western world. However, Mr. Speaker, I think I have said enough to indicate that if we are going to meet the crisis of higher education in Canada it will require a massive effort that is far, far greater than anything we have ever imagined possible.
Another aspect of the education crisis arises from automation and technological change. Canada is just beginning to feel the effects of this change, and in the next decade there is probably no aspect of Canadian life that will not be affected. In order to be sure that people adjust to such changes, we must develop far more effective retraining schemes than those in effect today. As workers' jobs disappear through the use of new scientific machines, they will have to be retrained for other jobs. During such retraining their in-22620-18
The Address-Mr. Scott come will have to be maintained until they are relocated. Such income will have to be a proper income, and not the pittance now paid. Failure to erect such educational schemes will result in widespread hardship and unemployment.
We shall have to encourage the building of technical colleges to turn out the thousands of technicians that the scientific age will require. It is freely predicted that young people starting to work today may have to be retrained four or five times during their working lives. I could go on outlining the years of crisis in our educational system, but I think I have given enough examples to indicate that a problem of gigantic and staggering proportions confronts Canada. It is obvious that a serious attempt to grapple with the problem is going to result in skyrocketing costs and massive outlays of money. And yet, it is imperative that we succeed because the whole future of Canada is at stake, since education has a direct relationship to a nation's economic growth.
It must be obvious also that if a realistic approach is going to be taken, the Provinces simply do not have the financial resources to do the job alone. They will need and must receive very large financial assistance from the Federal Government. I realize, of course, that education is an area of Provincial responsibility under the British North America Act, and I am not suggesting that we interfere in this exclusive jurisdiction. At the same time, it is hard to see how we are to proceed as a united nation unless education is regarded as a matter of national concern and of direct interest to all Canadians. A competent and well balanced work force is required for the healthy growth of our Canadian economy and the maintenance of our standard of living. If Canada is to be successful in carrying on the economic and political struggles of the future, a much greater percentage of her citizens must possess a higher degree of education or skill.
The principle of Federal aid to education is nothing new. The education of Indians and Eskimos, as well as children of the armed forces overseas, is a Federal responsibility. Through the years, substantial grants have been made available to the Provinces for technical and agricultural education. More recently some $340 million have been advanced under the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act. Following the war an immense D.V.A. program of education was financed by Ottawa. A per capita grant of $2 has been paid to universities as well as various

April 12. 1965
The Address-Mr. Scott grants to research and scholarships. The Glassco Commission refers to some 20 different Federal departments which provide some educational service today. Today more than ever, there is a greater need for Federal support for education through financial agreements with the Provinces. For such Provinces as might object, some formula can no doubt be worked out to meet such objections, similar to the opting out formula since, as I have emphasized, we are not advocating that the Government enter the educational fields of the Provinces except in a financial way.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
In order to assist the Provinces in carrying out their responsibilities in this vital field we advocate the following 10 point program.
1.	The establishment, in co-operation with the Provinces, of a Federal secretariat of education to perform the following services, (a) To supervise the educational activities of more than 80,000 students at present attending Federally operated schools at an annual cost of $50 million, (b) To assist the Department of Labour in carrying out a continuous survey of labour needs in Canada. Such studies would permit the programs of the retraining schools to be adjusted to meet trends in the labour market as they are revealed. Unless this is done we are educating in a vacuum and our expensive retraining facilities will prove ineffective, (c) To encourage and publicize the comprehensive programs of adult education at present offered by extension departments of universities across this country, (d) To act as a clearing house for matching grants and other contributions paid to the Provinces for university construction, vocational schools, student loans, scholarships, special courses for new Canadians, handicapped children, apprentices, unemployed, etc. (e) To provide a medium for the distribution among Provinces of information resulting from research studies and experiments conducted at the local level by school and university authorities, (f) To facilitate student exchange and teacher exchange abroad, (g) To co-ordinate the educational work of the Canada Council, the National Research Council, the Medical Research Council, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and UNESCO.
Let me emphasize that all of these educational services are being performed now, but in a fragmentary and hit-or-miss fashion. It would seem the time is at hand to set up,

with the approval and support of the Provinces, this type of co-ordinating agency.
2.	The Federal Government should assume 75 per cent of the capital cost of university construction costs. The total cost of public education is now $2 billion a year and will double in the next 10 years. If the Government assumed the major portion of university construction costs, the Provinces would be better able to carry their resposibilities on lower levels.
3.	Immediately raise the per capita grant from $2 to $3. Operating costs of universities double every five years and immediate relief from this pressing burden is needed. The last increase was in 1962-63 but costs have continued to rise. This would be the most effective way of preventing an alarming increase in student fees. The objective should be the lowering of fees and their eventual removal altogether.
4.	A special grant of $1 million yearly for distribution among Maritime Provinces to assist them with their special university problems. At the same time review and if necessary, increase the equalization grants so that all areas can develop educational programs equal to that in the wealthier areas.
5.	Assume 75 per cent of the cost of vocational and technical training, and in particular full cost of research in universities including facilities, salaries, equipment, etc. Such a step would make a vital and stimulating contribution to education at all levels and, at the same time, to the total development of Canada.
6.	Provide for a broad program of bursaries and scholarships as well as the present system of loans. It is imperative to make sure that every student obtains as much education as his ability will allow.
7.	Increased financial support for graduate schools. Unless we have a spectacular increase in graduate studies we shall never be able to train the scientists and teachers which our expanding schools and modernized industries require. The shortage of skilled people is world wide and we can no longer look to other countries. We must train our own educators.
8.	Intensify enormously our long term analysis of the economy as a guide to the provinces in drawing up curricula and courses.
9.	Encourage the practice of student exchange. In 1963, 8,115 Canadians studied outside Canada and about 8,500 foreign students studied in Canada. In terms of international
April 12, 1965

good will such programs should be expanded. To supplement the Commonwealth scholarship plan a similar one should be established for student exchange within the whole French cultural community.
10.	Treat all university donations from private sources as deductible for income tax purposes and exempt universities from federal sales taxes, as is done with hospitals.
I realize that, to some, these proposals may seem extreme, but to my mind they are the very minimum which will suffice. It is suggested as an interim measure, pending the report of the Commission on the Financing of Higher Education in Canada, whose report is expected late this year.
It may well be that the above measures will prove to be totally inadequate. The crisis in Canadian education is neither new nor is it likely to become easier in the very near future. It is estimated that the rapid expansion of students will be with us throughout the 1970's and well into the 1980's.
That being the case, the problems I have outlined today are going to intensify. Strong financial assistance such as I have suggested would also relieve the pressure on the individual home owner, who still carries the main burden of education costs in Canada. This has always struck me as being an unfair burden. No doubt many people would ask if such assistance would result in higher taxation. The answer of course is no. The report of the Economic Council of Canada estimates that if the Government is prepared to institute growth programs sufficient to bring unemployment down to 3 per cent, even existing tax levels will produce surpluses of over $2 billion. There is no reason why such surpluses cannot be channeled into the critical area of education.
May I again emphasize, as emphatically as it is possible for me to do, that Canada faces an education crisis of the first magnitude. While recognizing the constitutional position with regard to education the Federal Government must still step in with strong financial help to the Provinces.
Canada is a Confederation of ten Provinces, but it is also a nation. To move forward as a nation into the scientific age with imagination and confidence the Federal Government must play its part in providing what President Claude Bissell of the University of Toronto describes as "heroic measures" to meet the pressing demands of modern education.
The Address-Mr. Pilon
In conclusion, I wish to quote a brief passage from the second volume of the Report of the Royal Commission on Health Services. I quote:
We have in Canada a land of immense resources. We must use them for the good of all Canadians. We have an opportunity to build upon the northern half of this continent a nation of educated and healthy people. Nature itself favours such a possibility.
It is for us to to organize our resources in harmony with our favoured situation that Canada may become a show-place of man's humanity to man.
We will rightly stand condemned by history if we fail to do what our people need and what our resources make readily possible.
Nothing less than this is acceptable to the New Democratic Party.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks, may I congratulate very warmly the mover (Mr. Cashin) and the seconder (Mr. Chretien) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I do so because, in the first place, it is the custom, but mostly because they carried out their task with mastership, conviction and displayed much eloquence. I hope this optimism they have shown will spread in high government circles so as to inspire them with ideal and instil in them the required energy to apply the program proposed in the speech from the throne, and this for the benefit of all Canadians.
But what exactly does the program which the government holds out to us mean? To embellish it, the government has succeeded in adorning it with lots of flowers which, unfortunately, are a little faded since they date back several years and which, it seems to me, are doomed to a slow death, precisley because of the inaction and lack of imagination on the part of the present government.
Mr. Speaker, the program advocated in the speech from the throne constitutes a real electoral manifesto, but that does not necessarily make it reprehensible provided the government introduces the necessary measures to implement it. I think it is absolutely impossible to consider passing such a program without first initiating a basic reform, that of parliamentary procedure.
I for one sincerely regret that the report of the special committee on procedure and organization was not agreed to at the end of last session. In fact, I believe that to be realistic, any program of parliamentary reform should call for a time limit for the debates of this house and also propose the necessary means to refer to committees specially set up for that purpose the detailed consideration of estimates and study section by section of government bills. In my opinion, it will be impossible to carry out a large part of the government program as long as the government does not give proof of energy and determination in that regard.
Mr. Speaker, I find it impossible, in reading the speech from the throne, to determine where the government wants to lead us. To
April 12, 1965	COMMONS
be sure, it wants to please everybody, and I cannot blame it for that, but quite a few of the measures it is putting forward seem contradictory.
For instance, the government claims it is committed to a policy meant to promote the strength and unity of the Canadian confederation. To this end, it proposes the maintenance of consultation at the federal-provincial level. Such consultation is indeed most desirable, but specific measures still have to be put forth, if this co-operation which the government apparently wants to see established in the field of federal-provincial relations is to become a reality. Now, the one concrete measure the government seems to be setting forth has to do with its intention of repatriating the Canadian constitution through a formula already approved by all provincial premiers, but which has not yet been ratified by all the provincial legislatures.
As everyone knows, that is a highly controversial issue in Canada, especially in the province of Quebec, and I feel that before proceeding with the adoption of the formula, the government would be well advised to set up immediately a committee of the house which would hear evidence from constitutional experts and submit a report on which the government should base its future action.
As far as Senate reform is concerned, Mr. Speaker, I feel the government should forget about an old proposal which is not even a measure but which has been put forward on many instances. Instead, it should give serious consideration to the reform of the other place by transforming it into a constitutional committee or assembly to which recognized experts in constitutional matters would be appointed.
In my opinion, the Prime Minister could very well call to the Senate, immediately, for instance, Messers. Robert Fowler and Marcel Faribault, the authors of this treatise on the constitution which has already attracted much attention, namely, the book entitled "Ten for One". There is surely room in the upper chamber for people of such a standing as Marcel Faribault and Robert Fowler. I believe that if reforms of that nature were effected, we could restore to that legislative chamber most of the prestige it enjoyed in days gone by.
Mr. Speaker, the government claims that it intends to promote national unity, but let us examine the contradictions which exist in several of its measures: on the one hand,

The Address-Mr. Martineau it says that the rights of the provinces must be respected; and on the other, after it had parliament approve a bill allowing provinces who so wish to opt out from joint programs, it announces new measures which are but new joint programs.
There are, for instance, measures designed to promote rural development, the re-employment and training of workers, social assistance, urban renewal; all those measures will be co-ordinated by a secretariat within the Prime Minister's office, necessarily involving further agreements between the provinces and the central power.
Premier Lesage has already termed those measures as gifts from the Greeks. He said that the province of Quebec was thinking of opting out of those new joint programs.
The government also seems quite pleased with the economic situation. It states its satisfaction at the growth rate of the economy, at the volume of our external trade and at the fewer number of unemployed.
But the vagueness of the measures proposed gives clearly to understand that the government is at the end of its resources, and I rather get the impression that we are drifting, that we are buffeted by forces the government is powerless to control.
And all the time chronic poverty prevails and we cannot solve the problems created by a new technology.
The government adopts a carefree attitude which is not warranted by the economic situation. Unable to act, it is helpless in the face of run-away inflation. It admits that the cost of living, already at its highest in the history of Canada, is still going up; and the only remedy it can find is to freely advise the private sector to practise self-discipline. And yet the government continues to spend at a dizzy rate and controls all sectors of the economy.
The economic council is doing something, of course, since it submitted a report but did the government act on it? There has been no evidence of that until now. Besides, what are the powers of that economic council?
Moreover, I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate the government on its initiative to establish a company of young Canadians, through which the energies and talents of youth can be enlisted toward useful projects both in Canada and abroad. Surely the time has come to fully use that vis viva which is youth.
And talking about young people I should like to insist upon the proposal of establishing

The Address-Mr. Martineau a model parliament in order to celebrate Canada's centennial. That initiative was conceived by William Fair, from Saskatoon, who has been working on it firmly and intelligently for more than two years. It has already received the approval of both the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition.
It is a most interesting proposal, first from the point of view of the representatives sitting on it who will come from the electoral constituencies. The selection will be made on a merit basis and, to be elected, it will not be sufficient to enjoy a certain popularity, but also to have been selected by an impartial jury for one's qualities as speaker and for one's ability to express ideas.
I think that such a parliament should be free from any partisanship. It will discuss matters regarding Canadian unity and the future of confederation. Finally, it is proposed that it sit in this very house during parliamentary recesses, if, there are any in the year of the centennial. It seems that, to prepare adequately this model parliament of young people, the senior parliament, that is our own parliament, could right now get seriously to work on its present task of improving the situation of all Canadians and thus serving the whole people. And, the most important task it has to accomplish, is to restore the dignity of parliament itself.

Mr. Speaker, we are living in Canada through troubled days, and perhaps no single event illustrates more this crisis than the event which occurred in this Chamber last week, when the hon. Member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) crossed the floor, leaving the party to which he had dedicated so many years and all his loyalties and energies to sit as an independent. At the loss of a close friend and associate, I can only express grief and dismay.
As for the reasons which prompted him to make his dramatic decision, after months of soul searching, I speak more in pity than in anger. Here is a man of abiding loyalties, an urbane, civilized, erudite Canadian, with a broad political concept; a man of moderation, quiet and competent and of sound judgment. He is a man who wore lightly the mantle of high office and who enjoys the friendship of so many on all sides of this House. Surely the departure of such a man from the ranks of any party must signify

tragedy for the party that bears this loss. And the tragedy involves much more than just the person or personality of the hon. Member for Three Rivers; it affects all of us. For if there is no room for such a man in the Party, what kind of a man from Quebec or even elsewhere can the Party accommodate?
It has been said that certain elements rejoiced at the departure of the hon. Mem-for Three Rivers from their ranks. I cannot believe that such sentiments, if indeed they were exhibited, could be genuine. For if they were expressed, what happy turn of events, what victory could they possibly portray? If there was a victory for anyone, it was indeed a hollow victory. Was it a victory for the unity of the Party that has lost one of its most loyal supporters? Was it a victory for Canadian unity? Will it inspire confidence throughout the land? Very few people, I believe, not even political adversaries, can rejoice in their heart of hearts, or lightly dismiss the gesture posed by the hon. Member for Three Rivers, or feel anything but deep regret and frustration.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
Yet, the historic Conservative Party, to which I belong, must carry on. Its past role has been honourable and, at times, decisive. Its present potential is great-never has such an opportunity been given to a political group to exercise responsibility, leadership and comprehension-to rise above the petty issues of the day and, by highly asserting leadership and principles, win the allegiance of the great mass of Canadian voters, many of whom remain undecided and even confused at the spectacle daily reported from Parliament.
This is the Party that affirms its faith in "One Canada". Like the Member for Three Rivers, I believe in "One Canada", but it must be a Canada broad enough and generous enough to encompass all of its people and particularly to give to one of its founding races-the people of Quebec-to which I belong, ample scope for the fulfilment of deep yearning for autonomy, and an autonomous cultural destiny. That "One Canada" must aver itself full of understanding for the particular history, traditions and aspirations of the people who were, after the Indians, the first settlers to its shores. It must not be a recognition given grudgingly or with restriction, or on such a narrow basis that the recipient can only stifle or wither away,
April 12, 1965	COMMONS
cast off as a lonely branch on the great Canadian Tree.
The Member for Three Rivers, along with others of his colleagues from Quebec, understands the need for comprehension. On an historic occasion in this Chamber, he spoke loudly against separatism and expressed so eloquently authentic Canadian sentiments in these terms:
We have not been elected to bisect this country but rather to unite it and weld it together and to encourage comprehension, not only between the two great races which compose its population, but also between the different provinces of Canada-
And, again, he said:
I am here to take an interest in the affairs of the country as a whole-I am convinced that Quebec will be strong and prosperous inasmuch as the whole of Canada is strong and prosperous, and vice-versa.
They speak of the need for a strong, central power. I believe in a strong central Government capable of exercising all its attributes under the Constitution, but governing within the limits of this Constitution and dedicated to the spirit of federalism which is nothing if not based on diversity, or a respect for the autonomy of the provinces, and to the recognition of the basic partnership implicit in Confederation.
Some claim for the central Government greater powers in the interest of efficiency and strength. But let me ask them this: Will Canada be more efficient or stronger when one of its founding races feels itself frustrated, unhappy, even alien within its own country, or merely tolerated?
And yet, this is surely where an inflexible policy would lead. What inspiration or leadership, that vaunted leadership based on moderation, which is supposed to be Canada's special trademark and contribution, can this country give to the world if it cannot even solve the problems of unity within its own borders. How, indeed, can it speak with any authority to Africans, Asians and so many other people of the world where racial, cultural, religious and social differences are so much greater and deeper than our own, when it cannot settle differences between two peoples, both the heirs of the same Western civilization, each professing Christianity and who, moreover, have lived side by side for two centuries?
Yet, I am not one of those who harbour feelings of despair. My hope is founded on the firm basis that there are men and women in this Chamber, and in this they reflect the views of the millions across the land whom

The Address-Mr. M. Lessard they represent, who are firmly dedicated toward the attainment of comprehension, mutual understanding and respect as their primary goal and the most noble achievement toward which this Parliament can aim.
Indeed, what else but such a broad, flexible policy can weld together the mosaic of peoples, regional interest, and geographical and economic differences that make up this uncertain entity that is Canada?
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I believe in Canada, and my faith grows stronger when I see these men and women of so many different origins and backgrounds, drawn from all parties, and outside parties, speaking out, appealing for unity and understanding with an authentic Canadian voice-men from English speaking Canada appealing to my own compatriots, telling them of their understanding, indicating their willingness to meet, to parley, to negotiate honourably and openly in an attempt to spell out the needs and ideals of a Canada acceptable to all, men who are willing to innovate to gain this end.
Should not such overtures inspire all of us who are concerned about Canadian unity and the future of Canada to greater efforts in achieving it? This is no time for withdrawal or retrenchment, but rather for greater effort and involvement.
To those who have extended the hand of friendship and understanding, I say, thank you. We will clasp that hand of friendship and will with your help together build the kind of Canada which we know is possible, faithful to all of its past, yet looking toward the future, the sort of Canada wh.ch alone can be a beacon of light in a difficult age.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few brief remarks during the debate on the Speech from the Throne. First of all, I would like to congratulate the mover, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin) and the seconder, the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien), of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne.
