I believe these two young members of the house have made us realize to what extent we can be optimistic as far as the future of our country is concerned.
April 12, 1965

The Address-Mr. M. Lessard
I would also like to congratulate the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) who just resumed his seat, for the magnificent speech he delivered.
It is very difficult to make a speech after such a speaker as the one who preceded me. I cannot help agreeing totally with most of the points in his statement.
It is really a pity that in our country we cannot have men of good will or find some ground for agreement that would allow us to find solutions to the problems with which we are now faced.
Mr. Speaker, we are now discussing the proposals set forth by the government in the Speech from the Throne. Very briefly, I should like to say that, after going over all those proposals, I realize that the government is being quite bold, but also that its program will probably give rise to a great deal of discussion, a lot of negotiations, and could only result in legislation after quite a few lengthy conferences with the various provincial governments.
I am aware that the government has put forward certain measures which concern the activities and responsibilities of provincial governments. Here again, of course, one is tempted to say that the government is intruding into provincial jurisdiction and that such encroachments are unacceptable. For my part, I am inclined to ask certain questions.
Are all those efforts of the government really blameworthy? Not necessarily. So long as the government will agree to discuss with the provincial governments so that the latter might draw such legislation in agreement with the central government, so long as the central government will agree to include in its programs a provision enabling the various provincial governments to opt out when they so desire, while collecting the monies required for the administration costs of those projects, I am sure they will not be bad.
There might be some disadvantages. There will certainly be some. There is probably a positive aspect also and it is this aspect that we should stress. Personally, I see the possibility of an advantage which would be enjoyed throughout our great country. When I speak of uniformity, I mean that some provinces may have special needs because of very special problems. Those provinces will surely want the joint programs to contain provisions respecting their particular situation.
There is another aspect of joint programs which I find advantageous. You may say that

it is a bit selfish on my part but I feel that during the first few years following the establishment of a joint program by the federal government, with the approval of the provinces, there is a certain amount of groping; one has to experiment. Experience is there to prove it. During the first two or three years of operation, the need for several changes comes to light. Distributing the cost of experimenting and implementing such a plan among the whole population of the country is not a bad idea in itself. I think there is no point in each and everyone going about his own experimentation. This is an economical, logical and practical way. When several plans are tried out on a national basis in agreement with provincial governments, from an economical and practical point of view, I think it is not a bad thing provided a province has the opportunity to opt out when it deems it necessary and collect that part of the tax it is entitled to for contracting out of that particular plan.
Mr. Speaker, here is another point I should like to deal with. I was listening earlier to the remarks made by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) on this matter and I could not help but agree with him in this connection, for on several occassions I personally advocated that this was perhaps not the appropriate time in our history to undertake to amend our constitution.
I think some amendments could be made to it but, there again, in the heat of this debate we often hear constitution or so-called constitution experts make ex cathedra statements on what amendments should be made. So far as I am concerned-and I am no expert in this field, I am only a member of the mass of the workers-I am rather inclined to think that it would be wise to put off repatriation of the constitution. I think nobody is strongly objecting to this repatriation but to tie it to a certain amendment formula is another thing.
This matter is so wrapped up in emotions at the present time that I think perhaps it would be better if repatriation of and amendment to our constitution were put off for the time being. There are now in the province of Quebec two agencies which have been set up precisely in order to consider the amendments which should be made to the constitution. Those two organizations have not reported yet.
I think that the Lesage government should be careful and should wait for those agencies to submit their reports before treading a path where it will perhaps be very difficult
April 12, 1965
to turn back. The Laurendeau-Dunton commission does research work and will certainly be in a position to make very appropriate recommendations with respect to the amendments which will have to be made to the constitution. Is this not another good reason to delay the repatriation of the constitution or at least the proposed amendments?
Perhaps it would be good for the central government to consider the setting up of a special commission made up of members of the house and experts from outside who might be selected throughout the country, real specialists who would report. Then we might legislate in the field with a deeper knowledge of the real needs of the time.
There are also in the Speech from the Throne several suggestions respecting measures which the government intends to take in order to solve the problem of unemployment in this country and promote economic development. In two parts of that speech I see things in which I am interested and which I take to heart. At one place, it says:
You wilj be asked to approve the creation of a fund for rural economic development-
Well, Mr. Speaker, personally, I am anxious to see that measure because we have already a fund for economic development. It is only a matter of giving it the extension it requires to face the present needs and use it in order to promote greater industrial development.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
I would think, Mr. Speaker, that that bank is the instrument we are looking for. It has been in existence for a long time and in operation for several years. Therefore, let us provide that organization with the powers it requires, particularly in order to meet the demand of capital for the development of secondary industry in Canada.
The Speech from the Throne also announces that the government is planning legislation to set up a Canadian Development Corporation.
I would say that both projects are almost similar since both have the same goal, namely the expansion of the Canadian economy.
It is obvious that it is only in developing the secondary industry sector that we will eradicate unemployment which is affecting our country and make up the exchange or monetary deficits we have been experiencing for a number of years.
As all other countries, Canada must have as an objective maximum or optimum production, if you like, of consumer goods under any form. We realize that it is impossible to
26S
The Address-Mr. M. Lessard produce everything that we consume, but there is quite a wide margin between what we produce, what we consume and the potential of this country.
Before I conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to a trip I had the opportunity to make recently when the government delegated some members of the special committee on defence as observers during naval exercises held under NATO in the Caribbean Sea.
I should like first of all to commend the R.C.N. officers for the fine welcome they gave us on board. They treated us very well, and I have nothing but praise and thanks for them. I also want to congratulate them on the way they executed the manoeuvres.
However, because there is a qualification- I would even say there are several of them -like the other members of the expedition, I noticed that the living conditions of our men were far from satisfactory, especially on our only carrier, the Bonaventure.
I am not making these remarks to be critical or to condemn anyone in particular. Perish the thought. I merely wish to draw those facts to the attention of hon. members and to show the sailors we visited that we did not fail to notice the problems which existed on the Bonaventure even if we pretended not to see them. Our aircraft carrier is 20 years old. It was assigned a specific task which called for a crew of about 800. However, with the passing of time and with the evolution of Canada's and North America's defence systems, in one word, following our commitments to NATO, we had to entrust the Bonaventure with the new tasks with the result that, today, it has a crew of 1,300 and those men have to live in extremely cramped quarters.
Mr. Speaker, if Canada wishes to continue playing in the major leagues, it should be ready to pay the price; otherwise, it should go back to the minor leagues. By that I mean that if we cannot afford to buy adequate material to provide decent living conditions for our sailors, it would be just as well for us to withdraw from the game and to be content with a field of endeavour which is within our means.
Canada has only one aircraft carrier. The crew of the Bonaventure is very able and I was truly amazed to see how its members behaved in those circumstances.
But if the operation of an aircraft carrier is warranted, we must consider either getting a modern one, or have two so that they could

April 12, 1965

The Address-Mr. M. Lessard spell each other in naval exercises in order that the crew members will not be kept away from their homes as long as they were recently, that is three months.
Moreover, considering the conditions under which those men work, they must be well rested and have a clear mind because they always have to be on the alert.
Mr. Speaker, I can hardly see how men as competent as our Canadian seamen, working in such conditions and having such inadequate facilities to rest, can be in physical condition and have the open mind to perform the task they are required to do.
Men living aboard the Bonaventure or at least some of them, are lacking the bare essentials as far as facilities are concerned.
We are told that the ship will be put in dry dock next year to be completely rebuilt inside. We are even told that some facilities now lacking will be added, but I do not see how the ship could be enlarged, and unless the crew is reduced and the tasks assigned to that ship, made fewer, I think it would be impossible to give this aircraft carrier modern and up-to-date comfort. Facilities on that ship were good for the turn of the century but not for the year 1965.
If it can be justified to lay that ship in dry dock for a period of one year, if it has been found that we could dispense with that aircraft carrier for a year, it can only mean one of two things: either we have no more use for that ship or our defence system will be inadequate for the period during which the ship will be under repairs. Either we will have to abandon that field of activity completely or we will have to rent a similar ship so that its present crew may continue the training it is undergoing at the present time.
I know nothing about the plans of the Department of National Defence in that field. I know it is a very expensive piece of equipment, but if we decided that it was needed then we should secure what is best, a ship on which men can live decently.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with another subject, housing. I see on the other side of the house the hon. Member for Halifax (Mr. Lloyd), formerly mayor of Halifax. I know he is aware of this problem, as are other members of the house, but for the information of my colleagues, I would like to point out that certain members of the Bonaventure crew have expressed major criticisms.


One of these concerned living conditions aboard the ship and the other related to housing in Halifax.
Incidentally, I would like to say that the situation is not something of which the former mayor of Halifax should be proud. In fact, I think he should have brought pressure to bear on his fellow citizens during his mayoralty in order to promote certain developments in his city and provide for reasonable cost housing, where our seamen could live decently.
They are now forced to pay fantastic amounts, sometimes even higher than what hon. members have to pay here in Ottawa. In my opinion, this is a situation which is absolutely unacceptable on the part of the authorities of the city of Halifax and the military authorities of this country.
We should see to it that our Canadian sailors enjoy low rental housing.
Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to the criticisms which were levelled by our sailors, because they came from responsible people. In fact, some criticisms were made by young men who had joined the navy six months, one year or two years ago. I listened to their grievances, but I paid more attention to those which came from the petty officers. The latter play a most important role on board because they are responsible for the efficient and continuous handling of the ship. Most of those petty officers have 10, 15, 18 and even 20 years service in the Canadian navy, and many say that they are ready to quit the navy if they are to remain on that ship.
I feel that, after having invested so much money to train men, it would be simply ridiculous to let them go because we are not supplying them with the proper equipment they need to do the jobs we give them. It is one or the other: either we give them the tools to perform those jobs or we simply eliminate both the jobs and the men.
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is traditional in the Throne Speech debate to congratulate the Mover and the Seconder of the Address in Reply. In following that path tonight I am more than just following tradition. I believe the speeches of the hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin) and the hon. Member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien) are worthy of high commendation.
April 12, 1965

1 would also like to congratulate the hon. Member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) on the speech he delivered in this Chamber tonight. As an English Canadian I thought the points of view he expressed on the problems and tensions within our country were extremely well put, and I would hope he would distribute copies of his speech to his own caucus colleagues because, if the views he holds were more widely held throughout the country, the tensions he was discussing would be largely diminished.
Often in the Throne Speech debate a Government Member gives a scenic tour of his riding and discusses with fulsome praise the items contained in the Speech from the Throne. I am not going to follow that path tonight. We on the back benches on this side of the House have little enough opportunity to get up and talk about issues in which we are particularly interested. If we do so on the estimates, when Opposition members have an opportunity to do that, we are often accused of filibustering our own estimates. It is sufficient I think to say that I, as a supporter of the Government, am delighted with the contents of the Throne Speech. It is a program that offers excitement and challenge. It is a program aimed at many of the fundamental problems existing in the country.
The only description I am going to give of my riding is of one of the boundaries of it. Flowing down the western boundary of my riding is the Don River. It is a colourful river, but unfortunately the colour is generally supplied by the waste dyestuffs that flow out from the industry located along its banks, so that at times the river is red, blue, deep green or purple. The river flows through a valley rich in vegetation, fruit, trees and flowers, but in summertime when you travel up the river you are not able to enjoy the fragrance of the valley. You get the fragrance of the river; and that fragrance, unfortunately, tends to be coloured by the sewage that is flowing down it. In the sunlight, the river sparkles, but it is not the water that is sparkling; it is the pile of foamy detergent that is flowing out into the river. In short, the river is polluted and it is carrying its polluted products down into Lake Ontario. The topic therefore I would like to discuss tonight is the problem of pollution that exists within the Great Lakes area. This may seem like a parochial issue, but I do not think it is. The Great Lakes are important to all Canada. Some 30 million people live in the basin surrounding them. A
The Address-Mr. Hahn third of the Canadian population lives in the area surrounding the Great Lakes.
The Great Lakes were the cause of the tremendous build-up in population and of the tremendous industrial growth in the central part of our country. They offered water for navigation, water for cheap power and, above all, the water that was needed for consumptive purposes, for industry, for human beings, for communities. The abundance of clean water made possible the growth of this part of our country, and I think made possible the industrial growth of our country. As a by-product of these things we have since developed a fishing industry, and we have many recreational uses for water in this area.
Water is an important resource to any country, and we in this country are lucky. We have an abundant supply. Some 50 years ago or so, we never worried about our water supply. We appeared to have it in ample quantity, and we could use it as we liked; but now we are beginning to be concerned about it because we realize that a few generations hence water on this continent will be in short supply.
We who live in Canada, which has a vast supply of this commodity, are particularly lucky, but I think we realize that we must plan now for the future use of this resource, so that when we do need it, it will be available. I think we realize that within our borders we have a commodity that in the future is going to be a valuable export item, something that will be needed by our neighbours to the south, something they will not have that we do have.
The recent problem of water levels on the Great Lakes has highlighted the importance of water supplies to this area. It has produced * the low water levels of the last few years, which affected navigation on the lakes and the production of power on them. I was a member of the committee that was looking into the problem of water levels on the lakes, and, as a result of the preliminary examination we were able to make last session, I think it is pretty clear that the problem of regulation of water levels can be solved, and, in fact, will be solved. I would think that because of the time required to build the works necessary, we shall probably have the cyclical improvement so that the problem will tend to rectify itself, at least temporarily, before we establish a permanent solution. Nevertheless, solved it will be.
In the evidence that was given before that committee one of the things that impressed

April 12. 1985
The Address-Mr. Hahn me was the role of the Federal Government in this problem. We found that many, many Government Agencies, Boards, Commissions and Departments were involved. We asked to have a chart prepared-which we did not get-showing the relationship of all these Federal Government bodies dealing with this problem. I would think that if an organization chart were prepared, showing the Federal Government's role in this area, it would tend to look like a plate of spaghetti. This is a fundamental problem we must bear in mind.
We are not co-ordinated at the Federal level. We have divided responsibility. We have overlapping jurisdiction. We have groups here, there and everywhere, scattered throughout the Federal Government, each doing a little piece, with nobody that I can really see completely responsible for the problem. We talk about these things being co-ordinated, but I am afraid too often coordination in this sense mostly means shifting the responsibility to somebody else, and this is a problem we have to bear in mind.
Out of the work we have done on the problem of water levels has come a realization that the Federal Government must establish clearcut responsibility for the future use of this great resource, dealing first of all with problems of the levels on the lakes, and then looking further ahead at the future requirements on a continental basis, and the future diversions that are going to be necessary- such things as the Grand Canal we have heard about, flowing the waters from the James Bay watershed into the Great Lakes area; and other diversions from the West coast, bringing water down to the Central plain where it can be used.
All these things were discussed before the Committee dealing with the problem of the conservation and regulation of the supply of water. They dealt with the quantity of water available, but what they did not deal with is the quality of water. There is not a great deal of use having a vast quantity of water if the water you have is unusable. Quality for the uses to which we want to put our water is vital.
It is true we can use dirty water for navigation and power production; but if we cannot use it for consumption we cannot support large communities, we cannot support industry, we cannot support population in the surrounding area. It seems to me that we in the Great Lakes area, and also in other parts of the country-but I think primarily in the

Great Lakes area-are now in the process of destroying this great resource that we have. Man in his wisdom is taking this one vital commodity that is essential for the economic survival of this area, and destroying it. If we are not careful we shall not have it in usable condition for much longer. I think everyone is aware that Lakes Erie and Michigan are in almost critical condition now. I think we all know there are 2,000 miles of Lake Erie which no longer support fish life or proper vegetation-algae are spreading everywhere. We are all aware of the decline in the fishing, particularly in Lake Erie. It is suggested that most of the beaches on the shores of Lake Erie and probably Lake Michigan as well, are now unfit for swimming and recreational use. It is known that no raw sewage should be pumped into water to be used for consumption; yet the city of Windsor pumps all its sewage, raw and untreated, into the Detroit river and the city of Welland is still pumping raw sewage into the Welland canal area. There are plans to rectify this situation, but as of this moment the old practice is still being followed.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
Toronto has made vast improvements in its treatment of sewage, but despite this in heavy storms raw sewage is pumped into Lake Ontario off the shores of Toronto, and it is estimated that $300 million would be required to provide completely adequate treatment in Toronto to ensure that no raw sewage would get into the lake.
Dr. Langford, Director of the Great Lakes Institute and associated with the University of Toronto, said recently that the next ten years would be critical. This is about the amount of time we have; if we fail to deal with the problem soon we shall have passed the point of no return. I could go on to give further statistics, but I think it is generally accepted that the Great Lakes are reaching the critical point. We must find a solution to this problem and find it quickly. We, with our ingenuity, will fairly soon I think control water levels in the Great Lakes, and we shall probably spend a billion dollars doing it. Having done that, if we are not careful we shall create a new world wonder; we shall then have what is probably the largest, the most expensive and the best regulated cesspool on earth. It is something we should not allow to happen.
One might think that a solution to the pollution problem would be simple. After all, pollution comes from only three sources-
April 12, 1965

sewage dumped by municipalities, industrial waste, and garbage and sewage discharged from ships. The effect of all this on the water is varied. There is the serious hazard to human life. Fatal and contagious diseases can result from infected water. I should like to read a quotation from a speech given on December 9 last by the Secretary General of the Canadian Council of Resource Ministers on the subject of water pollution. The Secretary General said:
The St. Lawrence Seaway has opened the Great Lakes to 90 per cent of the world's commercial vessels. The increase in pollution by these vessels is a matter of great concern, involving water supplies, recreational beaches and real estate values. The discharge of shipboard sewage near public water supply intakes is of special concern. With ships from all parts of the world entering waters adjacent to public water supply intakes, the chances are greatly enhanced for waterborne disease transmission, and particularly those diseases from other countries which have long been gone from the Canadian scene or never have obtained a foothold here. Few ships plying the Great Lakes have some kind of shipboard waste control device aboard. Most dump their garbage directly into the lakes. It has been estimated the amount reaches between 1,000 and 2,000 tons annually.
This is the first serious effect of polluted water-the danger to health. The second is the effect on the fishing industry and the effect on the fish that live in the waters concerned. The third is the effect on humans of a less dangerous but nevertheless unpleasant nature -water which, because of its appearance or its odour, is unfit for human consumption or use. There is also the effect of polluted water on industrial growth. Industry needs clean water, for use in its processing; it will not locate by a polluted lake. Finally there is the recreational aspect, the effect on the tourist industry, on wildlife and all the other things which make life really worth living.
The solution to this problem should be simple. If the municipalities would stop dumping raw sewage, if industry would stop dumping its waste and if ships and pleasure craft would stop dumping garbage and sewage into the water there would be no problem. But the solution is not as simple as it appears. There is the question of jurisdiction. Pollution is mainly a provincial matter, yet many of the waters about which we are speaking flow from one province to another. The Federal Government is involved to some degree. We have federal legislation now under the Fisheries Act, under the Navigable Waters Protection Act, under the Criminal Code and under the Shipping Act. All these statutes deal in minor ways with the problem of
The Address-Mr. Hahn pollution. Yet within the Departments of Fisheries, Justice, and Transport who really is concerned about water pollution at the federal level? I do not think we know.
In addition to split jurisdiction between the Federal Government and the Provincial Governments the Federal and State Governments of the United States are obviously involved as they, too, share the lakes and are polluting the waters just as badly as we are.
The next major hurdle is probably the highest of all. It is, of course, the amount of money which it will cost all municipalities to treat every bit of sewage before dumping their waste into the lakes. How much will it cost to eradicate sewage and industrial wastes? I do not think we know. I have tried to get figures indicating the total cost of clearing up pollution in the Great Lakes, but so far I have not succeeded. I think it is sufficient to say that the cost would be tremendous. This is the reason why in the past adequate treatment has not been provided.
A final difficulty which has to be overcome is the apathy of the public generally. It is not very glamourous to spend tax dollars on sewage plants. As an example, there is a story that the Mayor of Toronto was recently questioned about a project to build an arts centre in that city. The comment which followed, was this "What do you want,-a centennial sewer?" Well, maybe that is exactly what we do need, but it is not an easy policy to sell.
I should like to consider for a few moments what is being done at the present time to try to tackle this problem. First, there is a meeting scheduled for the spring of 1966-a meeting of the Resource Ministers Council which consists of the ten Provincial Ministers and the Federal Minister involved in this question. The meeting will discuss all aspects of pollution whether of a water, air or land. I think this conference will produce extremely beneficial results in the long range, but I am concerned about its timing. It is scheduled for the spring of 1966 and I am sure it will be at least a year after that before any positive action is taken as a result of that meeting. We would then be in the spring of 1967. Dr. Langford about a year ago said we had ten years left in which to act Three of those years would already be gone.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
I feel that this conference is covering too broad an area. I feel that this conference is going to arrive at long term solutions. But I

April 12, 1965
The Address-Mr. Hahn do not think it is going to move quickly enough to deal with the specific problem which exists in the Great Lakes area.
The second thing I am concerned about is the lack of really good liaison with the United States on this problem. We have some liaison with them now, and I gather that the International Joint Commission issued a preliminary report about a week or so ago dealing with a limited segment of the pollution in the lakes area. But again we have not really got down to a hard bargaining position with the United States, trying to launch a major campaign to clean up the Great Lakes area. We are doing a bit of research on the problem, but the amount of research being done, particularly by the Great Lakes Institute, is woefully inadequate. The amount of money they are allocated by the Federal and Provincial Governments in relation to the size of the problem is minute, and we have a great deal more to do in this area.
The Province of Ontario has, I think, done a major job in the last few years with their part of the problem. In 1956 they established the Ontario Water Resources Commission. Within that Commission they have now coordinated their efforts, so there is one place in the Province of Ontario to which you go, knowing that there is where the responsibility lies. As a result of this co-ordinated effort they have recently announced, within the last few weeks, that they are embarking upon a five-year program, setting limits for industry so that the industry around the Province will stop polluting its waters. They are going to give industry five years to achieve this goal. I think this is a very practical, useful step; the only concern I have is whether industry will be able within this five-year period to finance the work necessary to stop its pollution.
The Federal Government is offering assistance to municipalities through the National Housing Act, to build sewage treatment plants. This too is beneficial, but again I raise the question, is it enough? Is this going to get the job done?
Finally, there is a certain amount of work being done now in the field of educating the public. I think particularly of the series of articles which ran during the last week or so in the Toronto Telegram outlining the problem of water pollution. I think this is a very necessary step, and it is something which has to be done on a much wider scale so that the public at large, who are going to have to raise the tax money to cure the problem,

are aware of the need for expenditures in this area.
The steps which have been taken thus far are all practical, useful steps. They are all moving in the right direction. They are all working toward a co-ordinated water policy for the country. They are working toward eventual solution of regulation of the Great Lakes. They are working toward eventual elimination of the pollution problem. But again I am concerned that they are too slow, on too broad a front and they are not dealing specifically enough and quickly enough with this prime problem.
I think there are a number of things that could and should be done right away. I think that the principle we have to follow, if we are going to save this water resource is, first of all, to put our own house in order in this country. We must make sure we are doing what needs to be done, and then having done that we can sit down with the United States government and say:	"Look
this is the effort that we are putting forth to clean up our side of the lake; it is now on your plate to handle your problem and clean up your side". I think that if we were able to sit down and bargain on that basis we could get full co-operation from the other side.
In order to put our house in order we have several things to do. First of all, we have to establish clearly and distinctly who is responsible at the Federal level, and what is the organization at the Federal level that will cut out this problem of shifting responsibility from one side to another. We must tie in definitely and clearly responsibility, with an ability to act in the field of water resources. Having done that, I think then we should get together with the Provincial Government, and in this case it is relatively easy because there is only one province directly concerned, the Province of Ontario. Having got together with the Province of Ontario I think it would be quite easy to work out with them a joint program.
First of all, we have to look at the preventive legislation which is on the books and see what legislative changes are necessary. I think we should arrive at an estimate of cost both to the municipalities and industry to clean up our side of the lakes. Having arrived at an estimate of cost, we then have to see who is going to pay the cost and how it is going to be financed.
There are several means of financing available. The sewage treatment plants needed
April 12. 1965

by municipalities are essentially a municipal responsibility, and I think that the extension of low cost loans from the Federal Government might induce the municipalities to proceed at a much faster rate. As far as industry is concerned I think it might well make it possible for industries to do the job if they were to be offered accelerated depreciation, fast write-offs on the special plant and equipment they would need in order to treat their waste products, before they dump them into the waters. I think that between these two levels of government public information must be stepped up so that when it comes to a choice between an arts centre and a sewer, the choice is not as ludicrous as it seems, and perhaps the right choice may be not an arts centre but a sewer. I think the public have at least to be able to make an intelligent discrimination when they are offered choices of this type.
We must also look at the laws respecting navigation of the lakes, to see whether we should not change our laws and prevent our own ships and foreign ships from polluting our waters. We must step up the grants that we are giving in the field of research so that we can know much more than we know now how much pollution the lakes can take, what type of pollution the lakes can stand. They can stand certain types of chemicals, and certain types they cannot stand. We do not know nearly enough about this, so we must increase the research in this area.
Finally, in the research area there is a great deal which might be done to lower the cost of treating sewage, to lower the cost of treating industrial wastes. I think that research into this effort would produce very beneficial results. If we can discuss this whole range of topics and reach agreement with the province on solutions to these problems, then we are in a position to go to the United States with our program laid out and see whether we cannot get them to do the same thing on their side of the border. If we are able to do this-and I think it imperative that we do this-we can stop the destruction of the Great Lakes and we can stop the waste of this resource that we are now spoiling. If we do not do this, Mr. Speaker, and if we do not do it quickly, I am afraid that the gloomy predictions of Dr. Langford and others might well come true, and we in our great wisdom may well succeed in destroying an essential resource, essential not only to Central Canada but to the economy of the whole country.
The Address-Mr. A. C. Cadieu

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this Throne Speech Debate it gives me a great deal of pleasure to congratulate the hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin) and the hon. Member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien) on the very efficient manner in which they performed their task. However, Mr. Speaker, I cannot say that the Speech from the Throne means very much to the people in the constituency of Meadow Lake.
I note there is a section of the Speech dealing with the abolition of poverty.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
I listened with a great deal of interest to the Throne Speech Debate and I noted that the Liberal Government has advocated an attack on poverty. Liberal Governments down though the years have created poverty by their lack of development and organization and their lack of assistance to those early settlers who pushed forth into these unlimited yet undeveloped areas. This same Government which has enunciated an attack on poverty, only a few days before the Throne Speech voted against an amendment to give $25 per month to that old age group 65 years to 70 years, and voted against an increase in pensions payable to individuals 70 years and over to $100 a month. Such an increase in pensions and a lowering of the age requirement would in itself have provided a great deal of assistance in the fight against poverty throughout this country.
The Meadow Lake constituency encompasses a vast area and takes in about 40 per cent of the area of the Province of Saskatchewan. It does not represent that percentage of the population, but the population of that area has dwindled since the Liberal Government took office. No one can predict with any certainty what will happen to the Meadow Lake constituency after redistribution.
I should like this evening to draw the attention of this House to several problems of concern to many of the people in my constituency. Perhaps to begin with I should refer to proposed rail line abandonments. Our memories reach back to years when the pioneers moved into this area, and what took place when the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. operated what they called Colonization Settlement Boards which, in many cases, preceded the settlers in the search for arable lands, and then returned with large placards advertising these fine fertile areas they had discovered, in an attempt to encourage people to go in and settle these productive
April 12, 1965

The Address-Mr. A. C. Cadieu lands. A great many war veterans returning from overseas, having fought over there on behalf of this country, were encouraged to go into these areas and to develop them. They were assured that rail line surveys had been made and that these lines would be constructed. Provincial Governments offered large tracts of land for homesteading purposes. People moved in by the hundreds and thousands, to settle these vast areas in the Meadow Lake constituency.
These pioneers were led down the garden path by the railway companies and the various Governments. The C.P.R., for instance, in collusion with others, was allowed to mislead these people. In that area at the south end of my constituency, where I live, the C.N.R. surveyed a rail line and brought in settlers. The C.P.R. realized that this was a prosperous area and also looked at the area with some prospect of moving in. The C.P.R. was granted running rights over the C.N.R. track from Prince Albert to Debden, a distance of some 90 miles built an additional 90 miles and were allowed to reap the wealth of this area. No assurance or guarantee was required of that company that it would push on further. Why were they allowed these running rights without the assurance that they would continue the line? Surely those settlers in the areas of Goodsoil and Pierce-land could expect that the C.P.R. would continue this line in return for running rights. These officials should have been compelled to continue this line. Many of the people in this area have to haul their farm produce to Meadow Lake, the nearest rail point, and in some cases over 65 miles. I suggest these people were betrayed.
Why has the C.N.R. not been compelled to build a line between Frenchman Butte and Heinsburg, Alberta, thus creating a direct line from Prince Albert and North Battle-ford and on into northern Alberta? Such a line would service all the people on the north side of the Saskatchewan River. This would mean a direct line link along the natural barrier of the North Saskatchewan River into Alberta. Why was the C.N.R. not compelled to build this line, closing the gap over a 38-mile area?
I am not one to advocate the nationalization of the C.P.R., as I believe in private enterprise, but I believe that if two farmers who lived side by side found that their holdings were not sufficient to provide both with a decent standard of living, one would sell out to the other. I think all the rollingstock

in this area should be operated by one railway company concentrating its efforts on providing the service these people can justifiably expect. The C.N.R. pioneered this part of the country and should have the opportunity of operating this service. It should have been incumbent upon the Federal Government to see that this company provided the services warranted by the area and its development. I am sure when one looks at the fine farm towns that have sprung up in this area, the mineral resources which have not been tapped and the number of settlers who have moved in and developed the country, he can only come to the conclusion that these people have been deceived. Their rail line was abandoned before it was ever completed. If the gap were completed from Frenchman Butte to Heinsburg, Alberta, I am sure it would be a rail line that would pay dividends. One should look at its geographical location on the north side of the North Saskatchewan River.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Look at some of the losing propositions in which the C.N.R. has invested and which the taxpayers have had to subsidize. There are so many that I could go on at great length. Take their adventure into the provision of hotel accommodation. I think they would have been well advised to leave the hotel business to private enterprise. The loss on the Chateau Laurier hotel alone would pay in a very short time for the bridging of the gap between Frenchman Butte and Heinsburg, Alberta, and I am sure it would do a great deal more for the development that this country needs than the Chateau Laurier hotel is doing for the welfare of the country.
So far as this problem is concerned, I think it is the duty of this Government or any government of the country to get down to straight facts and sound business principles, and to see to it that before the railway companies are allowed to talk about rail line abandonment they must lay their cards on the table and produce facts. This is particularly so in the case of the Government owned railway, and the Government should see to it that it does the things by way of development which are required of it.
When one looks at the Town of Meadow Lake he sees the largest grain storage facilities of any town in the Province of Saskatchewan. One can see that the products and the development are there. We do not know what they are paying to maintain 90 miles
April 12, 1965

of track in order to reap the benefit of this whole country, but we do know that both railway companies are complaining that they are not making any money on these lines. Let them get together on their books and see where the real trouble lies, before they are allowed to talk about coming in and tearing up the tracks.
Let us look at some of the blunders that were made by the railway companies. Let us look at some of the miles of grade they built on which they never laid the track. I am speaking now of the miles of grading they did from St. Walburg up through to Pierce-land on which they never laid any track, whereas only a few miles away they should have linked up the gap between Heinsburg and Frenchman Butte, and they overlooked this completely.
I should like to speak for a few minutes about another grievance in my constituency about which quite a few people are concerned, and I think they have a right to be concerned.
I refer to the Cold Lake bombing range. The land was taken over by the former Liberal Government to establish a bombing range at Cold Lake, and when settlement was first made early in the summer of 1957 a group of settlers in the area were discriminated against. I am speaking now of the Metis people in the Canoe Lake, Beauval and tie a la Crosse areas. They were tricked in the settlement that was made and were not paid on the same basis as other groups or individuals in the area.
When this was drawn to my attention in 1958 I set about to try to get these people further consideration. I was successful in doing this under the former government. While the payment was not made equal to the settlement received by the other groups, I was encouraged to believe that the payments would be brought up to an equal basis. Our Government was defeated early in 1963, but when I later approached the Associate Minister of National Defence of the present Government and presented the plight of these people to him, any further payment was completely rejected. I was told by the Minister that no further settlement would be made.
I think it was a shame that the Liberal Government of 1957 took advantage of these people. Later the Conservative Government, under the leadership of the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), proved that there was a discrepancy in the settlement with these people. We made a further payment to them and planned to bring them

The Address-Mr. A. C. Cadieu up in line with other groups that had been affected by the bombing range.
I think the present Government had a responsibility to complete this settlement, and I do not intend to let them forget this injustice so easily. It is quite possible that some people will think that these people were well paid, but when a government takes away the livelihood of people and does nothing to rehabilitate them and their families, there certainly should be no discrepancy. All groups or individuals should be paid on an equal basis. The livelihood of these people was taken away from them because of this bombing range. Their forefathers came to this area and lived by fishing, trapping and hunting in the area. I think the Government of the day has a responsibility and these people certainly should have been rehabilitated in some other way, and not by paying them a certain amount of money on the eve of an election and taking away their livelihood from them. I think this was a shame. I am receiving letters every day about this matter and I do not think the Government has any right to say to these people: We are going to take away your livelihood from you; you will have to go on living there in your shacks and cabins and all we will pay you is a measly token.
The Indian Affairs Branch looked after the Indian population and they received a considerably different settlement from that given the Metis. I think it is the duty of the Government to open up this file and take a good look at it. We can easily go through the file and find out where the discrepancy lies, and give these people the justice to which they are entitled.
There is another matter which I brought up earlier. It has gone by the boards now and nothing can be done about it, but I think it is a shame. I am referring to the destruction of the mid-Canada radar line. How secret this was kept. I was the Member for that constituency and I was not told a single thing about it. I saw an article which said, I believe, that the Saskatchewan Government was notified, but did nothing about it because when the time was ripe for offering suggestions the Provincial Minister, who did not realize what this meant to northern Canada, was misled. This radar line across the vast northland of Canada cost millions of dollars and it was ordered to be scrapped. Crews were hired to go in, cut the guywires, and let the installations go to waste. They were told to wreck fine cabins and other such accom-
278	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. A. C. Cadieu modation for the caretakers, and to destroy all the equipment.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
As soon as word leaked out of the possible destruction of these towers, the Minister was questioned. He wanted to remain ignorant of the fact. He let on it was too late, then, but we found out 15 hours before these radar towers were to be destroyed. We questioned the Minister and he had received word that the C.B.C. was interested. He indicated that word of their interest had been received too late, but it was 15 hours before these towers were to be destroyed. You can declare war in a quarter of that time. With modern communications systems, this destruction could have been stopped. If the C.B.C. were interested, there was a possibility of bringing radio and perhaps even television into this vast area of the northland. One only has to think of the many isolated people, the thousands of young people in that area, to realize the benefit that might have been derived from such a development. However, nothing was done to stop this destruction.
This Government knew, and the Minister knew that there were crews stationed at these towers. He came out with the weak excuse that the towers were dangerous to airplanes flying in the area. Very few airplanes fly in the area, but the towers were equipped with beacon lights. We had the equipment and we even had the fuel to keep these lights going for the next ten years. This was a weak excuse. This destruction had to take place. These are some of the things that make one wonder. As I say, this destruction could have been stopped because the lighting equipment was there and the caretaker was there. There was no danger to airplanes. The C.B.C. could have been given time to study the possibilities of these towers which were built throughout this country at great cost, whether we paid for them or the United States government paid for them. If the C.B.C. was interested, then God knows they spend enough money, and in the interests of economy we should have given them an opportunity to study the matter.
I should like to speak for a few moments about northern development. During the past few days I received a copy of a speech, as I suppose many other hon. Members did, from a C.C.F. member of the Saskatchewan Legislature. He was giving his version of northern development. He advocated that a vast part of the Northwest Territories adjacent to northern Saskatchewan be included in that

DEBATES	April 12. 1965
Province. I am sure the people of the Northwest Territories, when they look at the development that has taken place in Saskatchewan during the last 20 years under a C.C.F. government, would have little desire to be linked up with that Province. I could not blame them. When one looks at the development that has taken place in northern Saskatchewan under a C.C.F. government for the last 20 years and a Liberal government for 30 years, he finds that all that has been done has been the removal of minerals during wartime. Little has been done since.
The Leader of the Conservative Party in Saskatchewan proposed the construction of a rail line from Meadow Lake to Hudson Bay. This was no pipe dream. This is an area which has a vast potential in timber, minerals and fish products. I believe the Federal Government should take a good look at this proposal. We built the Pine Point Railway in Alberta and now that Provincial Government is proposing to build another rail line to develop the northern part of the province. Yes, there is great need for development of the northland. A number of years ago some of the businessmen in Meadow Lake, who could get no action from the Government, took it upon themselves to blaze a winter road through to Lake Athabasca in order that some of this freight that was going into Uranium City could go in through northern Saskatchewan, rather than through Alberta. They proved the feasibility of such a road. They blazed the road through and took freight in through Lake Athabasca across to Uranium City.
Under the former Government, and the Provincial Government of Saskatchewan, we started a winter access road. We built it as far as La Loche. When one looks at the terrain beyond that point, he cannot see any reason why this project should be stopped at La Loche. It should be continued to Lake Athabasca, then down to Stony Rapids where it could go into the Northwest Territories. I think Mr. Petersen, the Leader of the Conservative Party in Saskatchewan, had a brilliant idea when he proposed the construction of a railroad from northern Saskatchewan to Hudson Bay.
There is an unlimited potential for development in northern Saskatchewan, especially when one thinks of the mineral resources north of Buffalo Narrows such as iron and copper. There is a vast population in this area with nothing to do; there is nothing for them in the future, except socialist aid. Since this Government took office not
April 12, 1965	COMMONS
one move has been made to continue the winter access roads or to undertake any developmental projects. There is a great need, for instance, for a bridge at Buffalo Narrows where there was a tragic accident last winter. These are developments which, I am sure, would pay great dividends. I believe it is the duty of this Government to take a good look at the possibilities of northern development and to continue the work which was started by the former Government.
I recall so well that when I was elected there were hundreds of Indian boys and girls who did not have a school to attend. During the campaign of 1963 I could brag that not one Indian boy or girl was unable to attend school. We built wharves and we assisted the Provincial Government in the construction of winter access roads. Today we find everything at a standstill, the same sort of standstill we went through for 20 years under a Liberal regime. Why can these people not take an honest-to-God look at a country that has so much potential, and then let us get down to our northern development policy that was started under the Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker?
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate very warmly the mover (Mr. Cashin) and the seconder (Mr. Chretien) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
They discharged extremely well one of the most difficult tasks; did they not succeed in putting a new face on their old party?
Tradition was well served and the party's honour is safe.
Some criticism was most constructive, in particular what the hon. member for Vil-leneuve (Mr. Caouette), the leader of our party, the Ralliement Creditiste, had to say. I think everyone will agree that the first two days of debate were very interesting and useful to the house.
During those days every party had the opportunity to speak on behalf of its own group, and all members delivered well prepared and fine speeches.
On subsequent days, however, speakers were inclined to repeat simply the main ideas put forward by their first spokesman. We would have been ready to vote after the first stage; but since an eight-day throne speech debate is provided under the standing orders, members must speak during those
DEBATES	279
The Address-Mr. Gauthier eight days. We must vie with one another at all costs.
I shall try as much as possible not to repeat the remarks already put on the record, so as to spare you the torture of the drop of water.
As a matter of fact, since the beginning, we have been listening unconcerned and helplessly to a series of speakers and to what avail? Let us vote on the document read to us so that we can get on with it.
It is unthinkable that no government over the past 97 years felt the need to improve the beginning period of a session. Has it ever occurred to anyone that it was urgent to shorten this tedious period? Will an end ever be put to all these repetitions which are such a waste of the time of the house?
Governing, Mr. Speaker, is not a question of days or hours but a question of judgment.
Is there anything more painful than to drink even though one is no longer thirsty? And yet that is what we are asking the members of the house to do at the opening of each session.
The first time I attended this wordy battle, I thought it was to harden new members; such a performance on the part of adults is inadmissible because in a meeting intelligent men should have enough sense to keep quiet when they have nothing to say; however, timidity did not prevent some remarks to be made.
Today, at the opening of my third session, I notice a repetition of this comedy because, I am told, it is done in England. Mr. Speaker, you will agree with me that there is a limit to everything. We have today the absolute proof that our standing orders are outmoded.
I welcome this proposal to amend those dusty standing orders and I would even ask the Prime Minister to make it the first item of business.
Concerning this famous program containing the future business of the house, I would like to ask those in charge to establish a list of priorities for all those items and that it be scrupulously respected so that we may know what work we will be undertaking in the months to come.
Nothing is more disarming for opposition members not to know what tomorrow holds in store for them.
We are given notice of the business of the house for the next day only at ten o'clock in the evening while it is time to go to bed, and sometimes we are notified the same day. How can we proceed rapidly when we have not
April 12, 1965

The Address-Mr. Gauthier been informed of the subject matter to be debated.
The last session, Mr. Speaker, was an unprecedented monument built to the painful memory of a government groping ceaselessly to find its way.
Is it due to the incompetence of its leaders? Is it due to the lack of experience of some members of the cabinet? Is it due to this internal disorder brought about by this wave of scandals that unfurled on key members of the administration and reached the rank of the most humble members?
Is it due to a hidden, extra-governmental influence, by which government itself is outstripped?
Who is the master in your house? Is it the private secretaries? The technicians or officialdom?
To all those questions, only the party in office holds the answers. It is certainly not compelled to reveal them publicly, although the Prime Minister has made unquestioned efforts in order to set afloat his ship which dangerously keels over.
However, I am afraid the crew is too contaminated.
At all events, the Prime Minister will certainly have his hands full with his own party, his own government.
That is why I advise him not to complicate his position by interfering with the neighbour's business, namely the provinces.
There is an old saying: "Grasp all, lose all".
So I say to the Prime Minister that if he insists on continuing his illegal interference in fields exclusively reserved to the provinces, he will run with closed eyes to disappointments much more bitter than those he has known in the last few months, while leading his group of adventurers.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
We are, therefore, warning the Prime Minister and his cabinet that eight or ten items contained in the Speech from the Throne constitute a revolting change of policy toward the provinces and a direct insult to the province of Quebec where I live.
A few days ago the Prime Minister, through legislation passed here, offered the provinces the option to take over certain joint programs into which the federal government had wormed its way, but today, the same government is suggesting the establishment of further joint programs.
It is truly the game of old-line governments who hand $1 to the provinces so as to

better take $10 away from them. And this is what has always been called treating the provinces fairly.
When will you stop laughing at the people?
Do you take all Canadians for complete morons or are you that irresponsible?
When Quebec asks the federal government to get out of those fields of taxation, that does not mean the federal government should merely change place or position, but that it should disappear from Quebec's territory and mind its own business in Ottawa. Do I make myself clear enough with those simple words?
Will the Liberal government finally be intelligent enough to learn to respect provincial rights?
Back home, we say "like father like son". A government that shows so little respect for other people's property is setting a very poor example to the other members of the family, as we can judge by what is happening within the Liberal party.
The Prime Minister knows, better than anyone else, that education, agriculture, health, natural resources are fields exclusively reserved to the provinces. He is, therefore, the less excusable for interfering with such offhandedness in the business of the Quebec government. One should, therefore, not wonder anymore at the beginning of a quite legitimate revolt among the very leaders of Quebec.
As evidence, the last warnings given by Mr. Jean Lesage to the federal government that he will not tolerate that what was given by the right hand should be taken back by the left hand. Such action is hypocrisy, and nothing more, and it is not honest.
Consequently, we demand from the Liberal government the cancellation of these items, and I beg all my Liberal fellow citizens, if they still have the right to speak in their party, to take every possible means to call their leaders to reason.
If we scan quickly the speech from the throne, what is obvious is the socialistic legislation advocated by an ultra-centralizing government.
While 60 per cent of the 30 items of the speech from the throne are only a jumble of rehashed proposals, repetitions, aiming only at one goal, "to increase the volume", the end of this deluge of words ends on a discovery: war against poverty.
Do you know at least that since the dawn of history associations and governments everywhere have been fighting against poverty? As you can see, yours is not exactly a new idea.
April 12, 1965

However, what you seem to forget more than anything else is that in order to help, you have to give not take.
What is lacking today is purchasing power. It is not by increasing contributions and taxes that you will restore the purchasing power that the labour classes need for their economic recovery.
Indeed, we notice that the government has failed to put forward a single measure to fill that gap, which is the same as saying that the most remarkable aspect of the speech from the throne is its shortcomings.
It is not by setting up commissions of inquiry to provide employment for those who served the party well but by launching concrete reforms which will directly affect the working class that you will solve the existing problem.
That is why we, of the Ralliement Credi-tiste, request an immediate increase in family allowances, which have been forgotten since 1945.
We also request that income tax exemptions be raised to $2,500 for single persons and to $5,000 for married couples, with an additional exemption of $600 for each child.
We shall continue to fight so that our senior citizens receive $100 per month at the age of 60, without a means test, in order to do away once and for all with this army of inquisitive patronage agents who continuously harass our old people.
Everyone agrees that the Unemployment Insurance Act is unfair, especially with respect to farmers. The present act discriminates against many workers.
When will the government finally present the bill amending this famous act, and for which we have been waiting so patiently? When will it stop penalizing the unemployed workers instead of giving them what they are entitled to, for which they paid and for which they were taxed?
The present act is only a penalizing system. A family head is penalized because he forgot to return his card every fortnight; he is penalized because he left his employer who was exploiting him; he is penalized because he was sick; penalized for having refused a job which was too far away; penalized for having worked two days away from his job where he was working for three months, and his 24 stamps were even withdrawn from him; penalized for reporting to the office half an hour after the time set by the manager. A farmer is penalized because he owns a farm; for having kept five dairy cows which
The Address-Mr. Klein yield nothing in winter; penalized under section 59 (b), (c), (d); penalized under sections 146, 60, 62, 64, 65, 66; always penalized but taxed from the very first hour of work.
The present government has the nasty habit of grabbing everything it can, of taxing everything to the limit and giving back only what it wants.
That is what the people find revolting. When will Canada have a government which will govern in the interests of the people? When the people leam to elect their representatives instead of having them elected by the financiers. It will then rest with the people to keep their eyes open in the future to elect their own members of parliament.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to extend my very warm congratulations to the mover of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne (Mr. Cashin) and to the seconder (Mr. Chretien) for their very appropriate speeches.

I wish to add that both these young men are splendid examples of their races and both are destined some day, I believe, to achieve great things because they are eminently qualified to occupy the highest positions in this land.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
I should like to speak tonight about the outcry which emanates from the Soviet Union and Red China whenever any action is undertaken by the Western allies or by the United States, whether it be in the Congo, Viet Nam, South Korea, when the West is constantly accused of being imperialistic. So I thought I would like to look at the record- and since 1945 the record of the number of countries which have achieved independence and the populations involved staggers the imagination.
I should like to put on the record the countries that have achieved independence since 1945. They are: Algeria, the Kingdom of Burundi, Burma, the Federal Republic of Cameroon, Cambodia, the Republic of Central Africa, Ceylon, the Republic of Chad, Cyprus, the Republic of Congo, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Dahomey, Gabon, Gambia, Ghana, Guinea, India, Indonesia, Ivory Coast, Jamaica, Kenya, Republic of South Korea, Malagasy Republic, Malawi, formerly Nyasaland, Mali, Malaysia, Malta, Mauritania, Morocco, Nigeria, Pakistan, the Phillipines, Rwanda, Senegal, Sierra Leone,

April 12, 1965
The Address-Mr. Klein Somali Republic, Sudan, Tanzania, Togo, Tunisia, Trinidad and Tobago, Uganda, Republic of the Upper Volta, Zambia, Israel, Lagos and the Republic of Viet Nam. The total number of countries which have gained their independence since 1945 is 49. A population of 948 million people is involved and 11,500,000 square miles of territory has been liberated.
As opposed to this Western record we have to ask ourselves the question: Where is Latvia, where is Estonia and where is Lithuania? Under the domination of the Soviet Union and Red China since the war are the countries of Bulgaria, Rumania, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, East Germany, Albania, Yugoslavia, Korea, the Republic of North Viet Nam, Tibet-Tibet is an example of what can be expected if United States troops withdraw from South Viet Nam-Cuba and Mongolia. The Western alliance has not taken a single mile of territory belonging to any other country since 1945.
The struggle in North Viet Nam and South Viet Nam, Mr. Speaker, is not the struggle between the north and the south any more than was the struggle in North Korea and South Korea. The struggle in North Viet Nam and South Viet Nam is the struggle between the East and West. I remember, as do many members in this House, when France fell and England stood alone, the isolationist policy which existed at that time in the United States. I remember the United States First Party. I remember the United States Ambassador to the court of St. James reporting to the United States Government not to intervene in the war because Hitler was going to win. I cannot help but feel that instead of having the isolationist policy which the United States had in 1940 if the United States had intervened or warned Hitler in 1933 when he crossed the Rhine that he was going to have to deal with the United States, perhaps the second world war would have been averted.
When people say that the United States should get out of South Viet Nam because they have no business in South Viet Nam, I cannot help but think back to the time of the Hungarian revolution in 1956 or 1957-I do not recall the exact time-when people pleaded with the United States to go into Hungary during the three days the revolution took place. If United States troops were in Hungary tonight, Hungary would be free. If United States troops were in Poland tonight, Poland would be free. Wherever United States troops are there is also to be found freedom.
IMr. Klein.]
As we are all aware, there have been renewed tensions in the Middle East, and while the Soviet Union makes an appeal to peace loving nations in the world to bring pressure on the United States in South Viet Nam, she is doing more to create problems in the world than any other nation by arming the Middle East. There have been renewed tensions in the Middle East, and the danger of a renewed outbreak of fighting cannot be absolutely excluded. I noticed in the press that despite the dominant preoccupation with the dangerous situation in Viet Nam the council of NATO has found the situation in the Middle East sufficiently dangerous as to merit its consideration last week. The most inflammable element in that situation is the build-up of armaments, on the one hand by the Arab States which say openly they are determined to destroy their neighbour Israel, and on the other hand by Israel, which feels her existence is under permanent threat and who is making desperate efforts to acquire military material by way of a deterrent. I feel it would be correct to say that if this arms race can be halted on both sides the dangerous situation might decrease. What is the use of discussing disarmament between the great powers if the Soviet Union continues to pour war materiels into the Middle East? It seems to me it would make better sense to take a first step toward disarmament, which does not involve the question of how the great powers should disarm, but would involve a pledge on the part of the great powers not to supply danger areas with arms, tanks, guns and planes.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
Another step which should be taken before disarmament can be discussed, is a step to obtain agreement on the part of the great powers in respect of boundaries of all countries in the world, because as long as boundaries are in dispute there can never be disarmament. Perhaps such an agreement would lend itself to a more calm period, and once any danger of military intervention was obviated substantive political problems in the Middle East might improve, even though this is bound to be a slow and gradual process.
There is no denial of the fact that the Soviet Union represents the major factor regarding a build-up in arms at least on the Arab side through a continuous, uncontrolled and unlimited supply of materiel to the United Arab Republic and other Arab countries. Surely the Soviet Union is as interested as
April 12, 1965	COMMONS
are we and our allies in preventing a new conflagration in that delicate part of the world.
Therefore, I would request the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) to consider approaches to the Soviet Union through diplomatic channels and, if possible, in concert with our allies in an attempt to find out whether something can be done by agreement with the purpose of putting a lid on the armament race which, if it continues unchecked, is almost bound to sooner or later cause further military clashes.
I do not believe that a third world war will come, as the result of a direct attack by one major party on another, but a third major war could come as the result of a smaller war in a danger area such as the Middle East or Viet Nam.
Another matter which I should like to commend to the attention of the Government, again in terms of diplomatic dialogue with the Soviet Union, is the problem facing religious and ethnic minorities inside the Soviet Union, particularly that of the Jewish community there which numbers close to three million. A process continues, by which the Soviet authorities are gradually but systematically stifling the possibility for Jewish people there, who wish to do so, of practising their religious beliefs and obtaining the means for observance of the dietary and other religious practices, and to express their specific culture by way of books, newspapers and language studies.
Recently we had an example in this country of two individuals applying for citizenship being denied citizenship because they did not believe in religion. Our Government is now financing their case before the courts in order to preserve what we think is their right. This is exactly opposite to the situation which exists in the Soviet Union.
This strangulation of religious and cultural life has been causing great anxiety to the Jewish people here in Canada, as well as to Jews everywhere in the world, and I would request the Government to seek every opportunity to explain to the Soviet Union that this anxiety is shared by humanitarian opinions in this and other countries. Assuming that the Soviet Union desires to build friendship with our country, not only in the sphere of Government relations but also in the sphere of wider public relations, they should realize that this policy which is directed particularly at this moment against the Jewish
DEBATES	283
The Address-Mr. J. H. Horner community is not only wrong in itself but is bound to militate against their efforts to create a better image of the Soviet Union in the world.
In this connection there exists a problem in respect of reunification of families torn apart by World War II. Many of my constituents and I myself have been most gratified to note that our Government has continued its efforts to persuade the Soviet Government to alleviate individual suffering by permitting members of broken families to join their dear ones here in Canada and in other countries, and I sincerely hope that these efforts will bear fruit.
In conclusion, I should like to point out one specific thing. We in this country are going to debate very shortly the abolition of the death penalty. I believe that the tenor of this House favours the abolition of the death penalty, but while we are debating that question the Soviet Union still maintains the death penalty for economic crimes. I hope the debates which take place in this House on the abolition of capital punishment will be forwarded to the Soviet Union, so that they might know how Canada feels in this regard and how a democracy operates, and that while the death penalty for economic crimes existed perhaps in the 17th and 18th centuries, it has no place in the 20th century.
