speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak during this debate on the Throne Speech. Like many other farmers I listened closely to the Throne Speech for some indication of hope for the farming industry. It contained a great deal of reference to poverty, yet in only one paragraph did it touch upon farm economy. Nowhere in that Speech was there set out any concrete or specific suggestion as to what will specifically be done in this regard.
The Throne Speech contained some reference to aid to uneconomical farms and assistance for small farmers, through ARDA and other measures, to put the agricultural industry on an economic basis, as they term it. Let us consider quickly the position in which farmers find themselves today. In doing so we must remember that the price of wheat dropped last fall approximately 18 cents per bushel. We must also remember that beef prices fell three cents per pound, pork prices were down and that there was general concern in respect of dairy products, and prices of other farm products, including eggs. We have recently heard a good deal of talk about farmers marching on Ottawa. This must drive
April 12, 1965

The Address-Mr. J. H. Horner home to the Government that there is a great deal of fear and unrest among the farming population today. There is a lot of talk about how the small farmer has to be moved so as to make room for the big farmer. How small is small? The large farmer today may be a small farmer tomorrow. This is the concern of the agricultural industry as I see it.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Surely as legislators we must realize that for a farmer to make a success of farming he must love the occupation. He must love the land, he must love animals, and he must love the outdoor life and the freedom to do what he wants to do when he wants to do it. I think that basically farmers do like farming for these four reasons.
But what is the trend today? The farmers are saying: Where are we going? Last fall the farmers faced a general decline in farm prices. They are not really desperate yet, but they are concerned. What is the trend today? What does the future hold for the farmer? In the United States, President Johnson is talking about the great society. What does the great society of Canada hold for farmers today? The fact is that their numbers will become smaller and smaller, their land larger and larger, their cares greater and greater and their pocketbooks slimmer and slimmer. This may well be the trend of agriculture today. How can the trend best be arrested? That is the question that I think the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) and others should be concerning themselves with.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: He is not here.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Well, the Minister is busy making speeches and trying to be the farmers' friend, but rarely if ever visualizing the farmers' plight as the farmer sees it. Some time ago the Minister referred to himself as the food minister or the grocery minister. I saw him on television one night about six months ago when he said that we have a meat problem in Canada. What is he doing about it? I looked for something in the Speech from the Throne. Where is it? Where is the great aid for the basic problems confronting agriculture? It is not a question of giving handouts to farmers or more money to small farmers to drive out their neighbours.
I should like to direct the Government's thinking today to the other side of the coin. People are continually saying that we must drive out the inefficient farmer and force him out of business by one method or another. Editorials in newspapers say: Do not subsidize

the inefficient. Let us look at the other side of the coin. Is there not inefficiency in the marketing of the farmers' products? Surely we all know that the lower the price the farmer gets for his product, the more he must produce of that product; and the more he produces of the product, the greater the surplus and the lower the price he gets. The farmer finds himself on a terrible treadmill.
Let us have a look at the selling methods so far as the farmers' products are concerned. As cities grow and expand we see suburbia springing up here, here and here, and the establishment of great shopping plazas with food stores. Today these shopping centres do something like 75 per cent of the retail food business. The Price Spreads Commission, which dealt with the matter up until 1958, said that by that time shopping centres had gobbled up 64 per cent of the retail business and the small independent grocers had only 36 per cent. I would venture to say that today the shopping centres have close to 75 per cent, if not more than that.
I know there is a general concept today that these large, well lighted food stores with their big buildings must be efficient because of their size. This is not the case. The Price Spreads Commission of 1960 found the very opposite to be the case. They found that the supermarkets are not necessarily efficient. As I mentioned, the farmer is concerned about his share of the consumer dollar. In the report of the Price Spreads Commission of 1960 I notice that in 1949 the farmers' share of the retail dollar in the case of a loaf of bread was 23 per cent, while in 1958 it was 12 per cent. I would think that today it would be close to 9 per cent. That is found on page 312, volume 3, of the Price Spreads Commission report.
The same thing is true of beef, eggs and every agricultural product that the farmer markets today. Taking 1949 as the base year and representing 100, the retail price of beef today is 140. Yet there is only 2 cents a pound difference in the price the farmer receives. In 1949 the average price of beef on the hoof at the stockyards was 20 cents a pound. Today it is 22 cents. Yet there is a difference of 40 index points in the retail price of beef over the same period of time. Where has the inefficiency been in the marketing of that product?
Over the week end I visited the shopping centres of Ottawa and watched consumers buying in Loblaws, A & P and Dominion
April 12, 1965

Stores. I would say that the grocery chains in Ottawa are a prime example of what the Commission pointed out, the inefficiency in the marketing of the farmers' products. I have here a flyer from a Calgary newspaper and I will refer to it as an example. In Calgary there is keen competition in the meat industry right through the packing plant and shopping centres down to the consumer. I dare anybody in Ottawa to tell me where weiners can be bought in this city for three pounds for a dollar. I use weiners as an example because they are a typical food, and similar in Western and Eastern Canada. You can buy the best steak in Calgary for 75 cents a pound, but at Loblaws in Ottawa on Saturday steak was $1.05 a pound. Where has the 30 cents gone? That is what the farmers want to know. In the old days when grocery stores were owned by individuals and the grocers had a guild they would take the owners of Loblaws, tar and feather them and drag them through the streets to convince customers that they were a firm with which they should not do business.

speechtext:
Some smart aleck who does not know the seriousness of the plight of the farmer is making some loud remark. There is talk about the inefficient farmer. Let us look at the inefficient marketing of his products. This is what the Price Spreads Commission had to say about the food industry in 1960 in their report. I quote from page 60:
The evidence we have studied has led us to the conclusion that there is an essential difference between the determination of prices at the farm level and the determination of prices in other markets between the farm and the consumer.
They then go on to say:
The general recommendations we have made are designed to bring about changes in the process of price-making in the food marketing system which would be of benefit to consumers.. .and to primary producers...
They may have made recommendations but those recommendations did not bring about a general revision of price-making in the shopping centres. One only has to go to the shopping centres in Ottawa and see the prices that A & P, Loblaws and the rest of them charge for meat, and then compare the prices in Calgary for similar meat. I used the example of three pounds of weiners for a dollar. Bologna is another product that is the same all across Canada. It is four pounds for a dollar in Calgary. You cannot get two pounds for a dollar in Ottawa.
The Address-Mr. J. H. Horner
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
No, there is just no rhyme or reason for that price differentiation. The trouble is that there is no competition in the marketing of food, particularly meat products, in the large shopping centres. They are competing in the marketing of services, as was pointed out on page 26 of the Price Spreads Commission report. They said they were convinced that the structure of the food marketing industry has contributed to the advancement of prices to consumers, although they were unable to measure the effectiveness of the structure or the amount by which added services were really widening the spread in the price to the consumer.
I point this out because I seriously believe that this part of the agriculture industry needs greater study. You can take the Hedlin and Menzies report on poverty on the farm, and on inefficient farms, but let us look at the need for competition in the area of marketing of farm products. Certainly, we all know that under a system of free enterprise you must have sharp and keen competition or things get out of line. This is exactly what has happened. Our city planners who have been planning suburbia and the shopping centres have given these shopping centres a captive market with very little competition. They have driven out the independent grocer solely because the independent grocer has not provided a parking place for his customers. This subject needs careful study, and I would recommend a royal commission to do that.
One only has to talk to people who are buying beef at the stockyard, and ask them what determines the price. They will say: We have an order-and I am a buyer for Canada Packers or for Burns-from Safeway for such and such a poundage of beef. They will tell you out and out that today the shopping centres are able to dictate the price the farmer receives for his beef. There is evidence of this in the Price Spreads Commission report. The shopping centres, the chain stores, show a greater profit when the price to the farmer is the lowest. This is understandable, if you know their system. They charge all the market will bear. If the price of cattle is high and the shopping centre has to pay dearly for beef, that narrows the spread between what the shopping centre pays and what the consumer will pay. The consumer will only pay so much. If the price to the farmer is low and the shopping centre can buy beef cheaply, that widens the spread.
286	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. J. H. Horner This is exactly what was pointed out by the Price Spreads Commission. The final price remains what the consumer will pay, and there was ample evidence of this as I toured the shopping centres here in Ottawa on Saturday. There was ample evidence that the shopping centres and chain stores were selling meat, in particular, at the highest level and were robbing the public of dollars which the public did not realize they were losing.
Somebody says, "Oh". I ask him to study the market to see if I am not correct. We hear a great deal of talk about productivity on the farm and how the farmer must be efficient. Let us have a little efficiency in the marketing of his products. Somebody may wonder why the shopping centres are able to widen the spread. This is solely because today the average worker spends 20 per cent of his wage on food, whereas a few years ago he spent 25 per cent. In other words he has more money to spend on food today than he had a few years ago. The shopping centres, therefore, can charge more for this food and widen the margin of profit. There is evidence of this in the Price Spreads Commission report. I have a number of pages marked, but I do not believe I will have time to read them.
One only needs to look at the Financial Post of September 26 which dealt with wholesale chain stores marketing food to see that the dividend on those shares doubled in the last four years. Certainly, I believe we must take a very close look at these facts before we condemn the small farmer, before we condemn the inefficient farmer. We should take a look at the inefficient system that great society, as President Johnson calls it, has evolved. Certainly the profits of chain stores and grocery stores that handle meat are higher than any other part of the industry.
On page 28 of the Price Spreads Commission report, volume 1, there is a table which outlines the gross margins of food retailing and wholesaling outlets up until 1957. This indicates that chain meat stores have the widest margin; 20.2 per cent of their sales was profit. It rose from something like 15 per cent in 1951 to 20 per cent in 1957. I suggest that if one could find similar figures today he would find it would be practically 24 per cent or 25 per cent. This is their profit margin on the products we are asking the farmers to produce.
During the last session of this House we had a committee set up to study the prices of feed grain for farmers in Eastern Canada.

DEBATES	April 12. 1965
This committee would have been better off studying the relationship of the price a farmer receives for his product and the price the consumer has to pay for it. This would have done the farmer a lot more good, in my opinion. Perhaps the committee could have recommended an agency to watch over the shopping centres rather than recommending an agency to watch over feed grain prices. A civil servant told me this interesting story, and I was not going to tell it, but I will. He said that we were importing mutton from Australia. I asked how it happened we were importing mutton from Australia when we had such a difficult time selling our own mutton or lamb. Nobody really likes mutton. This man deals with the packing plants and the chain stores every day. He said they are taking beef blood plasma and mixing it with Australian mutton, then selling it as ground meat. This is the kind of thing that is happening to our meat industry in Canada.

We are getting the wool pulled over our eyes.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)

speechtext:
Somebody says we are getting the wool pulled over our eyes, and that is certainly true so far as the consumer is concerned, and so far as the primary producer is concerned. These people are charging all the market will bear, and their profits are largest when the price to the primary producer is lower. It is therefore their prime purpose to keep the price of the primary producer as low as possible so their profits will be as large as possible. I am convinced that is the basic rule of thumb on which shopping centres and meat chain stores work. I am sure you, Mr. Speaker, and other hon. Members know about this. The housewives have heard the price of meat has gone down and that the farmers are in terrible shape because the price on the hoof has dropped. But when they go to the butcher shop they never see that reduction in the price they pay.
I am sure all housewives in Canada have asked their husbands at some time or another, "Why don't we see this reduction in the price of meat when we go the meat store?" The reduction is rarely seen there or, if it is, it is a gradual reduction, not a sharp one which could be brought about by keen competition at the retail level.
I do not believe that the packing plants are making a killing. In fact I think they are operating a very efficient type of business;
April 12. 1965
but it is the chain store, the final outlet, which is the culprit in this industry.
About two years ago the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission dealt with the merger of Canada Packers with Calgary Packers of Calgary, and Wilsil Meat Packers of Montreal. The price squeeze commission brought down their evidence, which was referred by the Minister of Justice to counsel who recommended that no prosecution be undertaken. The Throne Speech is concerned with the livelihood of farmers and we as legislators are concerned with this problem. Canada Packers today processes 30 per cent of the meat consumed and produced in Canada. This is a huge supply to put in the hands of one company, especially when one understands the principle that competition must be keen and active in order to maintain, for any length of time, the free enterprise system which we all cherish so much.
At the time the price squeeze commission reported there was great concern among farmers because nobody in government proceeded to prosecute Canada Packers. Recently we had the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) tour Australia and New Zealand and return with a terrific report. He spent a lot of money and I hope the taxpayers of Canada will get something for it. He gave us a great report to the effect that a steer could be produced in Australia for $7 while it would cost $100 for the same steer in Canada. What has happened to Australian beef production over the past two years? They have pretty nearly doubled their beef production and that increase is continuing at a rapid rate.
What do we see Canada Packers doing now? The Financial Post of April 10, 1965 gave an outline of the great profits Canada Packers are making and how much dividend they were paying on class A and B shares. I quote from that paper as follows:
Recently the company announced it had formed a partnership with Jackson's (Corio) Meat Packing Pty. Ltd., of Geelong, Australia, to operate a packing and canning plant there.
This will be interesting to farmers in Canada because we know that, in years ahead, what happened in the United States during the past two years, due to the importation of Australian beef at a tremendous rate-which caused a great deal of concern to the U.S. beef industry-will happen here. Will it matter to Canada Packers Limited if they make a dollar processing Canadian meat or processing Australian meat and selling it in Canada? It will make no difference. Canada
287
The Address-Mr. J. H. Horner Packers can see what is coming and that is why that company is buying plants in Australia.
The biggest threat I can see today is Australian beef production. The Minister has admitted quit frankly that we have a meat problem in Canada. At one time or another he has called himself the minister of food and the minister of groceries. We cherish the idea that this is a free enterprise system and that we must maintain competition, but there is plenty of evidence from the Commission on Price Spreads of 1959 and 1960 to suggest shopping centres do not especially try to become efficient, so far as keeping the price spread narrow. In fact they try to keep the spread as wide as possible.
Though I do not see it mentioned in the Speech from the Throne I would like the government to follow what the United States is doing in the same industry, and in this connection I would like to read a short paragraph from the National Livestock Producer, a United States magazine, which I believe is published in Denver. It deals with the U.S. National Commission on Food Marketing and with what the U.S. expects this Commission to do. I quote as follows:
"In the study of meats and livestock," said Dr. G. E. Brandow, Commission executive director, "attention will be directed in part to the sale of meat by packers to wholesalers and large retailers. Practices of buyers and sellers will be studied from the standpoint of efficiency of distribution, fairness of competition, manner of price determination, product differentiation, and relative bargaining power of participants. A second area dealing with livestock markets and feedlot operations of packers will be similarly examined.
I quote this to show what they are doing in the United States. The U.S. combines investigation branch directed its attention to the electrical industry in the States over the past few years, and not so many days ago it prohibited the merger of a couple of breweries. Now its investigations are being directed to the shopping centres, and the problem brought about by this new system of marketing the farmers' produce. They are showing a real concern for it, and I would hope our Minister of Agriculture could take up from where the Price Spreads Commission left off, which pointed out a similar trend in the food marketing industry.
Many farmers across Canada would like to see a study made of this problem and I hope the government will meet this demand to study efficient marketing of the farmers' produce. I am convinced that here lies a large part of the answer to the problems of

As I see it, it is the Government's duty to create a climate in which the large and the small can work side by side, not a climate in which the large can strangle the small.
In many cases in farming, the small farmer is the most efficient. Mr. Speaker, this debate is usually noted for its variety, both in style and subject matter. I would like my opening words to be traditional; that is, I would like to join in the congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the Address in Reply on their very well delivered speeches at the opening of the debate. I think they deserve congratulations.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
My colleagues in the New Democratic Party have presented in this debate a series of policy statements as an alternative to the policies outlined in the Speech from the Throne. They have proposed immediate action to implement the report of the Hall Commission for universal Government financed medicare. They have dealt with the steps required to achieve the goals set up by the Economic Council of Canada. They have dealt with manpower and employment policies and with steps at the federal level needed to protect the consumer. They have indicated the vitally important role of the Federal authority in the field of education, if Canada is to meet the challenge of the age of automation.
But all of this will be difficult if not impossible without a new sense of national purpose and unless we solve the crisis of Canadian unity. This sense of national purpose, this solution to the crisis of Confederation, will have to be embodied in a new Constitution. I urge that the most important task confronting this Parliament is the task of developing and framing a new Constitution for Canada.
It is for this reason that I find the Speech from the Throne a bitterly disappointing document. Not only is there no suggestion that the Parliament of Canada will be allowed to take a serious look at a new Constitution
XMr. Homer (Acadia).]
DEBATES	April 12. 1965
for Canada by means of a special Committee set up for the purpose but, on the contrary, the Speech from the Throne promises to bring into effect the constitutional amending formula which will-for reasons I will speak about later-sound a death-knell to any hope of a dynamic re-thinking and revision of our constitutional structure.
There are both negative and positive reasons why a new Constitution for Canada is required. One of the negative reasons is expressed by two distinguished Canadians in a book called "Ten to One". One of the authors, Mr. Fowler, is a Liberal of English or Scots background; the other, Mr. Faribault, a Conservative of French background. Both are distinguished businessmen. Although I would hesitate to endorse all that they say in "Ten to One", I think Canadians will be much indebted to them for their tackling boldly the problems that face Canada. They say:
The present Canadian Constitution as set out in the British North America Act and subsequent amendments, is inadequate to meet the needs of Canada in 1965.
And again.
In any event the kind of constitution we envisage for Canada-a document that will be a resounding declaration of our present national agreement and a point of departure for our future unity-will not be achieved by tinkering with clauses of the British North America Act. We must find some way to make a bold fresh start. We think that the new Constitution Canada needs, is a much more comprehensive undertaking.
I could not agree more. Canada and Canada's Parliament should now be embarking on the preparatory work for such a bold and comprehensive undertaking. Instead, the Government by urging on us a too rigid and inflexible formula, is asking us to foreclose forever such a possibility and to condemn ourselves to a static-not a dynamic-conception of Canada's future.
I am sure that many people, including perhaps a few in this House, think of constitutions as dull, legal documents fit only for the discussion of constitutional lawyers, political scientists and other self-appointed experts. There may be times when this is true, but not, I venture to assert, in Canada today. I prophesy that there will be an increasing and intense public concern amongst Canadians about the Constitution for the next few years. The Constitution is the framework within which Governments can act or can be prevented from acting to meet human needs. Constitutions, if they are inflexible, can prevent governments in the future from
April 12, 1965

dealing effectively with basic practical needs, for example for full employment, for economic growth, for minimal labour standards, for adequate marketing of farm products, for Canada's full international stature, and many other vital requirements of a dynamic changing society.
The Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism has in its preliminary report given us a solemn warning that we must make adjustments if we are to meet "the greatest crisis in our history". Can anyone doubt that the richer, more dynamic Canada whose rebirth is called for by the Commission will require new constitutional forms to be evolved? This in turn will require much effort, examination, travail and "dialogue", to use a term now so much in favour.
It is for this reason that the insistence of the Government that we should accept a rigid amending formula would be funny if it were not tragic. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) speaking in Montreal on February 27 said:
I have no doubt that the population of Quebec will understand that the formula, even if certain intransigent ideologists find it less than ideal, represents an indispensable step in our constitutional evolution. Obviously it is only a preliminary step to a formal revision of the Constitution.
Thank God the people of Quebec have more intelligence than the hon. gentleman credits them with. At the risk of being called an intransigent ideologist-and I would be in good company-let me state as clearly as I can that this so-called indispensable step may yet turn out to be the last step, because in the guise of taking the first preliminary step Canada would be hobbling herself for all time. What is the core of the amending formula and why are we in this party fighting it with all the force we can muster? It is contained in section 2 which makes subject to the unanimity rule, as it is called, that is, the veto of each one of the Provinces, all substantial amendments affecting in any way the powers of the Provinces to make laws. This would have a threefold effect.
But I see it is now ten o'clock and I will leave the denouement of the threefold effect until tomorrow, if I may.

AGRICULTURE-BRITISH COLUMBIA-REQUEST FOR LONG TERM LOANS TO TREE FRUIT GROWERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise a question this evening about something of which I have personal experience, having been a practising orchard-

ist for nearly 50 years. In discussing this at the present time let me say that I have grown fruit even earlier than the somewhat junior graduate. At one time I even ran poultry. In fact, I come from a family which I think is the only family in British Columbia I know of that operated a travelling rooster.
Let me say that we paid $100 an acre for forest land which we were told would grow apples and grow us rich. We grew apples but we did not grow rich.
I am well acquainted with the problems that I wish to present to the Parliamentary Secretary this evening. I know these problems which face the tree fruit growers in British Columbia both in respect of production and marketing. I represent a part of the country which is ideal for the growing of tree fruit. Unfortunately, owing to the flooding that will be occasioned by the building of the High Arrow dam many thousands of acres of some of the best land in my constituency for growing peaches, cherries, apples and pears will be destroyed.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
I want to bring to the attention of the Parliamentary Secretary a resolution that was adopted at the last annual convention of the British Columbia Fruit Growers Association. That organization has been in existence since 1889 and represents the tree fruit growers of the Okanagan and Kootenay districts in the southeastern part of British Columbia. This organization has had long experience in respect of the problems which face the fruit industry. This question was raised at their convention which was held between January 19 and 21 of this year and it was the subject of considerable discussion because it is a problem that faces tree fruit growers in British Columbia and in other parts of Canada. I am sure the same problem will be found in Ontario and Quebec, and no doubt in the Maritimes. As the result of this discussion the following resolution headed "Financial Assistance Program" was adopted:
Whereas there is no act or arrangement at present under which fruit growers may borrow long term, low interest funds to renovate their orchards by cutting out trees of low marketable varieties or on low volume rootstocks and replacing the removed trees with varieties acceptable to the consuming public and on high volume type rootstocks, and
Whereas many orchards were planted 30 to 40 years ago and the production has fallen to 500 to 700 bushels per acre of average to low quality fruit and are therefore uneconomical, and
Whereas it is estimated in the United States that production of 1,500 bushels of high quality apples
April 12, 1965

per acre must be produced in the years to come to meet competition.
Therefore be it resolved that the British Columbia Fruit Growers Association approach the Canadian Government and request that the Farm Credit Corporation or other Government plan be amended to the extent that loans be made available to fruit farmers to enable them to cut out all or a part of their trees, if thought necessary, or plant or replant with acceptable market varieties on quick bearing high volume rootstocks, said loans to cover not only the removing of old trees and replanting of new ones, but the continued care and maintenance of the new trees until they have grown to an economic size, and moreover funds be loaned to take care of the livelihood of the farmer to enable him to carry out the above renovations.
This very important resolution was passed by this convention as the result of considerable study of this question. Our foreign markets are changing. We are losing the market in Britain and Europe for certain varieties. We used to have a very large market for Cox's Orange in Britain. There have been very heavy plantings there since the second world war and there are large imports from Italy and other parts of Europe and from Australia and New Zealand. The competition there is keener.
The Canadian consumer now has a different taste and requires a different type of apple. More and more the Canadian consumer has changed from the green and high quality apple to red apples like the McIntosh, Red Delicious, Rome Beauty and apples of that type. This has caused the growers to realize that they have got to change some of their varieties, if they are going to compete in the foreign and domestic markets, and they have also got to change to varieties, particularly dwarf specimens, that produce on quick bearing, high volume root stocks at a much higher rate than at the present time.
It is because of the problem that faces the growers that they gave it such consideration at the convention, and I was asked to raise the matter here. I always like raising matters and asking questions of the Parliamentary Secretary because I take great delight in the fact that I attended Ontario Agriculutral College in 1909 and he was born the following year. So it is a question of an aging man talking to a juvenile-but a very wise one, I trust, in these circumstances. My question is: Has the Department heard of these representations from the British Columbia Fruit Growers Association? Are they giving them serious study and what is the intention of the Government with respect to this request?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to express appreciation to the hon. Member for Kootenay West for bringing this important matter before the House. I also want to express appreciation for the fact that he has completed his autobiography so far as I am concerned. I always knew he was a tree farmer but I did not know his experience extended to orcharding and, of course, I am particularly happy about that.
In the absence of the Minister I am unable to confirm or deny whether or not representations have been received by the Minister on behalf of the British Columbia Fruit Growers Association, but I would assume that representations have been made. I am conscious, of course, of the changes that have taken place in recent years and that tastes have changed as indicated by the hon. Member. I realize that orcharding is a business that has gone through various stages of specialization and that orchardists no longer grow 10 or 20 varieties as they used to do in years gone by. I realize they are now concentrating on the more desirable varieties in order to meet consumer demand. I can only assure the hon. Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) that this matter will be brought to the attention of the Minister. I am confident that very careful consideration will be given to it. Of course, the hon. Member will appreciate that I am unable to give him any firm commitment, since his question involves a matter of Government policy, which would be announced by the Minister in due course. I wish to assure him, however, a question so pressing will be brought to the Minister's attention.

ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-PREPARATION OF PAMPHLET ON CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday afternoon the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) was speaking in the Throne Speech debate and he made an announcement that was new to the Members of the House. He indicated that he had given instructions to his departmental officials to prepare, for the information of hon. Members and the general public, not a white paper, because it will not involve a matter of Government policy, but an information pamphlet bearing on capital punishment. This pamphlet will be made available to all Members, and will contain statistics, along with the pros and cons of the problem involved. Finally, there will be a historical record and the result of facts observed in various
April 12, 1965

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion countries which, to a varying degree, have retained or abolished capital punishment. This was the announcement made by the Minister.
As one who favours the retention of capital punishment, I wish to ask the Minister of Justice if he will see that this information pamphlet is as fair as it is possible to be in presenting both sides of the matter, because this is an information pamphlet which is going to be paid for by the taxpayers of Canada. Since it is not a Government white paper, it should be impartial when discussing a matter that affects the hearts and consciences of Canadians as does this question of capital punishment. I am not one to argue that the Cabinet is the repository of all the virtues. I do not believe that it is impossible for them to commit an error. This is particularly so when I can show you a copy of the April 1 issue of the United Church Observer, the official publication of the United Church, where on page 14 of this edition, in discussing the question of capital punishment, this publication makes the flat-footed statement that the British Parliament has voted capital punishment out, while public opinion favoured its retention.
This is a definite misstatement of fact because the British House of Commons did vote against capital punishment, but the question has yet to go up to the House of Lords. It has since been stymied in the House of Commons. If an official organ of the United Church of Canada cannot present the facts accurately, then I am asking you, can an information pamphlet be prepared accurately presenting both sides of the case, when you bear in mind that this Cabinet has commuted every death sentence which has been imposed since they came into office two years ago this month? This certainly gives an indication of their way of thinking.
When the Minister of Justice was speaking on Friday afternoon he stated that we are no longer in an era of punishment for vengeful purposes. The only people I hear making such statements are those who are in favour of the abolition of capital punishment. The Minister of Justice not only made that comment on Friday afternoon, but the day he announced the commutation of the death sentence of the Santa Claus murderer Marcotte, he announced this free vote on capital punishment. Later, when speaking in Montreal, he said he was against capital punishment except in three specific instances, which he mentioned. Marcotte fitted into all three. He had murdered a policeman, he had
[Mr. Cowan.1
been convicted and he is now being tried on a second charge of murdering a policeman.

Could I suggest to the Minister of Justice or the Department, in order that this pamphlet may be as fair as possible, before it is published, and certainly before it is printed, that it be shown to and considered by one or two, or three representatives of that school of thought who still believe in the moral law.
We do not think it is a good policy to appoint cats as guardians of goldfish bowls, and since the United Church Observer states that those who favour the retention of capital punishment are fundamentalists or policemen,

Shea, secretary of the Canadian Association of the Chiefs of Police, of Montreal, to consider the pamphlet before giving it to the printers; or the Rev. Perry Roclswood, of Halifax, Nova Scotia; or Hon. Claude Wagner, Attorney General of Quebec, the man who prosecuted the Santa Claus murderer in the first case; and I would suggest with all respect Mr. Heath Macquarrie, the hon. Member for Queens, P.E.I. I would even suggest the name of Mr. Cassidy of Ottawa, President of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Veterans Association. Another man I would name is the Attorney General of Newfoundland, Hon. L. R. Curtis, and Elmer L. Steeves of Moncton, New Brunswick -and in passing may 1 say one of the Steeves was a Father of Confederation.
They are men of the utmost probity and integrity who favour the retention of capital punishment in this country. I believe this information pamphlet will be open to criticism on the grounds that it is biased, unless it is considered by the representatives of the school of thought that I represent before it is sent to the printers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-PREPARATION OF PAMPHLET ON CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the start I would like to re-emphasize that
April 12, 1965	COMMONS
the proposed debate on the abolition of capital punishment is not one in which the Government intends to take a position which would make the vote one of confidence. On this question it is expected that there will be diverse points of view taken by people in all parties, and therefore the debate will not be along party lines.
But the Government is prepared to assist the debate, as the hon. Member pointed out and as the Minister pointed out last Friday, by presenting an information pamphlet in order to put into the hands of all interested persons, both inside and outside the House, such of the relevant material as will permit an informed consideration of this important question.
Perhaps I should emphasize the word "information" in this regard. It is not intended in this particular document to set out the arguments pro and con. It is felt the various protagonists will be able to do this most effectively. But in setting forth the facts we must remember there is no absolute of objectivity. Inevitably everyone approaches any problem with a certain number of preconceptions. Subject to that limitation the information pamphlet will seek to be, as was said of Thomas Paine, "As impartial as sun and rain", and in its preparation the Government will seek to demonstrate, in the words of Burke, "The cold neutrality of an impartial judge." The hon. Member has made a useful suggestion which I will bring to the attention of the Minister and the officers of the Department.

maintopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION- VANCOUVER-POSSIBLE USE OF FORMER R.C.A.F. BASE
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION- VANCOUVER-POSSIBLE USE OF FORMER R.C.A.F. BASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was told on Orders of the Day this morning that no decision has yet been reached by the Government in its consideration of the latest resolution passed by the City Council of Vancouver with regard to the disposition of the former R.C.A.F. base located at Kitsilano Beach in Vancouver.
In 1942, when this property was acquired by the Department of National Defence as an R.C.A.F. supply depot, there was, as far as I can determine, a clear and unmistakable understanding on the part of the then council that the use of this property by the R.C.A.F. would be for the duration of the war, that any buildings erected on the property would be of a temporary nature, and that after the war the property would be
DEBATES	293
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion surrendered to the City of Vancouver for park purposes, as has been recommended by every planning report prepared for, or by, the City of Vancouver.
After the defence reorganization by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) last year, this supply depot was closed, and I was hopeful that 30 years of public controversy in Vancouver would come to an end and that this property would be granted to the city for park purposes as is desired, I am firmly convinced, by an overwhelming majority of the citizens of Vancouver.
At that time proposals were put forward to use part of the base for new C.B.C. radio and television headquarters. Due to decisions made by the previous Government, Vancouver is fourth in line after Montreal, Toronto and Winnipeg, for new C.B.C. facilities. Our C.B.C. facilities are a disgrace to Canada's third largest city and are a discredit to a national broadcasting corporation. Over the last year negotiations went on to determine whether there was a compromise arrangement which would be acceptable to most people, by which the C.B.C. could locate on part of the base and the balance be given to the City of Vancouver for park purposes. It has become obvious that permanent location of the C.B.C. at Kitsilano is unacceptable.
City council's latest resolution calls for the city to acquire the whole of the base on a 99-year lease for $1 a year, but will permit the C.B.C. to lease approximately 11 acres of it for 15 years, with a possible right to renegotiate a further extension of ten years. I am inclined to believe that when this resolution was passed unanimously by Council, the aldermen must not have thought out the matter to its logical conclusion.
This resolution, this proposal now being considered by the Government, falls between two stools. It represents a second best settlement; a second best park of 11 acres, rather than 26 acres, and a second best C.B.C. centre, because how can the Corporation be expected or allowed, with any logic or economic sense, to spend the large amounts of money required to build the type of C.B.C. centre worthy of Vancouver, when they only have the property for 15 years?
If City Council is prepared to allow the C.B.C. to locate on part of Kitsilano, surely they should want the C.B.C. to be in a position to make the sort of capital expenditures necessary to make it a first class headquarters. We do not want some gerrybuilt structure down there on the beach for the next 15 years. Jf
April 12, 1965

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion City Council's latest resolution is accepted by the Government, I am sure it will result in a freeze on C.B.C. developments in Vancouver for the next 15 years. Within five or ten years, we will, for example, undoubtedly be going into colour television. How can the C.B.C. be expected to spend large sums of money developing a colour studio on property which they may have for only another five or ten years?
If City Council is not prepared to allow the C.B.C. to locate on the Kitsilano base for a sufficiently long time to warrant a large capital expenditure, I strongly urge them to say so. I ask the Council to reconsider its position. If they are not prepared to make a logical and economically sound proposal with regard to the C.B.C. at Kitsilano they should indicate that they want it for park purposes as an integral part of Vancouver's beautiful waterfront development, as recently urged by the Vancouver parks board. Let not Vancouver make the mistakes of Toronto where
millions are now being spent trying to reclaim the waterfront for the benefit of the citizens.
I urge City Council to indicate their position to the Government quickly, because we have been dealing with this for 18 months and time is running out, if any of this potential parkland is to be used this summer. I assure Council that, armed with the sort of resolution I have indicated, I am hopeful we can obtain the desired end.
